title: Advances in the biology and chemistry of sialic acids.
abstract: Sialic acids are a subset of nonulosonic acids, which are nine-carbon alpha-keto aldonic acids. Natural existing sialic acid-containing structures are presented in different sialic acid forms, various sialyl linkages, and on diverse underlying glycans. They play important roles in biological, pathological, and immunological processes. Sialobiology has been a challenging and yet attractive research area. Recent advances in chemical and chemoenzymatic synthesis, as well as large-scale E. coli cell-based production, have provided a large library of sialoside standards and derivatives in amounts sufficient for structure-activity relationship studies. Sialoglycan microarrays provide an efficient platform for quick identification of preferred ligands for sialic acid-binding proteins. Future research on sialic acid will continue to be at the interface of chemistry and biology. Research efforts not only will lead to a better understanding of the biological and pathological importance of sialic acids and their diversity but also could lead to the development of therapeutics.

title: Advances in the biology and chemistry of sialic acids.
abstract: Sialic acids, a diverse family of nine-carbon nonulosonic acids, are critical components of glycans in vertebrates and certain bacteria, contributing to a wide range of biological, pathological, and immunological processes. Their remarkable structural diversity arises from extensive natural modifications, varied glycosidic linkages, and presentation on multiple glycan backbones, reflecting evolutionary pressures such as host-pathogen interactions. Recent advances in chemical and chemoenzymatic synthesis, as well as microbial production methods, have enabled the generation of extensive libraries of sialoside standards and derivatives, facilitating detailed structure-activity relationship studies. Analytical challenges persist due to the unique chemical properties and instability of sialic acid modifications, but innovative synthetic strategies and the development of sialoglycan microarrays are enhancing the ability to probe sialic acid biology. Continued interdisciplinary research at the interface of chemistry and biology promises to deepen understanding of sialic acid functions and diversity, with potential implications for therapeutic development.

title: All biology is computational biology
abstract: Here, I argue that computational thinking and techniques are so central to the quest of understanding life that today all biology is computational biology. Computational biology brings order into our understanding of life, it makes biological concepts rigorous and testable, and it provides a reference map that holds together individual insights. The next modern synthesis in biology will be driven by mathematical, statistical, and computational methods being absorbed into mainstream biological training, turning biology into a quantitative science.

title: All biology is computational biology
abstract: This paper argues that computational thinking and methods are now fundamental to all of biology, making computational biology central to the discipline. Computational approaches have transformed biological research by organizing knowledge through databases and ontologies, enabling large-scale data analysis, and providing statistical tools to uncover patterns and correlations invisible to traditional methods. These advances have produced a reference map of life that guides experimental research and turns conceptual ideas into testable hypotheses. Despite persistent skepticism from some in the biological community, the integration of mathematical, statistical, and computational techniques is reshaping biology into a quantitative science. The next modern synthesis in biology will be driven by these methods becoming core components of mainstream biological training, ultimately dissolving distinctions between computational and experimental biologists.

title: Biology of the Laboratory Mouse
abstract: There are a number of illustrations and figures which, on the whole, are quite well selected and of good quality. In some instances, the material presented happens to represent an area over which considerable controversy exists at present and, unfortunately, both sides of the controversy do not receive the same treatment. A student perusing this book should be aware of this so that he may keep an open mind. It would, of course, be beyond the scope of such a conference to try to present all sides of the subject completely, for the book would then become unwieldy in size. On the whole, this is a very useful and informative study which provides and conveys a good impression of the current work being done on the subjects covered.
venue: The Yale Journal of Biology and Medicine

title: Biology of the Laboratory Mouse
abstract: This comprehensive volume provides an in-depth exploration of the laboratory mouse, offering detailed coverage of its biology, embryology, reproduction, histology, pathology, genetics, and care. Edited by George D. Snell and featuring contributions from leading experts at the Jackson Laboratory, the book presents a uniquely thorough composite account of the laboratory mouse as a research model. Key sections address spontaneous neoplastic diseases, gene and chromosome mutations, tumour genetics and transplantation, and the milk factor, with particular emphasis on the value of inbred and hybrid strains for genetic and cancer research. While the illustrations are noted as subpar by American standards, the meticulous detail throughout makes this work an indispensable reference for laboratories maintaining large mouse colonies, providing essential knowledge that can improve research outcomes and reduce material wastage.
venue: The Yale Journal of Biology and Medicine

title: Computational cell biology
abstract: This text is an introduction to dynamical modeling in cell biology. It is not meant as a complete overview of modeling or of particular models in cell biology. Rather, we use selected biological examples to motivate the concepts and techniques used in computational cell biology. This is done through a progression of increasingly more complex cellular functions modeled with increasingly complex mathematical and c- putational techniques. There are other excellent sources for material on mathematical cell biology, and so the focus here truly is computer modeling. This does not mean that there are no mathematical techniques introduced, because some of them are absolutely vital, but it does mean that much of the mathematics is explained in a more intuitive fashion, while we allow the computer to do most of the work. The target audience for this text is mathematically sophisticated cell biology or neuroscience students or mathematics students who wish to learn about modeling in cell biology. The ideal class would comprise both biology and applied math students, who might be encouraged to collaborate on exercises or class projects. We assume as little mathematical and biological background as we feel we can get away with, and we proceed fairly slowly. The techniques and approaches covered in the ?rst half of the book will form a basis for some elementary modeling or as a lead in to more advanced topics covered in the second half of the book.

title: Computational cell biology
abstract: The complexity of biological systems has outpaced the capacity of traditional reductionist approaches in cell biology, necessitating new strategies to understand the interconnected and dynamic nature of cellular processes. This commentary highlights the transformative role of computational methods in cell biology, which now extend beyond supporting experimental tools to become essential for acquiring, analyzing, and interpreting large-scale data. Advances in computational image analysis, modeling, and systems biology are enabling unprecedented quantitative insights into cellular dynamics, interaction networks, and regulatory patterns. The Journal of Cell Biology recognizes this paradigm shift by presenting reviews and research exemplifying interdisciplinary computational approaches, aiming to foster collaboration between cell and computational biologists. Embracing computational cell biology promises to reveal novel concepts of cellular organization and function, broadening the scope of biological inquiry while maintaining molecular detail.

title: Copper active sites in biology.
abstract: Based on its generally accessible I/II redox couple and bioavailability, copper plays a wide variety of roles in nature that mostly involve electron transfer (ET), O2 binding, activation and reduction, NO2− and N2O reduction and substrate activation. Copper sites that perform ET are the mononuclear blue Cu site that has a highly covalent CuII-S(Cys) bond and the binuclear CuA site that has a Cu2S(Cys)2 core with a Cu-Cu bond that keeps the site delocalized (Cu(1.5)2) in its oxidized state. In contrast to inorganic Cu complexes, these metalloprotein sites transfer electrons rapidly often over long distances, as has been previously reviewed.1–4 Blue Cu and CuA sites will only be considered here in their relation to intramolecular ET in multi-center enzymes. The focus of this review is on the Cu enzymes (Figure 1). Many are involved in O2 activation and reduction, which has mostly been thought to involve at least two electrons to overcome spin forbiddenness and the low potential of the one electron reduction to superoxide (Figure 2).5,6 Since the Cu(III) redox state has not been observed in biology, this requires either more than one Cu center or one copper and an additional redox active organic cofactor. The latter is formed in a biogenesis reaction of a residue (Tyr) that is also Cu catalyzed in the first turnover of the protein. Recently, however, there have been a number of enzymes suggested to utilize one Cu to activate O2 by 1e− reduction to form a Cu(II)-O2•− intermediate (an innersphere redox process) and it is important to understand the active site requirements to drive this reaction. The oxidases that catalyze the 4e−reduction of O2 to H2O are unique in that they effectively perform this reaction in one step indicating that the free energy barrier for the second two-electron reduction of the peroxide product of the first two-electron step is very low. In nature this requires either a trinuclear Cu cluster (in the multicopper oxidases) or a Cu/Tyr/Heme Fe cluster (in the cytochrome oxidases). The former accomplishes this with almost no overpotential maximizing its ability to oxidize substrates and its utility in biofuel cells, while the latter class of enzymes uses the excess energy to pump protons for ATP synthesis. In bacterial denitrification, a mononuclear Cu center catalyzes the 1e- reduction of nitrite to NO while a unique µ4S2−Cu4 cluster catalyzes the reduction of N2O to N2 and H2O, a 2e− process yet requiring 4Cu’s. Finally there are now several classes of enzymes that utilize an oxidized Cu(II) center to activate a covalently bound substrate to react with O2. Figure 1 Copper active sites in biology. Figure 2 Latimer Diagram for Oxygen Reduction at pH = 7.0 Adapted from References 5 and 6. This review presents in depth discussions of all these classes of Cu enzymes and the correlations within and among these classes. For each class we review our present understanding of the enzymology, kinetics, geometric structures, electronic structures and the reaction mechanisms these have elucidated. While the emphasis here is on the enzymology, model studies have significantly contributed to our understanding of O2 activation by a number of Cu enzymes and are included in appropriate subsections of this review. In general we will consider how the covalency of a Cu(II)–substrate bond can activate the substrate for its spin forbidden reaction with O2, how in binuclear Cu enzymes the exchange coupling between Cu’s overcomes the spin forbiddenness of O2 binding and controls electron transfer to O2 to direct catalysis either to perform two e− electrophilic aromatic substitution or 1e− H-atom abstraction, the type of oxygen intermediate that is required for H-atom abstraction from the strong C-H bond of methane (104 kcal/mol) and how the trinuclear Cu cluster and the Cu/Tyr/Heme Fe cluster achieve their very low barriers for the reductive cleavage of the O-O bond. Much of the insight available into these mechanisms in Cu biochemistry has come from the application of a wide range of spectroscopies and the correlation of spectroscopic results to electronic structure calculations. Thus we start with a tutorial on the different spectroscopic methods utilized to study mononuclear and multinuclear Cu enzymes and their correlations to different levels of electronic structure calculations.

title: Copper active sites in biology.
abstract: Copper plays diverse and essential roles in biological systems due to its accessible redox states and bioavailability, enabling it to mediate electron transfer, oxygen activation and reduction, nitrite and nitrous oxide reduction, and substrate activation in a variety of enzymes. This review comprehensively examines the structural, electronic, and mechanistic features of copper active sites across different classes of copper enzymes, including mononuclear blue copper and CuA sites involved in electron transfer, as well as multicopper oxidases and cytochrome oxidases responsible for efficient O2 reduction. The discussion integrates insights from enzymology, kinetics, spectroscopy, and electronic structure calculations to elucidate how copper centers achieve rapid electron transfer, overcome spin-forbidden reactions, activate strong bonds such as C-H in methane, and minimize overpotential in catalytic cycles. Special emphasis is placed on the correlation between spectroscopic signatures—particularly X-ray absorption and emission methods—and the geometric and electronic structures of copper centers. The review also highlights the contribution of model studies to understanding O2 activation mechanisms and explores recent discoveries of novel copper-mediated processes. Overall, this work provides a detailed framework for understanding the fundamental principles governing copper biochemistry and its implications for biological catalysis and energy conversion.

title: Cu-free click cycloaddition reactions in chemical biology.
abstract: Bioorthogonal chemical reactions are paving the way for new innovations in biology. These reactions possess extreme selectivity and biocompatibility, such that their participating reagents can form covalent bonds within richly functionalized biological systems--in some cases, living organisms. This tutorial review will summarize the history of this emerging field, as well as recent progress in the development and application of bioorthogonal copper-free click cycloaddition reactions.

title: Cu-free click cycloaddition reactions in chemical biology.
abstract: Copper-free click cycloaddition reactions have emerged as powerful tools in chemical biology, enabling highly selective and biocompatible covalent labeling of biomolecules within complex biological environments, including living systems. This review traces the evolution of bioorthogonal chemistry, focusing on the development and mechanistic underpinnings of copper-free cycloaddition strategies designed to overcome the limitations posed by cellular environments, such as cytotoxicity, competing nucleophiles, and redox sensitivity. Key advances discussed include the design of strained cyclooctynes and their derivatives for rapid azide-alkyne cycloadditions, as well as alternative approaches utilizing oxanorbornadienes and tetrazine-based inverse-electron-demand Diels–Alder reactions. The review highlights how these innovations have expanded the toolkit for probing dynamic biological processes with minimal perturbation, facilitating applications ranging from biomolecular imaging to targeted therapeutics. The continued refinement of copper-free click reagents promises to further enhance the precision and versatility of chemical biology research.

title: Evolutionary biology of aging
abstract: The evolutionary theory of aging Observation of aging Experimental tests of the evolutionary theory of aging Genetic mechanisms form the evolution of aging Comparative biology of aging An evolutionary perspective on organismal theories of aging An evolutionary perspective on cellular and molecular theories of aging The future of gerontology.

title: Evolutionary biology of aging
abstract: This book provides a comprehensive and accessible introduction to the evolutionary biology of aging, focusing on the theoretical foundations and empirical evidence supporting evolutionary explanations for senescence. Rose presents historical context and mathematical models, notably antagonistic pleiotropy and mutation accumulation (reframed as age-specificity of gene action), and reviews experimental tests of these theories, primarily drawing on his own research. The text argues that aging is genetically and evolutionarily distinct from fitness, though the empirical scope is somewhat narrow and alternative data are sometimes too readily dismissed. Later chapters critique non-evolutionary theories of aging and propose an evolutionary paradigm for gerontology, emphasizing the lack of conserved senescence mechanisms and advocating for physiological over molecular studies. While the book succeeds in clarifying evolutionary perspectives and minimizing mathematical complexity for non-specialists, it is less comprehensive in experimental coverage and offers limited guidance on mechanistic research directions. Overall, it is a valuable resource for researchers interested in the genetic and evolutionary aspects of aging but leaves open questions regarding underlying physiological and molecular processes.

title: Host Biology in Light of the Microbiome: Ten Principles of Holobionts and Hologenomes
abstract: Groundbreaking research on the universality and diversity of microorganisms is now challenging the life sciences to upgrade fundamental theories that once seemed untouchable. To fully appreciate the change that the field is now undergoing, one has to place the epochs and foundational principles of Darwin, Mendel, and the modern synthesis in light of the current advances that are enabling a new vision for the central importance of microbiology. Animals and plants are no longer heralded as autonomous entities but rather as biomolecular networks composed of the host plus its associated microbes, i.e., 'holobionts.' As such, their collective genomes forge a 'hologenome,' and models of animal and plant biology that do not account for these intergenomic associations are incomplete. Here, we integrate these concepts into historical and contemporary visions of biology and summarize a predictive and refutable framework for their evaluation. Specifically, we present ten principles that clarify and append what these concepts are and are not, explain how they both support and extend existing theory in the life sciences, and discuss their potential ramifications for the multifaceted approaches of zoology and botany. We anticipate that the conceptual and evidence-based foundation provided in this essay will serve as a roadmap for hypothesis-driven, experimentally validated research on holobionts and their hologenomes, thereby catalyzing the continued fusion of biology's subdisciplines. At a time when symbiotic microbes are recognized as fundamental to all aspects of animal and plant biology, the holobiont and hologenome concepts afford a holistic view of biological complexity that is consistent with the generally reductionist approaches of biology.

title: Host Biology in Light of the Microbiome: Ten Principles of Holobionts and Hologenomes
abstract: The holobiont and hologenome concepts redefine animals and plants as integrated units comprising hosts and their symbiotic microbes, challenging traditional, nucleocentric views of biology. This essay synthesizes historical and contemporary perspectives to articulate ten foundational principles that clarify the nature, scope, and implications of holobionts and hologenomes. These principles distinguish holobionts from other biological assemblages, position the hologenome as a comprehensive gene system, and highlight the roles of both selection and neutrality in shaping host-microbe associations. The framework extends classical evolutionary theory by incorporating intergenomic interactions, mechanisms of inheritance beyond Mendelian genetics, and multilevel selection. By providing a predictive and testable foundation, this work aims to unify subdisciplines across the life sciences and catalyze hypothesis-driven research that fully integrates microbiology into our understanding of host biology.

title: Scale-free networks in cell biology
abstract: A cell's behavior is a consequence of the complex interactions between its numerous constituents, such as DNA, RNA, proteins and small molecules. Cells use signaling pathways and regulatory mechanisms to coordinate multiple processes, allowing them to respond to and adapt to an ever-changing environment. The large number of components, the degree of interconnectivity and the complex control of cellular networks are becoming evident in the integrated genomic and proteomic analyses that are emerging. It is increasingly recognized that the understanding of properties that arise from whole-cell function require integrated, theoretical descriptions of the relationships between different cellular components. Recent theoretical advances allow us to describe cellular network structure with graph concepts and have revealed organizational features shared with numerous non-biological networks. We now have the opportunity to describe quantitatively a network of hundreds or thousands of interacting components. Moreover, the observed topologies of cellular networks give us clues about their evolution and how their organization influences their function and dynamic responses.

title: Scale-free networks in cell biology
abstract: Cellular function arises from intricate networks of interactions among genes, proteins, and metabolites, whose global organization is increasingly accessible through integrated genomic and proteomic analyses. Recent advances in network theory have revealed that many cellular networks, including gene regulatory, protein-protein interaction, and metabolic networks, exhibit scale-free topologies characterized by power-law degree distributions and high clustering coefficients. These structural features, shared with diverse non-biological networks, suggest the absence of a typical node and the presence of highly connected hubs. The scale-free architecture influences network robustness, functional redundancy, and dynamic responses to perturbations. Graph theoretical concepts such as node degree, clustering coefficient, path length, and component structure provide quantitative frameworks for analyzing local and global properties of cellular networks. This review synthesizes current understanding of how graph representations elucidate the principles governing cellular network organization, their evolutionary implications, and their impact on cellular behavior and adaptability.

title: Spatial autocorrelation in biology: 1. Methodology
abstract: Spatial autocorrelation analysis tests whether the observed value of a nominal, ordinal, or interval variable at one locality is independent of values of the variable at neighbouring localities. The computation of autocorrelation coefficients for nominal, ordinal, and for interval data is illustrated, together with appropriate significance tests. The method is extended to include the computation of correlograms for spatial autocorrelation. These show the autocorrelation coefficient as a function of distance between pairs of localities being considered, and summarize the patterns of geographic variation exhibited by the response surface of any given variable. Autocorrelation analysis is applied to microgeographic variation of allozyme frequencies in the snail Helix aspersa. Differences in variational patterns in two city blocks are interpreted. The inferences that can be drawn from correlograms are discussed and illustrated with the aid of some artificially generated patterns. Computational formulae, expected values and standard errors are furnished in two appendices.

title: Spatial autocorrelation in biology: 1. Methodology
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive methodology for analyzing spatial autocorrelation in biological data, addressing variables measured at nominal, ordinal, and interval levels. The authors detail the computation of autocorrelation coefficients for each data type and provide appropriate significance tests, extending the analysis to the construction of correlograms that depict autocorrelation as a function of geographic distance. The methodology is illustrated through both artificial patterns and an empirical case study examining microgeographic variation in allozyme frequencies in the snail Helix aspersa, revealing differences in spatial variation across two urban blocks. The paper discusses the implications of various spatial patterns detected through correlograms and offers practical computational formulas, expected values, and standard errors in appendices. This work introduces biologists to formal spatial autocorrelation analysis, enhancing the interpretation of geographic variation in evolutionary and ecological studies.

title: Systems biology and the virtual physiological human
abstract: Mol Syst Biol. 5: 292 The virtual physiological human (VPH) initiative is intended to support the development of patient‐specific computer models and their application in personalised and predictive healthcare. The VPH, a core target of the European Commission's 7th Framework Programme, will serve as a ‘ methodological and technological framework that, once established, will enable collaborative investigation of the human body as a single complex system ’ (http://www.europhysiome.org/roadmap/). As such, the VPH initiative constitutes an integral part of the international Physiome Project (http://www.physiome.org.nz/), a worldwide public domain effort to develop a computational framework for the quantitative description of biological processes in living systems across all relevant levels of structural and functional integration, from molecule to organism, including the human (Kohl et al , 2000; Bassingthwaighte et al , 2009). So, what is the connection between this grand challenge and systems biology? To explore this, we must first agree on what we take systems biology to mean. ### Description versus definition Descriptions of systems biology range from the view that it is merely ‘new wording, more fashionable, for physiology’ (http://is.gd/tQJL), to the all‐inclusive ‘systems biology involves the application of experimental, theoretical, and computational techniques to the study of biological organisms at all levels, from the molecular, through the cellular, to the organ, organism, and populations. Its aim is to understand biological processes as integrated systems instead of as isolated parts’ (http://is.gd/tQK0). At the same time, attempts to concisely define systems biology have not yielded definitive form of words that is acceptable to the majority of researchers engaged in what they consider to be systems biology. One of the reasons for this situation may be that many different scientific streams have come together in the systems biology pool (see also Bassingthwaighte et al , 2009), each with its own conceptual and terminological …

title: Systems biology and the virtual physiological human
abstract: This editorial explores the relationship between systems biology and the virtual physiological human (VPH) initiative, highlighting how systems biology serves as a conceptual and methodological approach that integrates reductionist and integrative research across multiple biological scales. The VPH, a major European effort aligned with the international Physiome Project, aims to develop patient-specific computational models for personalized healthcare by treating the human body as a complex, multi-level system. The article discusses the challenges of defining systems biology, emphasizing its role as an approach rather than a discipline, and traces its roots to both historical physiology and recent advances in computational modeling. It argues that systems biology’s strength lies in its ability to unify experimental and computational techniques for quantitative analysis of biological entities and their interactions. The VPH exemplifies this approach by pursuing a 'middle-out' strategy—integrating data and models from genes to the whole organism—to achieve dynamic, multi-scale understanding of human physiology. The editorial concludes that systems biology provides the essential framework for realizing the VPH vision, enabling collaborative, quantitative investigation of biological systems for predictive and personalized medicine.

title: The anomaly of silicon in plant biology.
abstract: Silicon is the second most abundant element in soils, the mineral substrate for most of the world's plant life. The soil water, or the 'soil solution,' contains silicon, mainly as silicic acid, H4SiO4, at 0.1-0.6 mM--concentrations on the order of those of potassium, calcium, and other major plant nutrients, and well in excess of those of phosphate. Silicon is readily absorbed so that terrestrial plants contain it in appreciable concentrations, ranging from a fraction of 1% of the dry matter to several percent, and in some plants to 10% or even higher. In spite of this prominence of silicon as a mineral constituent of plants, it is not counted among the elements defined as 'essential,' or nutrients, for any terrestrial higher plants except members of the Equisitaceae. For that reason it is not included in the formulation of any of the commonly used nutrient solutions. The plant physiologist's solution-cultured plants are thus anomalous, containing only what silicon is derived as a contaminant of their environment. Ample evidence is presented that silicon, when readily available to plants, plays a large role in their growth, mineral nutrition, mechanical strength, and resistance to fungal diseases, herbivory, and adverse chemical conditions of the medium. Plants grown in conventional nutrient solutions are thus to an extent experimental artifacts. Omission of silicon from solution cultures may lead to distorted results in experiments on inorganic plant nutrition, growth and development, and responses to environmental stress.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: The anomaly of silicon in plant biology.
abstract: Silicon is the second most abundant element in soils and is present in plant tissues at concentrations comparable to or exceeding those of essential macronutrients, yet it is not generally recognized as essential for higher plants except for certain groups such as the Equisitaceae. This review examines the paradoxical status of silicon in plant biology, highlighting its ubiquity in soils and nutrient solutions, its ready uptake by plants, and its significant but variable accumulation in plant tissues. Despite the lack of consensus on its essentiality—stemming from difficulties in creating silicon-free environments and ambiguous experimental results—ample evidence indicates that silicon availability can enhance plant growth, mineral nutrition, mechanical strength, and resistance to biotic and abiotic stresses. The omission of silicon from conventional nutrient solutions may lead to experimental artifacts and misinterpretations in studies of plant nutrition and stress physiology. The review concludes that while silicon cannot currently be classified as an essential element for most higher plants, its prominent role in plant biology warrants greater consideration in both research and agricultural practice.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: The genetic transformation of bone biology.
abstract: The skeleton, like every organ, has specific developmental and functional characteristics that define its identity in biologic and pathologic terms. Skeleton is composed of multiple elements of various shapes and origins spread throughout the body. Most of these skeletal elements are formed by two different tissues, cartilage and bone, and each of these two tissues has its own specific cell types: the chondrocyte in cartilage, and the osteoblast and osteoclast in bone. Finally, each of these cell types has its own differentiation pathway, physiological functions, and therefore pathological conditions. The complexity of this organ in terms of developmental biology, physiology, and pathology, along with the multitude of important conceptual advances in our understanding of skeletal biology, are such that it has become impossible to present in a short review an up-to-date summary of both cartilage and bone biology. Thus, this review will concentrate only on bone biology beyond embryonic patterning. The entire bone field is dominated by the impact of degenerative diseases, such as osteoporosis. title: The genetic transformation of bone biology.
abstract: Recent advances in genetic research have profoundly transformed our understanding of bone biology, particularly in elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying bone development, physiology, and pathology. This review focuses on the genetic regulation of bone cell differentiation beyond embryonic patterning, emphasizing the pivotal roles of osteoclasts and osteoblasts in bone remodeling and disease. Genetic studies in mice and humans have identified key transcription factors such as Pu.1, c-Fos, and NF-κB as central regulators of osteoclast differentiation, with loss-of-function mutations resulting in distinct skeletal phenotypes like osteopetrosis. The interplay between genetic pathways and extracellular signals orchestrates the balance between bone formation and resorption, a process disrupted in conditions such as osteoporosis. Despite significant progress in understanding osteoclast biology, the molecular control of osteoblast function remains less defined, highlighting critical gaps and emerging questions in the field. Overall, genetic approaches continue to drive conceptual advances in bone biology, offering new insights into skeletal diseases and potential therapeutic targets.

title: The Marine Microbial Eukaryote Transcriptome Sequencing Project (MMETSP): Illuminating the Functional Diversity of Eukaryotic Life in the Oceans through Transcriptome Sequencing
abstract: Current sampling of genomic sequence data from eukaryotes is relatively poor, biased, and inadequate to address important questions about their biology, evolution, and ecology; this Community Page describes a resource of 700 transcriptomes from marine microbial eukaryotes to help understand their role in the world's oceans.

title: The Marine Microbial Eukaryote Transcriptome Sequencing Project (MMETSP): Illuminating the Functional Diversity of Eukaryotic Life in the Oceans through Transcriptome Sequencing
abstract: The Marine Microbial Eukaryote Transcriptome Sequencing Project (MMETSP) addresses the critical gap in reference sequence data for marine microbial eukaryotes by generating and analyzing transcriptomes from a broad diversity of ecologically relevant marine taxa. Recognizing the limitations and taxonomic biases inherent in existing genomic resources, particularly the underrepresentation of key marine lineages, MMETSP leverages large-scale mRNA sequencing to rapidly characterize the functional gene repertoire of these organisms. By providing well-annotated transcriptomic datasets linked to taxonomically identified cultures, this initiative enhances the capacity for comparative and functional analyses in marine microbial ecology. The resulting resource not only improves the interpretation of environmental sequence data but also illuminates the evolutionary and ecological roles of eukaryotic microbes in ocean ecosystems, thereby supporting future research into their contributions to global biogeochemical cycles and ecosystem functioning.

title: Translational Systems Biology of Inflammation
abstract: Inflammation is a complex, multi-scale biologic response to stress that is also required for repair and regeneration after injury. Despite the repository of detailed data about the cellular and molecular processes involved in inflammation, including some understanding of its pathophysiology, little progress has been made in treating the severe inflammatory syndrome of sepsis. To address the gap between basic science knowledge and therapy for sepsis, a community of biologists and physicians is using systems biology approaches in hopes of yielding basic insights into the biology of inflammation. “Systems biology” is a discipline that combines experimental discovery with mathematical modeling to aid in the understanding of the dynamic global organization and function of a biologic system (cell to organ to organism). We propose the term translational systems biology for the application of similar tools and engineering principles to biologic systems with the primary goal of optimizing clinical practice. We describe the efforts to use translational systems biology to develop an integrated framework to gain insight into the problem of acute inflammation. Progress in understanding inflammation using translational systems biology tools highlights the promise of this multidisciplinary field. Future advances in understanding complex medical problems are highly dependent on methodological advances and integration of the computational systems biology community with biologists and clinicians.

title: Translational Systems Biology of Inflammation
abstract: Inflammation is a complex, multi-scale biological process essential for immune defense and tissue repair, yet its dysregulation underlies numerous diseases such as sepsis, trauma, and autoimmune disorders. Despite extensive molecular and cellular data, effective clinical therapies for severe inflammatory syndromes remain elusive due to the limitations of reductionist approaches. This review outlines the emergence of translational systems biology as an integrative discipline combining experimental data with dynamic mathematical modeling—such as agent-based and equation-based models—to bridge the gap between basic research and clinical application. Focusing on acute inflammation and sepsis, the paper highlights how these computational frameworks facilitate mechanistic insights across biological scales, support in silico clinical trials, and inform rational drug and device design. The authors emphasize the necessity of interdisciplinary collaboration among biologists, clinicians, and computational scientists to develop predictive models that can guide both fundamental discovery and translational strategies. Progress in this field demonstrates the promise of systems-level approaches for addressing complex medical challenges, with future advances hinging on methodological innovation and deeper integration of computational tools into biomedical research and practice.

title: tRNA biology charges to the front.
abstract: tRNA biology has come of age, revealing an unprecedented level of understanding and many unexpected discoveries along the way. This review highlights new findings on the diverse pathways of tRNA maturation, and on the formation and function of a number of modifications. Topics of special focus include the regulation of tRNA biosynthesis, quality control tRNA turnover mechanisms, widespread tRNA cleavage pathways activated in response to stress and other growth conditions, emerging evidence of signaling pathways involving tRNA and cleavage fragments, and the sophisticated intracellular tRNA trafficking that occurs during and after biosynthesis.

title: tRNA biology charges to the front.
abstract: Recent advances in tRNA biology have uncovered remarkable complexity and regulatory sophistication in tRNA maturation, modification, quality control, and intracellular trafficking. This review synthesizes new insights into the diverse pathways of tRNA processing, including end maturation, splicing, and the extensive repertoire of nucleotide modifications that influence tRNA stability and function. Special attention is given to the multilayered regulation of tRNA gene transcription by RNA polymerase III and its integration with cellular signaling pathways such as PKA and TOR, mediated by factors like Maf1. The review also highlights emerging mechanisms of tRNA turnover and stress-induced cleavage, revealing roles for tRNA fragments in cellular signaling. Additionally, recent discoveries illuminate the intricate dynamics of tRNA trafficking within eukaryotic cells and the evolutionary diversity of processing enzymes such as RNase P. Collectively, these findings position tRNA biology at the forefront of RNA research, with broad implications for understanding gene expression regulation, cellular adaptation to stress, and the evolution of RNA-based processes.

title: Agent-Based Business Process Management
abstract: This paper describes work undertaken in the ADEPT (Advanced Decision Environment for Process Tasks) project towards developing an agent-based infrastructure for managing business processes. We describe how the key technology of negotiating, service providing, autonomous agents was realized and demonstrate how this was applied to the BT (British Telecom) business process of providing a customer quote for network services.
venue: International Journal of Cooperative Information Systems

title: Agent-Based Business Process Management
abstract: This paper presents an agent-based approach to business process management developed within the ADEPT project, addressing the challenges of distributed, dynamic, and decentralized organizational environments. The proposed framework conceptualizes business processes as communities of autonomous, negotiating agents that encapsulate problem-solving capabilities and interact through service provision, negotiation, and information sharing. Each agent manages specific services or tasks and coordinates with others via service level agreements established through negotiation protocols, accommodating heterogeneous information models and organizational autonomy. The ADEPT agent architecture supports hierarchical and hybrid organizational structures by nesting agents and tasks, enabling flexible modeling of real-world business processes. The approach is demonstrated through its application to British Telecom’s customer quote process, highlighting the benefits of agent-based systems in managing complexity, supporting proactive and responsive decision-making, and maintaining organizational integrity. The paper contrasts this methodology with traditional business process management techniques and discusses ongoing research directions and open challenges in agent-based process management.
venue: International Journal of Cooperative Information Systems

title: A dynamic capabilities-based entrepreneurial theory of the multinational enterprise
abstract: This paper develops a dynamic capabilities-based theory of the multinational enterprise (MNE). It first reviews scholarship on the MNE, with a focus on what has come to be known as “internalization” theory. One prong of this theory develops contractual/transaction cost-informed governance perspectives; and another develops technology transfer and capabilities perspectives. In this paper, it is suggested that the latter has been somewhat neglected. However, if fully integrated as part of a more complete approach, it can buttress transaction cost/governance issues and expand the range of phenomena that can be explained. In this more integrated framework, dynamic capabilities coupled with good strategy are seen as necessary to sustain superior enterprise performance, especially in fast-moving global environments. Entrepreneurial management and transformational leadership are incorporated into a capabilities theory of the MNE. The framework is then used to explain how strategy and dynamic capabilities together determine firm-level sustained competitive advantage in global environments. It is suggested that this framework complements contract-based perspectives on the MNE and can help integrate international management and international business perspectives.

title: A dynamic capabilities-based entrepreneurial theory of the multinational enterprise
abstract: This paper advances a dynamic capabilities-based entrepreneurial theory of the multinational enterprise (MNE), addressing limitations in prevailing internalization and transaction cost approaches. While traditional theories emphasize market failures and governance mechanisms as drivers of MNE formation, they insufficiently explain sustained competitive advantage and firm heterogeneity in global contexts. Integrating insights from organizational capabilities, business strategy, and entrepreneurship, this perspective positions dynamic capabilities—firms’ abilities to sense, seize, and transform opportunities—as central to MNE success. The framework highlights the importance of entrepreneurial management and transformational leadership in building and renewing competitive advantage across diverse markets. By synthesizing governance and capabilities perspectives, the theory provides a more comprehensive explanation of MNE boundaries, internationalization choices, subsidiary roles, and foreign direct investment. This integrative approach bridges international business and management scholarship, offering a robust foundation for understanding how strategy and dynamic capabilities jointly underpin superior performance in rapidly changing global environments.

title: Blockchain for Supply Chain Traceability: Business Requirements and Critical Success Factors
abstract: We seek to guide operations management (OM) research on the implementation of supply chain traceability systems by identifying business requirements and the factors critical to successful implementation. We first motivate the need for implementing traceability systems in two very different industries—cobalt mining and pharmaceuticals—and present business requirements and critical success factors for implementation. Next, we describe how we carried out thematic analysis of practitioner and scholarly articles on implementing blockchain for supply chain traceability. Finally, we present our results pertaining to the needs of different stakeholders such as suppliers, consumers, and regulators. The business requirements for traceability systems are curbing illegal practices; improving sustainability performance; increasing operational efficiency; enhancing supply‐chain coordination; and sensing market trends. Critical success factors for implementation are companies’ capabilities; collaboration; technology maturity; supply chain practices; leadership; and governance of the traceability efforts. These findings provide a nascent measurement model for empirical work and a foundation for descriptive and normative research on blockchain applications for supply chain traceability.

title: Blockchain for Supply Chain Traceability: Business Requirements and Critical Success Factors
abstract: This paper examines the implementation of blockchain technology for supply chain traceability by identifying key business requirements and critical success factors through thematic analysis of practitioner and academic literature. Using cobalt mining and pharmaceuticals as illustrative cases, the study highlights the need for traceability systems to address issues such as curbing illegal practices, enhancing sustainability, improving operational efficiency, strengthening supply chain coordination, and sensing market trends. The analysis identifies stakeholders’ needs—including those of suppliers, consumers, and regulators—and outlines critical success factors such as organizational capabilities, collaboration, technology maturity, supply chain practices, leadership, and governance. The findings provide an initial measurement model to support empirical research and offer a foundation for further descriptive and normative studies on blockchain applications in supply chain traceability.

title: Employability attributes and personality preferences of postgraduate business management students
abstract: Orientation: The demand for sustained employability and a proactive career agency has led to a renewed interest in the dispositional and psychological attributes of students and employees – like their employability attributes and personality preferences – because these relate to the proactive management of their career development in a changing employment world. Research purpose: The purpose of the study was to determine the relationship between employees’ employability attributes (as the Employability Attributes Scale measures them) and their personality preferences (as the Myers-Briggs Type indicator, Form M, measures them). Motivation for the study: There seems to be a paucity of information about how employees’ personality preferences relate to their employability attributes in South Africa’s multicultural organisational context. Research design, approach and method: The authors conducted a quantitative survey. It involved a non-probability sample of 304 early career adults enrolled for an Honour’s degree in business management in an open distance learning higher education institution. They used correlational statistics and multiple regression analyses to analyse the data. Main findings: The authors observed a number of significant relationships between the participants’ personality preferences and their employability attributes. Practical/managerial implications: Career counsellors and human resource practitioners need to recognise how employees’ personality preferences influence their employability attributes in the management of their career development and employability. Contribution/value add: The findings add to the existing career literature on the career metacompetencies that influence employees’ employability. They also provide valuable information that organisations can use for career development support and counselling practices in the contemporary world of work.

title: Employability attributes and personality preferences of postgraduate business management students
abstract: This study investigates the relationship between employability attributes and personality preferences among postgraduate business management students in South Africa. Employability attributes, encompassing career self-management, cultural competence, and self-efficacy, are increasingly recognized as essential for graduates navigating a dynamic and uncertain labor market. Using a quantitative survey design, data were collected from 304 early career adults enrolled in an Honours business management program at an open distance learning institution. The Employability Attributes Scale and the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (Form M) were administered to assess participants’ employability-related competencies and personality preferences, respectively. Correlational and multiple regression analyses revealed significant associations between specific personality preferences and employability attributes, highlighting the influence of dispositional factors on proactive career behaviors. The findings underscore the importance for career counselors and human resource practitioners to consider personality preferences in supporting students’ and employees’ career development and employability. This research contributes to the literature on career meta-competencies by providing insights into how personality shapes employability, offering practical implications for organizational career development interventions in multicultural contexts.

title: Innovation, Dynamic Capabilities, and Leadership
abstract: The world in which today’s businesses operate has become not only riskier but also more volatile, uncertain, complex, and ambiguous (VUCA). Organizations that hew too closely to traditional ways of operating will be hampered in their ability to succeed. In contrast, those that focus on new product and process developments coupled with business model innovation will leverage their dynamic capabilities. An essential overlay is entrepreneurial leadership from top management teams. Strong dynamic capabilities are impossible without it. This article examines how business model innovations, dynamic capabilities, and strategic leadership intertwine to help organizations thrive in VUCA worlds.

title: Innovation, Dynamic Capabilities, and Leadership
abstract: This paper explores how organizations can thrive amid the volatility, uncertainty, complexity, and ambiguity (VUCA) that characterize today’s business environment by leveraging innovation, dynamic capabilities, and strategic leadership. Drawing on recent research and illustrative cases, the authors distinguish between ordinary and dynamic capabilities, emphasizing that while ordinary capabilities support current operations, dynamic capabilities—such as sensing opportunities, seizing them, and transforming the organization—are essential for sustained competitive advantage in turbulent contexts. The paper argues that business model innovation is critical for adapting to disruptive change and that entrepreneurial leadership from top management teams is indispensable for building and orchestrating these higher-order capabilities. By examining the interplay between innovation processes, dynamic capabilities, and leadership approaches, the study provides a framework for understanding how organizations can navigate uncertainty and proactively shape their futures.

title: Innovation in Business Management Exploring the Path to Competitive Excellence
abstract: In the realm of business management, the focal point has shifted towards innovation as a pivotal endeavor for attaining a competitive edge. This study aims to delve into the repercussions of innovation in business management and accentuate its pivotal role in forging pathways to competitive advantage. The Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) analysis, employing the SmartPLS tool, was employed to scrutinize data gathered from 150 respondents representing Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (UMKM) in Indonesia across four distinct sectors: fashion, furniture, home decoration, and services. The analysis reveals a noteworthy impact of innovation on various facets of business management, encompassing strategy, organizational operations, and marketing. These findings underscore that organizations adept at integrating innovation into their management practices can cultivate sustainable competitive advantages. Furthermore, the research spotlights critical factors influencing the implementation of innovation, including leader support, organizational culture, and the ability to navigate risk. This study furnishes invaluable insights for practitioners and decision-makers by underscoring the significance of innovation in fortifying competitive positions. The practical implications of these findings suggest that MSMEs fostering a culture of innovation, backed by leadership support and adept risk management, stand poised to enhance their performance and competitiveness within the increasingly intricate and dynamic markets.

title: Innovation in Business Management Exploring the Path to Competitive Excellence
abstract: This study investigates the critical role of innovation in business management as a driver of competitive excellence among Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in Indonesia. Utilizing Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) with SmartPLS on data from 150 respondents across fashion, furniture, home decoration, and service sectors, the research examines how innovation influences strategic management, organizational operations, and marketing effectiveness. The findings demonstrate that integrating innovation into business practices significantly enhances sustainable competitive advantage. Key factors facilitating successful innovation implementation include leadership support, organizational culture, and effective risk management. The study provides actionable insights for practitioners and policymakers, highlighting that MSMEs fostering a culture of innovation—underpinned by strong leadership and risk navigation—are better positioned to improve performance and maintain competitiveness in dynamic markets.

title: Paradigm Shifts - E-Business and Business/Systems Integration
abstract: The last decade or so spawned a host of business and technology innovations. On the business side, we saw business process reengineering, the management philosophies of customer relationship management and supply chain management, virtual organizations, electronic commerce, and business-tobusiness trading exchanges. On the technology side, we saw client-server computing, enterprise resource planning systems, the widespread adoption of Internet protocols, intranets and enterprise information portals, software package support for customer relationship management, supply chain management and other activities related to electronic business, and applications service providers. This tutorial puts put these business and technology innovations into historical context and relates them to one another through the unifying concepts of business integration and systems integration. One theme of the tutorial is the incomplete linkage between business integration and systems integration. Another is the imperfect relationship between the management philosophies of customer relationship management, supply chain management and electronic
venue: Communications of the Association for Information Systems

title: Paradigm Shifts - E-Business and Business/Systems Integration
abstract: This paper examines the major paradigm shifts in business and technology over the past decade, focusing on the emergence of e-business and the growing need for both business and systems integration. It situates innovations such as business process reengineering, customer relationship management, supply chain management, enterprise resource planning systems, and electronic commerce within a historical context, highlighting their interconnections and mutual influences. The analysis distinguishes between internal and external business integration, illustrating the challenges organizations face in achieving seamless coordination across departments and with external partners. The paper argues that while technological advancements have enabled new forms of integration, there remains an imperfect linkage between management philosophies and the information systems designed to support them. Through case examples, it demonstrates how gaps in integration can create significant business problems, particularly in meeting customer expectations for unified service and global inventory visibility. The tutorial concludes by emphasizing the ongoing need to align business strategies with systems integration efforts to fully realize the potential of e-business innovations.
venue: Communications of the Association for Information Systems

title: The evolution and future of logistics and supply chain management
abstract: This article will be divided into three sections: past, present, and future. The past section will trace major events that created business logistics as it is practiced today. In particular, do the events portend the future of business logistics and supply chain management? The present section will attempt to summarize the state of business logistics. How business logistics relates to supply chain management will be addressed. The future section will make some predictions as to the issues that need to be addressed and the events that will likely take place in the near term.

title: The evolution and future of logistics and supply chain management
abstract: This paper traces the historical development of logistics and supply chain management, examining key milestones that shaped the field from its fragmented origins in the early twentieth century to its current integrated approach. The analysis highlights how logistics evolved from a focus on individual activities, such as transportation and warehousing, to a holistic discipline emphasizing cost trade-offs and coordination across business functions. The emergence of physical distribution and business logistics in the 1960s and 1970s is discussed, along with the growing recognition of logistics costs and their impact on firm performance. The relationship between logistics and supply chain management is explored, noting their increasing convergence as firms seek to optimize flows from suppliers to end customers. Looking ahead, the paper identifies future challenges and opportunities, including technological advancements, globalization, and the need for greater integration across supply networks. The study concludes that understanding the evolution of logistics provides valuable insights for addressing emerging issues in supply chain management and for guiding future research and practice in the field.

title: The role of digitalization in business and management: a systematic literature review
abstract: Digitalization is a powerful engine for economic growth in the world. In 2018, digitally transformed firms represented 13.5 billion US dollars of global GDP and, towards the end of 2023, they are expected to represent 53.3 billion US dollars, over half of the general nominal GDP (Statista, Nominal GDP driven by digitally transformed and other enterprises worldwide 2018–2023. https://www.statista.com/statistics/1134766/nominal-gdp-driven-by-digitally-transformed-enterprises/ , 2022). The main objective of this study is to provide information (highlighting principal research topics and research agendas) from the literature on state-of-the-art digitalization within firms through a Systematic Literature Review (SLR). In all, 119 review articles on the most mature functional areas of the firm are analyzed: management, marketing, and finance and accounting, published in the WOS over the period 2018-April 2022. In this study, key relevant tendencies are identified in the most mature areas of the firm, which are the impact of digital technologies on the analysis of consumer behavior; digitalization and green innovation within organizations; and blockchain technology applied to financial services. The main contributions of this work are as follows: (1) to provide the most complete and up-to-date review of digitalization from a global perspective, summarizing the current state of knowledge within an integrated framework; (2) to reduce the complexity of digitalization by offering structure and clarity; and (3) to offer links between digitalization and established points of view in the literature on management, marketing, finance, and accounting. The novelty of this paper is centered on a joint analysis of digitalization, digital transformation, and digital technologies, taking into account the most mature functional areas of the firm.

title: The role of digitalization in business and management: a systematic literature review
abstract: This paper presents a systematic literature review of digitalization in business and management, focusing on the mature functional areas of management, marketing, and finance and accounting. Analyzing 119 review articles published between 2018 and April 2022, the study identifies key trends such as the impact of digital technologies on consumer behavior analysis, the integration of digitalization with green innovation, and the application of blockchain in financial services. The review synthesizes current knowledge within an integrated framework, clarifies the complexity of digitalization, and establishes connections with established literature in core business disciplines. By highlighting research gaps and future agendas, this work offers a comprehensive and up-to-date perspective on digitalization’s transformative role in organizations, providing valuable insights for scholars and practitioners seeking to navigate ongoing digital transformation.

title: Atmospheric chemistry of iodine.
abstract: This review comprises the most recent advances in our understanding of the sources of iodine (i.e., biological, gas- and aqueous-phase chemical mechanisms), describes the results of field observations (i.e., ground, balloon, and satellite based), discusses the progress made in laboratory studies of elementary processes and nanoparticle formation as well as numerical modeling of reactive iodine chemistry and particle formation, and summarizes our current knowledge of the atmospheric impact of iodine (i.e., ozone depletion, HOx and NOx chemistry, Hg oxidation, and new particle formation).

title: Atmospheric chemistry of iodine.
abstract: Iodine plays a multifaceted role in atmospheric chemistry, influencing processes from ozone depletion to particle formation and mercury cycling. This review synthesizes recent advances in understanding the sources, transformations, and impacts of atmospheric iodine. Oceans are identified as the dominant source, emitting a range of inorganic and organic iodine compounds through biological and photochemical mechanisms. Field measurements using advanced spectroscopic and mass spectrometric techniques have revealed widespread occurrence of reactive iodine species—including atomic iodine, molecular iodine, IO, and OIO—in diverse environments such as coastal regions, the open ocean, polar areas, salt lakes, and volcanic plumes. Laboratory and theoretical studies have elucidated the kinetics, photochemistry, and heterogeneous reactions of these species, highlighting their roles in catalytic ozone destruction and modulation of radical balances that control atmospheric oxidizing capacity. A major recent focus is on the formation of ultrafine iodine oxide particles, which can act as cloud condensation nuclei and potentially influence climate. Iodine-mediated oxidation also enhances mercury deposition in polar regions. Despite significant progress, key uncertainties remain regarding emission rates, chemical mechanisms, particle growth processes, and global impacts. The integration of field observations, laboratory experiments, and modeling is essential for advancing our understanding of iodine’s complex atmospheric chemistry and its broader environmental implications.

title: A reflection on lithium-ion battery cathode chemistry
abstract: Lithium-ion batteries have aided the portable electronics revolution for nearly three decades. They are now enabling vehicle electrification and beginning to enter the utility industry. The emergence and dominance of lithium-ion batteries are due to their higher energy density compared to other rechargeable battery systems, enabled by the design and development of high-energy density electrode materials. Basic science research, involving solid-state chemistry and physics, has been at the center of this endeavor, particularly during the 1970s and 1980s. With the award of the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry to the development of lithium-ion batteries, it is enlightening to look back at the evolution of the cathode chemistry that made the modern lithium-ion technology feasible. This review article provides a reflection on how fundamental studies have facilitated the discovery, optimization, and rational design of three major categories of oxide cathodes for lithium-ion batteries, and a personal perspective on the future of this important area. The 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry has been awarded to a trio of pioneers of the modern lithium-ion battery. Here, Professor Arumugam Manthiram looks back at the evolution of cathode chemistry, discussing the three major categories of oxide cathode materials with an emphasis on the fundamental solid-state chemistry that has enabled these advances.

title: A reflection on lithium-ion battery cathode chemistry
abstract: This review examines the evolution of lithium-ion battery cathode chemistry, tracing its origins from early intercalation compounds to the development of high-energy-density oxide cathodes that underpin modern lithium-ion technology. Emphasizing the critical role of fundamental solid-state chemistry and physics, the article reflects on how advances in understanding structure-composition-property relationships enabled the rational design and optimization of three major classes of oxide cathodes: layered, spinel, and polyanion families. The review highlights the pivotal contributions of John Goodenough’s group in pioneering these chemistries, which have facilitated significant increases in cell voltage, energy density, and safety. By contextualizing these scientific milestones within broader societal impacts—such as portable electronics, electric vehicles, and renewable energy integration—the article underscores the importance of continued basic research for future innovations in battery materials.

title: Bioorthogonal chemistry: fishing for selectivity in a sea of functionality.
abstract: The study of biomolecules in their native environments is a challenging task because of the vast complexity of cellular systems. Technologies developed in the last few years for the selective modification of biological species in living systems have yielded new insights into cellular processes. Key to these new techniques are bioorthogonal chemical reactions, whose components must react rapidly and selectively with each other under physiological conditions in the presence of the plethora of functionality necessary to sustain life. Herein we describe the bioorthogonal chemical reactions developed to date and how they can be used to study biomolecules.

title: Bioorthogonal chemistry: fishing for selectivity in a sea of functionality.
abstract: Bioorthogonal chemistry has emerged as a powerful approach for the selective modification and study of biomolecules within the complex environment of living systems, where traditional chemical methods often lack the necessary specificity. This review traces the historical development of bioorthogonal reactions, from early protein bioconjugation techniques targeting natural amino acid residues to modern strategies employing unnatural functional groups and metal-mediated transformations. The unique requirements for bioorthogonality—rapid and selective reactivity under physiological conditions without interfering with native biological processes—have driven innovation in reaction design, enabling precise labeling and manipulation of diverse biomolecules such as proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and glycans. We discuss the evolution of residue-specific and site-selective modification methods, advances in incorporating orthogonal functionalities into biomolecules, and the application of these chemistries to probe cellular processes in real time. The review concludes by highlighting ongoing challenges and future directions for expanding the repertoire of bioorthogonal reactions to access new biological insights.

title: Black hole chemistry: thermodynamics with Lambda
abstract: We review recent developments on the thermodynamics of black holes in extended phase space, where the cosmological constant is interpreted as thermodynamic pressure and treated as a thermodynamic variable in its own right. In this approach, the mass of the black hole is no longer regarded as internal energy, rather it is identified with the chemical enthalpy. This leads to an extended dictionary for black hole thermodynamic quantities; in particular a notion of thermodynamic volume emerges for a given black hole spacetime. This volume is conjectured to satisfy the reverse isoperimetric inequality—an inequality imposing a bound on the amount of entropy black hole can carry for a fixed thermodynamic volume. New thermodynamic phase transitions naturally emerge from these identifications. Namely, we show that black holes can be understood from the viewpoint of chemistry, in terms of concepts such as Van der Waals fluids, reentrant phase transitions, and triple points. We also review the recent attempts at extending the AdS/CFT dictionary in this setting, discuss the connections with horizon thermodynamics, applications to Lifshitz spacetimes, and outline possible future directions in this field.

title: Black hole chemistry: thermodynamics with Lambda
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive review of black hole thermodynamics in extended phase space, where the cosmological constant is treated as a thermodynamic pressure and its conjugate variable as a thermodynamic volume. By reinterpreting the black hole mass as enthalpy rather than internal energy, an enriched thermodynamic framework emerges, leading to new insights such as the reverse isoperimetric inequality and the identification of novel phase transitions analogous to those in conventional chemistry, including Van der Waals fluids, reentrant phase transitions, and triple points. The review also discusses the extension of the AdS/CFT correspondence in this context, connections with horizon thermodynamics, applications to Lifshitz spacetimes, and possible future directions. This approach, termed black hole chemistry, reveals deep analogies between black holes and everyday thermodynamic systems and opens new avenues for understanding gravity, quantum theory, and holography.

title: Defect Engineering: Tuning the Porosity and Composition of the Metal–Organic Framework UiO-66 via Modulated Synthesis
abstract: Presented in this paper is a deep investigation into the defect chemistry of UiO-66 when synthesized in the presence of monocarboxylic acid modulators under the most commonly employed conditions. We unequivocally demonstrate that missing cluster defects are the predominant defect and that their concentration (and thus the porosity and composition of the material) can be tuned to a remarkable extent by altering the concentration and/or acidity of the modulator. Finally, we attempt to rationalize these observations by speculating on the underlying solution chemistry.

title: Defect Engineering: Tuning the Porosity and Composition of the Metal–Organic Framework UiO-66 via Modulated Synthesis
abstract: This study presents a comprehensive investigation into the defect chemistry of the metal–organic framework UiO-66 synthesized using various monocarboxylic acid modulators under standard conditions. By systematically varying the concentration and acidity of the modulators across 15 syntheses, we demonstrate that missing cluster defects are predominant and that their concentration—and thus the porosity and composition of UiO-66—can be precisely tuned. Characterization by PXRD, nitrogen sorption, dissolution/NMR, and TGA reveals clear trends: increasing modulator concentration or acidity leads to higher defect concentrations and enhanced porosity, with BET surface areas ranging from 1175 to 1777 m2g-1. Comparison of experimental nitrogen adsorption isotherms with simulated models further validates these findings. The results highlight the critical role of modulator properties in defect engineering, offering a rational approach to tailor UiO-66’s structure and properties for targeted applications.

title: Development cycle 2 of the Modular Earth Submodel System (MESSy2)
abstract: The Modular Earth Submodel System (MESSy) is an open, multi-institutional project providing a strategy for developing comprehensive Earth System Models (ESMs) with highly flexible complexity. The first version of the MESSy infrastructure and process submodels, mainly focusing on atmospheric chemistry, has been successfully coupled to an atmospheric General Circulation Model (GCM) expanding it into an Atmospheric Chemistry GCM (AC-GCM) for nudged simulations and into a Chemistry Climate Model (CCM) for climate simulations. Here, we present the second development cycle of MESSy, which comprises (1) an improved and extended infrastructure for the basemodel independent coupling of process-submodels, (2) new, highly valuable diagnostic capabilities for the evaluation with observational data and (3) an improved atmospheric chemistry setup. With the infrastructural changes, we place the headstone for further model extensions from a CCM towards a comprehensive ESM. The new diagnostic submodels will be used for regular re-evaluations of the continuously further developing model system. The updates of the chemistry setup are briefly evaluated.

title: Development cycle 2 of the Modular Earth Submodel System (MESSy2)
abstract: The second development cycle of the Modular Earth Submodel System (MESSy2) advances the framework for constructing comprehensive Earth System Models (ESMs) by introducing significant infrastructural enhancements and new submodels. MESSy2 features a redesigned, basemodel-independent memory and meta-data management interface (CHANNEL), enabling flexible coupling of process submodels across diverse basemodels and improving data handling and export capabilities. Additional generic submodels, such as TIMER and QTIMER, optimize time control and resource management. The system is further extended with new diagnostic and process submodels, as well as updates to the atmospheric chemistry setup, supporting more robust model evaluation against observational data. These developments establish a foundation for expanding from Chemistry Climate Models toward fully integrated ESMs, with an emphasis on modularity, flexibility, and continuous re-evaluation to accommodate ongoing scientific and technical advancements.

title: Harmonized guidelines for single-laboratory validation of methods of analysis (IUPAC Technical Report)
abstract: Abstract Method validation is one of the measures universally recognized as a necessary part of a comprehensive system of quality assurance in analytical chemistry. In the past, ISO, IUPAC, and AOAC International have cooperated to produce agreed protocols or guidelines on the 'Design, conduct and interpretation of method performance studies' [1], on the 'Proficiency testing of (chemical) analytical laboratories' [2], on 'Internal quality control in analytical chemistry laboratories' [3], and on 'The use of recovery information in analytical measurement' [4]. The Working Group that produced these protocols/guidelines has now been mandated by IUPAC to prepare guidelines on the single-laboratory validation of methods of analysis. These guidelines provide minimum recommendations on procedures that should be employed to ensure adequate validation of analytical methods. A draft of the guidelines has been discussed at an International Symposium on the Harmonization of Quality Assurance Systems in Chemical Laboratory, the proceedings from which have been published by the UK Royal Society of Chemistry.

title: Harmonized guidelines for single-laboratory validation of methods of analysis (IUPAC Technical Report)
abstract: This technical report presents harmonized guidelines for the single-laboratory validation of analytical methods, developed under the auspices of IUPAC in collaboration with ISO and AOAC International. Recognizing the critical role of method validation in laboratory quality assurance and regulatory compliance, the guidelines provide minimum recommendations for procedures to ensure reliable analytical results when full interlaboratory validation is impractical or unnecessary.
