The document consolidates existing international protocols and standards, clarifies relevant terminology, and outlines essential performance characteristics to be evaluated—including applicability, selectivity, calibration, trueness, precision, recovery, range, detection limits, sensitivity, ruggedness, and measurement uncertainty. Detailed guidance is given on the design and conduct of validation studies, the extent of required validation, and considerations for uncertainty estimation. These harmonized guidelines aim to promote best practices in single-laboratory validation across diverse analytical fields, supporting laboratories in demonstrating method fitness-for-purpose and meeting legislative or client requirements.

title: Nickel-catalyzed cross-couplings involving carbon-oxygen bonds.
abstract: Nickel-Catalyzed Cross-Couplings Involving Carbon-Oxygen Bonds Brad M. Rosen, Kyle W. Quasdorf, Daniella A. Wilson, Na Zhang, Ana-Maria Resmerita, Neil K. Garg,* and Virgil Percec* Roy & Diana Vagelos Laboratories, Department of Chemistry, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104-6323, United States Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry, University of California, Los Angeles, California 90095, United States

title: Nickel-catalyzed cross-couplings involving carbon-oxygen bonds.
abstract: Nickel-catalyzed cross-coupling reactions involving carbon-oxygen bonds have emerged as powerful tools for constructing complex molecular architectures, offering an attractive alternative to traditional palladium-catalyzed processes that typically rely on aryl halides. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the historical development, mechanistic insights, and recent advances in nickel-catalyzed homocoupling, cross-coupling, and functionalization of C–O bonds, with a particular focus on phenol- and enol-derived electrophiles such as sulfonates, sulfates, esters, and carbamates. The advantages of using nickel catalysts include lower cost, greater abundance, and unique reactivity that enables the activation of less reactive C–O bonds under milder conditions and with broader substrate scope. The review highlights the synthetic value of phenol-derived electrophiles due to their natural abundance and functional group compatibility, discusses strategies for overcoming the inherent strength of C–O bonds, and compares nickel catalysis to other transition metal systems. By organizing the literature according to electrophile class and coupling type, this work underscores the versatility and practical significance of nickel catalysis in sustainable organic synthesis and sets the stage for future developments in C–O bond activation chemistry.

title: Open Babel: An open chemical toolbox
abstract: A frequent problem in computational modeling is the interconversion of chemical structures between different formats. While standard interchange formats exist (for example, Chemical Markup Language) and de facto standards have arisen (for example, SMILES format), the need to interconvert formats is a continuing problem due to the multitude of different application areas for chemistry data, differences in the data stored by different formats (0D versus 3D, for example), and competition between software along with a lack of vendor-neutral formats.ResultsWe discuss, for the first time, Open Babel, an open-source chemical toolbox that speaks the many languages of chemical data. Open Babel version 2.3 interconverts over 110 formats. The need to represent such a wide variety of chemical and molecular data requires a library that implements a wide range of cheminformatics algorithms, from partial charge assignment and aromaticity detection, to bond order perception and canonicalization. We detail the implementation of Open Babel, describe key advances in the 2.3 release, and outline a variety of uses both in terms of software products and scientific research, including applications far beyond simple format interconversion.ConclusionsOpen Babel presents a solution to the proliferation of multiple chemical file formats. In addition, it provides a variety of useful utilities from conformer searching and 2D depiction, to filtering, batch conversion, and substructure and similarity searching. For developers, it can be used as a programming library to handle chemical data in areas such as organic chemistry, drug design, materials science, and computational chemistry. It is freely available under an open-source license from http://openbabel.org.

title: Open Babel: An open chemical toolbox
abstract: Open Babel is an open-source chemical toolbox designed to address the persistent challenge of interconverting chemical structures among diverse file formats in computational chemistry and related fields. Supporting over 110 chemical file formats, Open Babel facilitates seamless data exchange by implementing a broad range of cheminformatics algorithms, including partial charge assignment, aromaticity detection, bond order perception, and canonicalization. The software provides both command-line utilities and a programmable library, enabling tasks such as conformer searching, 2D depiction, molecular filtering, batch conversion, substructure and similarity searching. Its extensible architecture allows easy integration of new file formats and functionalities through plugins. Open Babel also offers advanced features such as path-based molecular fingerprints for rapid database searching and robust methods for bond perception and atom typing, accommodating the varying data representations found in chemical informatics. Freely available under an open-source license, Open Babel serves as a comprehensive solution for researchers and developers working in organic chemistry, drug design, materials science, and computational modeling, promoting interoperability and innovation across the chemical sciences.

title: Quantum Chemistry in the Age of Quantum Computing.
abstract: Practical challenges in simulating quantum systems on classical computers have been widely recognized in the quantum physics and quantum chemistry communities over the past century. Although many approximation methods have been introduced, the complexity of quantum mechanics remains hard to appease. The advent of quantum computation brings new pathways to navigate this challenging and complex landscape. By manipulating quantum states of matter and taking advantage of their unique features such as superposition and entanglement, quantum computers promise to efficiently deliver accurate results for many important problems in quantum chemistry, such as the electronic structure of molecules. In the past two decades, significant advances have been made in developing algorithms and physical hardware for quantum computing, heralding a revolution in simulation of quantum systems. This Review provides an overview of the algorithms and results that are relevant for quantum chemistry. The intended audience is both quantum chemists who seek to learn more about quantum computing and quantum computing researchers who would like to explore applications in quantum chemistry.

title: Quantum Chemistry in the Age of Quantum Computing.
abstract: Quantum chemistry faces significant challenges due to the exponential complexity of simulating quantum systems on classical computers, limiting the accuracy and scalability of electronic structure calculations for molecules and materials. The emergence of quantum computing offers a transformative approach by leveraging quantum mechanical phenomena such as superposition and entanglement to efficiently represent and manipulate complex wave functions. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the intersection between quantum chemistry and quantum computing, detailing the limitations of classical methods, the computational complexity of quantum chemical problems, and the development of quantum algorithms tailored for both fault-tolerant and near-term noisy quantum devices. Key topics include phase estimation, variational quantum eigensolvers, Hamiltonian simulation, hybrid quantum-classical algorithms, and mappings from chemical problems to qubit representations. By bridging concepts from chemistry, physics, and computer science, this work aims to inform both chemists seeking to harness quantum computational tools and quantum information scientists interested in chemical applications. The article concludes with a discussion of current progress, ongoing challenges, and future directions for realizing practical quantum advantage in chemical simulations.

title: Quantum computational chemistry
abstract: With small quantum computers becoming a reality, first applications are eagerly sought. Quantum chemistry presents a spectrum of computational problems, from relatively easy to classically intractable. Algorithms for the easiest of these have been run on the first quantum computers. But an urgent question is, how well will these algorithms scale to go beyond what is possible classically? This review presents strategies employed to construct quantum algorithms for quantum chemistry, with the goal that quantum computers will eventually answer presently inaccessible questions, for example, in transition metal catalysis or important biochemical reactions.

title: Quantum computational chemistry
abstract: Quantum computational chemistry is an emerging interdisciplinary field at the intersection of quantum computing and computational chemistry, aiming to leverage quantum algorithms and hardware to solve classically intractable chemical problems. This review provides a comprehensive introduction to both foundational areas, with a particular focus on the electronic structure problem, which underpins predictions of chemical reactivity, stability, and properties. The article surveys key developments in mapping chemical systems onto quantum computers using first and second quantization methods, discusses major quantum algorithms such as quantum phase estimation and variational approaches, and examines strategies for reducing quantum resource requirements and mitigating errors in near-term devices. Illustrative examples demonstrate how these methods are applied to representative molecular systems. The review concludes with a discussion of current limitations, resource estimates for future quantum simulations, and an outlook on the potential impact of quantum computational chemistry in advancing scientific discovery and industrial applications.

title: Reactions at surfaces in the atmosphere: integration of experiments and theory as necessary (but not necessarily sufficient) for predicting the physical chemistry of aerosols.
abstract: While particles have significant deleterious impacts on human health, visibility and climate, quantitative understanding of their formation, composition and fates remains problematic. Indeed, in many cases, even qualitative understanding is lacking. One area of particular uncertainty is the nature of particle surfaces and how this determines interactions with gases in the atmosphere, including water, which is important for cloud formation and properties. The focus in this Perspective article is on some chemistry relevant to airborne particles and especially to reactions occurring on their surfaces. The intent is not to provide a comprehensive review, but rather to highlight a few selected examples of interface chemistry involving inorganic and organic species that may be important in the lower atmosphere. This includes sea salt chemistry, nitrate and nitrite ion photochemistry, organics on surfaces and heterogeneous reactions of oxides of nitrogen on proxies for airborne mineral dust and boundary layer surfaces. Emphasis is on the molecular level understanding that can only be gained by fully integrating experiment and theory to elucidate these complex systems.

title: Reactions at surfaces in the atmosphere: integration of experiments and theory as necessary (but not necessarily sufficient) for predicting the physical chemistry of aerosols.
abstract: Understanding the physical chemistry of atmospheric aerosols is critical for predicting their impacts on climate, air quality, and human health, yet significant uncertainties remain, particularly regarding surface reactions that govern particle formation, transformation, and fate. This perspective highlights the central role of surface chemistry in determining aerosol properties, focusing on selected examples involving inorganic and organic species relevant to the lower atmosphere, such as sea salt chemistry, nitrate and nitrite photochemistry, and heterogeneous reactions of nitrogen oxides on mineral dust proxies. The article emphasizes that while the integration of experimental and theoretical approaches is necessary to achieve molecular-level insights into these complex interfacial processes, such integration alone may not be sufficient for comprehensive prediction due to the inherent complexity and variability of atmospheric systems. The discussion underscores the need for continued advances in both experimental techniques and theoretical modeling to bridge existing knowledge gaps and improve our ability to predict aerosol behavior in the atmosphere.

title: Ten Chemical Innovations That Will Change Our World: IUPAC identifies emerging technologies in Chemistry with potential to make our planet more sustainable
abstract: Abstract 2019 is a very special year in chemistry. 2019 marks two major anniversaries: the 100th anniversary of the founding of the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC), and the 150th anniversary of Dimitri Mendeleev’s first publication on the Periodic Table of Elements [1]. IUPAC is the global organization that, among many other things, established a common language for chemistry—enabling scientific research, education, and trade. In a similar manner, Mendeleev’s system classified all the elements that were known at the time, and even predicted the existence of elements that would only come to be discovered years later. These two anniversaries are closely entwined, as IUPAC has played a major role developing of the modern Periodic Table by ensuring that the most authoritative version of the table is accessible to everyone [2], establishing names and symbols for the newly discovered elements, and also constantly reviewing its accuracy through the IUPAC Commission on Isotopic Abundances and Atomic Weights.

title: Ten Chemical Innovations That Will Change Our World: IUPAC identifies emerging technologies in Chemistry with potential to make our planet more sustainable
abstract: This paper presents the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry’s (IUPAC) initiative to identify ten emerging chemical technologies with the potential to significantly advance global sustainability. Marking the centennial of IUPAC and the 150th anniversary of Mendeleev’s Periodic Table, the study highlights how chemistry continues to shape society and address pressing challenges. Through a rigorous selection process involving global experts, IUPAC has spotlighted innovations such as nanopesticides, enantio-selective organocatalysis, solid-state batteries, flow chemistry, and reactive extrusion. These technologies promise to enhance agricultural productivity with reduced environmental impact, enable greener and more efficient synthesis of chemicals and pharmaceuticals, improve energy storage safety and performance, and minimize hazardous waste through solvent-free processes. The paper discusses both the scientific breakthroughs and the practical hurdles facing these innovations as they transition from laboratory research to industrial application. By showcasing these advances, IUPAC aims to inspire further research, foster interdisciplinary collaboration, and accelerate the adoption of sustainable chemical solutions worldwide.

title: The synthesis of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) using continuous flow chemistry
abstract: The implementation of continuous flow processing as a key enabling technology has transformed the way we conduct chemistry and has expanded our synthetic capabilities. As a result many new preparative routes have been designed towards commercially relevant drug compounds achieving more efficient and reproducible manufacture. This review article aims to illustrate the holistic systems approach and diverse applications of flow chemistry to the preparation of pharmaceutically active molecules, demonstrating the value of this strategy towards every aspect ranging from synthesis, in-line analysis and purification to final formulation and tableting. Although this review will primarily concentrate on large scale continuous processing, additional selected syntheses using micro or meso-scaled flow reactors will be exemplified for key transformations and process control. It is hoped that the reader will gain an appreciation of the innovative technology and transformational nature that flow chemistry can leverage to an overall process.

title: The synthesis of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) using continuous flow chemistry
abstract: Continuous flow chemistry has emerged as a transformative technology in the synthesis of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), offering enhanced control, safety, and scalability compared to traditional batch processes. This review highlights the evolution and current state of continuous flow methodologies for API production, emphasizing their holistic integration from synthesis through in-line analysis and purification to final formulation. Key examples from both academia and industry demonstrate how flow chemistry enables efficient, reproducible, and safer multi-step syntheses, including challenging or hazardous transformations. The modularity and automation potential of flow systems facilitate rapid process optimization and real-time monitoring, while also addressing issues of heat and mass transfer. Despite notable successes in scaling up API manufacture using flow reactors, challenges such as reactor fouling, high initial investment, and the need for specialized training persist. By critically examining both the achievements and limitations of continuous flow approaches, this review underscores their growing impact on pharmaceutical manufacturing and the collaborative efforts required to realize fully continuous drug production.

title: Algorithms on Strings, Trees, and Sequences: Computer Science and Computational Biology
abstract: Traditionally an area of study in computer science, string algorithms have, in recent years, become an increasingly important part of biology, particularly genetics. This volume is a comprehensive look at computer algorithms for string processing. In addition to pure computer science, Gusfield adds extensive discussions on biological problems that are cast as string problems and on methods developed to solve them. This text emphasizes the fundamental ideas and techniques central to today's applications. New approaches to this complex material simplify methods that up to now have been for the specialist alone. With over 400 exercises to reinforce the material and develop additional topics, the book is suitable as a text for graduate or advanced undergraduate students in computer science, computational biology, or bio-informatics.

title: Algorithms on Strings, Trees, and Sequences: Computer Science and Computational Biology
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive study of algorithms for strings, trees, and sequences, with a focus on their foundational roles in computer science and computational biology. It systematically explores exact and inexact string matching, including classical algorithms such as Boyer-Moore and Knuth-Morris-Pratt, as well as advanced preprocessing and comparison-based methods. The construction and application of suffix trees are examined in depth, highlighting their utility in problems ranging from substring search to genome-scale data analysis. Dynamic programming techniques for sequence alignment, edit distance computation, and local similarity detection are detailed alongside improvements for efficiency and space usage. The work extends to multiple sequence alignment, database search strategies using tools like FASTA and BLAST, and the algorithmic challenges posed by large-scale biological data. Additional topics include physical mapping, DNA sequencing, evolutionary tree reconstruction, gene prediction, molecular computation, and models of genome-level mutations. Through algorithmic innovations and practical applications, the paper bridges theoretical computer science with the demands of modern computational biology.

title: All-optical machine learning using diffractive deep neural networks
abstract: All-optical deep learning Deep learning uses multilayered artificial neural networks to learn digitally from large datasets. It then performs advanced identification and classification tasks. To date, these multilayered neural networks have been implemented on a computer. Lin et al. demonstrate all-optical machine learning that uses passive optical components that can be patterned and fabricated with 3D-printing. Their hardware approach comprises stacked layers of diffractive optical elements analogous to an artificial neural network that can be trained to execute complex functions at the speed of light. Science, this issue p. 1004 All-optical deep learning can be implemented with 3D-printed passive optical components. Deep learning has been transforming our ability to execute advanced inference tasks using computers. Here we introduce a physical mechanism to perform machine learning by demonstrating an all-optical diffractive deep neural network (D2NN) architecture that can implement various functions following the deep learning–based design of passive diffractive layers that work collectively. We created 3D-printed D2NNs that implement classification of images of handwritten digits and fashion products, as well as the function of an imaging lens at a terahertz spectrum. Our all-optical deep learning framework can perform, at the speed of light, various complex functions that computer-based neural networks can execute; will find applications in all-optical image analysis, feature detection, and object classification; and will also enable new camera designs and optical components that perform distinctive tasks using D2NNs.

title: All-optical machine learning using diffractive deep neural networks
abstract: We present a novel all-optical machine learning framework based on Diffractive Deep Neural Networks (D2NNs), where multiple passive diffractive layers, designed through deep learning, collectively perform complex computational tasks using only optical diffraction. By physically fabricating D2NNs with 3D-printed phase-only transmission layers operating at terahertz frequencies, we experimentally demonstrate their ability to implement handwritten digit classification and imaging lens functions, achieving high accuracy and efficiency. This scalable approach leverages the inherent parallelism and speed of light propagation in optical systems, enabling power-efficient and ultrafast execution of machine learning tasks without electronic computation. The D2NN framework opens new avenues for all-optical image analysis, feature detection, object classification, and the design of adaptive optical components, offering significant potential for future advances in optical computing and intelligent imaging systems.

title: Computational Modeling, Formal Analysis, and Tools for Systems Biology
abstract: As the amount of biological data in the public domain grows, so does the range of modeling and analysis techniques employed in systems biology. In recent years, a number of theoretical computer science developments have enabled modeling methodology to keep pace. The growing interest in systems biology in executable models and their analysis has necessitated the borrowing of terms and methods from computer science, such as formal analysis, model checking, static analysis, and runtime verification. Here, we discuss the most important and exciting computational methods and tools currently available to systems biologists. We believe that a deeper understanding of the concepts and theory highlighted in this review will produce better software practice, improved investigation of complex biological processes, and even new ideas and better feedback into computer science.

title: Computational Modeling, Formal Analysis, and Tools for Systems Biology
abstract: The rapid expansion of publicly available biological data has driven the adoption of advanced computational modeling and formal analysis techniques in systems biology. This review examines the integration of concepts and tools from theoretical computer science—such as process algebras, rule-based systems, Petri nets, model checking, and static analysis—into the modeling and investigation of complex biological processes. We discuss how these approaches enable precise, executable representations of biological systems, facilitate hypothesis testing, and support both qualitative and quantitative analyses. Emphasizing the importance of domain-specific languages and graphical modeling frameworks, we highlight their accessibility to biologists and their capacity to bridge mathematical and computational paradigms. The review also considers the potential for cross-disciplinary feedback, where advances in systems biology can inspire new developments in computer science. By surveying key methodologies and software tools, we aim to foster a deeper understanding of formal modeling concepts among systems biologists and encourage broader adoption of rigorous computational practices in the study of biological systems.

title: Euclid. I. Overview of the Euclid mission
abstract: The current standard model of cosmology successfully describes a variety of measurements, but the nature of its main ingredients, dark matter and dark energy, remains unknown. is a medium-class mission in the Cosmic Vision 2015--2025 programme of the European Space Agency (ESA) that will provide high-resolution optical imaging, as well as near-infrared imaging and spectroscopy, over about 14\,000\,deg$^2$ of extragalactic sky. In addition to accurate weak lensing and clustering measurements that probe structure formation over half of the age of the Universe, its primary probes for cosmology, these exquisite data will enable a wide range of science. This paper provides a high-level overview of the mission, summarising the survey characteristics, the various data-processing steps, and data products. We also highlight the main science objectives and expected performance.

title: Euclid. I. Overview of the Euclid mission
abstract: The Euclid mission, developed by the European Space Agency with contributions from an international consortium, is designed to investigate the nature of dark energy and dark matter by mapping the geometry of the Universe with unprecedented precision. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the mission’s scientific objectives, instrumentation, survey strategy, and operational framework. Euclid employs a 1.2-meter space telescope equipped with visible and near-infrared imaging and spectroscopy to survey 15,000 square degrees of extragalactic sky, enabling measurements of weak gravitational lensing and galaxy clustering over a wide redshift range. The mission’s data will constrain cosmological parameters, test theories of gravity on cosmic scales, and advance our understanding of galaxy evolution and large-scale structure formation. We summarize the mission architecture, calibration plans, data processing pipelines, and anticipated legacy value for the astronomical community. Euclid is poised to deliver transformative insights into fundamental physics and cosmology through its high-precision mapping of the dark Universe.

title: Knowledge Management and Organizational Learning
abstract: This series is introduced by the International Association for Knowledge Management (www.IAKM.net) with an aim to offer advanced peer-reviewed reference books to researchers, practitioners and students in the field of knowledge management in organizations. Both discussions of new theories and advances in the field, as well as reviews of the state-of-the art will be featured regularly. Particularly, the books will be open to these contributions: Reviews of the state-of-the art (i.e. syntheses of recent studies on a topic, classifications and discussions of theories, approaches and methods, etc.) that can both serve as a reference and allow opening new horizons Discussions on new theories and methods of scientific research in organisational knowledge management Critical reviews of empirical evidence and empirical validations of theories Contributions that build a bridge between the various disciplines and fields that converge towards knowledge management (i.e.: computer science, cognitive sciences, economics, other management fields, etc.) and propose the development of a common background of notions, concepts and scientific methods Surveys of new practical methods that can inspire practitioners and researchers in their applications of knowledge management methods in companies and public services

title: Knowledge Management and Organizational Learning
abstract: This volume provides a comprehensive examination of knowledge management (KM) and organizational learning (OL), presenting current research, theoretical developments, and practical applications in the field. Through contributions from leading scholars, the book explores foundational concepts such as the distinction between knowledge management and the management of knowledge, the transformation of tacit to organizational knowledge, and the role of organizational routines in knowledge creation and storage. It addresses key issues including knowledge diffusion, the challenges of transferring tacit knowledge, the enabling role of information technology, and the integration of KM systems. The volume also investigates applications such as virtual communities of practice, open innovation, and strategies for overcoming the digital divide. Measurement and evaluation frameworks for KM effectiveness are discussed alongside approaches to valuing knowledge within virtual communities. Finally, the book examines the interplay between organizational knowledge capabilities, learning processes, performance across cultures, and sustainability. By integrating diverse perspectives and empirical findings, this collection advances understanding of how organizations can effectively manage knowledge and foster continuous learning to enhance performance and adaptability in dynamic environments.

title: Quantum computing
abstract: The subject of quantum computing brings together ideas from classical information theory, computer science, and quantum physics. This review aims to summarize not just quantum computing, but the whole subject of quantum information theory. Information can be identified as the most general thing which must propagate from a cause to an effect. It therefore has a fundamentally important role in the science of physics. However, the mathematical treatment of information, especially information processing, is quite recent, dating from the mid-20th century. This has meant that the full significance of information as a basic concept in physics is only now being discovered. This is especially true in quantum mechanics. The theory of quantum information and computing puts this significance on a firm footing, and has led to some profound and exciting new insights into the natural world. Among these are the use of quantum states to permit the secure transmission of classical information (quantum cryptography), the use of quantum entanglement to permit reliable transmission of quantum states (teleportation), the possibility of preserving quantum coherence in the presence of irreversible noise processes (quantum error correction), and the use of controlled quantum evolution for efficient computation (quantum computation). The common theme of all these insights is the use of quantum entanglement as a computational resource. It turns out that information theory and quantum mechanics fit together very well. In order to explain their relationship, this review begins with an introduction to classical information theory and computer science, including Shannon's theorem, error correcting codes, Turing machines and computational complexity. The principles of quantum mechanics are then outlined, and the Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen (EPR) experiment described. The EPR-Bell correlations, and quantum entanglement in general, form the essential new ingredient which distinguishes quantum from classical information theory and, arguably, quantum from classical physics. Basic quantum information ideas are next outlined, including qubits and data compression, quantum gates, the `no cloning' property and teleportation. Quantum cryptography is briefly sketched. The universal quantum computer (QC) is described, based on the Church-Turing principle and a network model of computation. Algorithms for such a computer are discussed, especially those for finding the period of a function, and searching a random list. Such algorithms prove that a QC of sufficiently precise construction is not only fundamentally different from any computer which can only manipulate classical information, but can compute a small class of functions with greater efficiency. This implies that some important computational tasks are impossible for any device apart from a QC. To build a universal QC is well beyond the abilities of current technology. However, the principles of quantum information physics can be tested on smaller devices. The current experimental situation is reviewed, with emphasis on the linear ion trap, high-Q optical cavities, and nuclear magnetic resonance methods. These allow coherent control in a Hilbert space of eight dimensions (three qubits) and should be extendable up to a thousand or more dimensions (10 qubits). Among other things, these systems will allow the feasibility of quantum computing to be assessed. In fact such experiments are so difficult that it seemed likely until recently that a practically useful QC (requiring, say, 1000 qubits) was actually ruled out by considerations of experimental imprecision and the unavoidable coupling between any system and its environment. However, a further fundamental part of quantum information physics provides a solution to this impasse. This is quantum error correction (QEC). An introduction to QEC is provided. The evolution of the QC is restricted to a carefully chosen subspace of its Hilbert space. Errors are almost certain to cause a departure from this subspace. QEC provides a means to detect and undo such departures without upsetting the quantum computation. This achieves the apparently impossible, since the computation preserves quantum coherence even though during its course all the qubits in the computer will have relaxed spontaneously many times. The review concludes with an outline of the main features of quantum information physics and avenues for future research.

title: Quantum computing
abstract: This paper presents an accessible introduction to the principles of quantum computing using the framework of spin resonance methods. Emphasizing that quantum computing is fundamentally a reinterpretation of established concepts in quantum two-level systems, the discussion focuses on how qubits can be represented by spins and manipulated through well-known operations. The essential role of one-spin rotations and controlled-NOT (CNOT) gates is analyzed, demonstrating that any quantum computation can be decomposed into these basic operations. The challenges posed by decoherence and the practical limitations of current experimental realizations are addressed, highlighting the importance of selectivity in pulse application for accurate qubit control. The paper provides a pedagogical model for implementing quantum logic gates and offers exercises to reinforce understanding, making the subject accessible to undergraduate students and newcomers to the field.

title: Quantum random walks: An introductory overview
abstract: This article aims to provide an introductory survey on quantum random walks. Starting from a physical effect to illustrate the main ideas we will introduce quantum random walks, review some of their properties and outline their striking differences to classical walks. We will touch upon both physical effects and computer science applications, introducing some of the main concepts and language of present day quantum information science in this context. We will mention recent developments in this new area and outline some open questions.

title: Quantum random walks: An introductory overview
abstract: This article provides an accessible introduction to quantum random walks, highlighting their foundational concepts, key properties, and significant differences from classical random walks. Beginning with a physically motivated example, the paper develops the necessary terminology and mathematical framework for understanding quantum random walks, making the subject approachable for readers with a basic background in quantum mechanics but little exposure to computer science or quantum information theory. The survey covers both the physical underpinnings and computer science applications of quantum random walks, including their role in quantum algorithms and potential for computational speedup. Recent developments are discussed alongside open questions, with attention given to physical implementation and the emergence of classical behavior through decoherence. The article aims to equip readers with the intuition and background needed to engage with current research in this rapidly evolving interdisciplinary field.

title: The Bioperl toolkit: Perl modules for the life sciences.
abstract: The Bioperl project is an international open-source collaboration of biologists, bioinformaticians, and computer scientists that has evolved over the past 7 yr into the most comprehensive library of Perl modules available for managing and manipulating life-science information. Bioperl provides an easy-to-use, stable, and consistent programming interface for bioinformatics application programmers. The Bioperl modules have been successfully and repeatedly used to reduce otherwise complex tasks to only a few lines of code. The Bioperl object model has been proven to be flexible enough to support enterprise-level applications such as EnsEMBL, while maintaining an easy learning curve for novice Perl programmers. Bioperl is capable of executing analyses and processing results from programs such as BLAST, ClustalW, or the EMBOSS suite. Interoperation with modules written in Python and Java is supported through the evolving BioCORBA bridge. Bioperl provides access to data stores such as GenBank and SwissProt via a flexible series of sequence input/output modules, and to the emerging common sequence data storage format of the Open Bioinformatics Database Access project. This study describes the overall architecture of the toolkit, the problem domains that it addresses, and gives specific examples of how the toolkit can be used to solve common life-sciences problems. We conclude with a discussion of how the open-source nature of the project has contributed to the development effort.

title: The Bioperl toolkit: Perl modules for the life sciences.
abstract: The Bioperl toolkit is an open-source collection of Perl modules designed to address the diverse computational needs of the life sciences community. Developed through international collaboration, Bioperl provides a comprehensive, user-friendly, and extensible framework for managing, analyzing, and integrating biological data. Its object-oriented architecture supports a wide range of tasks, including sequence analysis, annotation, database access, phylogenetics, protein structure, and bibliographic reference management. By offering reusable components and a consistent programming interface, Bioperl streamlines complex bioinformatics workflows and reduces redundant software development efforts. The toolkit facilitates interoperability with external applications and data formats, supports integration with Python and Java via BioCORBA, and provides extensive documentation and tutorials to lower the barrier for new users. This paper describes the design principles, module organization, and practical applications of Bioperl, highlighting how its open-source model accelerates community-driven innovation in bioinformatics software development.

title: The iPlant Collaborative: Cyberinfrastructure for Plant Biology
abstract: The iPlant Collaborative (iPlant) is a United States National Science Foundation (NSF) funded project that aims to create an innovative, comprehensive, and foundational cyberinfrastructure in support of plant biology research (PSCIC, 2006). iPlant is developing cyberinfrastructure that uniquely enables scientists throughout the diverse fields that comprise plant biology to address Grand Challenges in new ways, to stimulate and facilitate cross-disciplinary research, to promote biology and computer science research interactions, and to train the next generation of scientists on the use of cyberinfrastructure in research and education. Meeting humanity's projected demands for agricultural and forest products and the expectation that natural ecosystems be managed sustainably will require synergies from the application of information technologies. The iPlant cyberinfrastructure design is based on an unprecedented period of research community input, and leverages developments in high-performance computing, data storage, and cyberinfrastructure for the physical sciences. iPlant is an open-source project with application programming interfaces that allow the community to extend the infrastructure to meet its needs. iPlant is sponsoring community-driven workshops addressing specific scientific questions via analysis tool integration and hypothesis testing. These workshops teach researchers how to add bioinformatics tools and/or datasets into the iPlant cyberinfrastructure enabling plant scientists to perform complex analyses on large datasets without the need to master the command-line or high-performance computational services.

title: The iPlant Collaborative: Cyberinfrastructure for Plant Biology
abstract: The iPlant Collaborative is a National Science Foundation-funded initiative designed to develop a comprehensive cyberinfrastructure that addresses the computational and data integration needs of the plant biology research community. By leveraging advances in high-performance computing, large-scale data storage, and open-source software, iPlant provides a sustainable and extensible platform that enables researchers from diverse disciplines to collaborate, integrate analytical tools, and manage complex datasets. The platform supports a wide range of users, from students to computational experts, facilitating cross-disciplinary research and training while promoting reproducibility and experimental verifiability. Through community-driven workshops and APIs for tool integration, iPlant empowers plant scientists to tackle Grand Challenges in agriculture, ecology, and bioenergy by enabling efficient analysis of genomic, phenotypic, and environmental data. This article reviews the design principles, implementation strategies, and anticipated impacts of the iPlant cyberinfrastructure on advancing plant biology research and education.

title: The Semantic Grid: A Future e‐Science Infrastructure
abstract: e-Science offers a promising vision of how computer and communication technology can support and enhance the scientific process. It does this by enabling scientists to generate, analyse, share and discuss their insights, experiments and results in an effective manner. The underlying computer infrastructure that provides these facilities is commonly referred to as the Grid. At this time, there are a number of grid applications being developed and there is a whole raft of computer technologies that provide fragments of the necessary functionality. However there is currently a major gap between these endeavours and the vision of e-Science in which there is a high degree of easy-to-use and seamless automation and in which there are flexible collaborations and computations on a global scale. To bridge this practice–aspiration divide, this paper presents a research agenda whose aim is to move from the current state of the art in e-Science infrastructure, to the future infrastructure that is needed to support the full richness of the e-Science vision. Here the future e-Science research infrastructure is termed the Semantic Grid (Semantic Grid to Grid is meant to connote a similar relationship to the one that exists between the Semantic Web and the Web). In particular, we present a conceptual architecture for the Semantic Grid. This architecture adopts a service-oriented perspective in which distinct stakeholders in the scientific process, represented as software agents, provide services to one another, under various service level agreements, in various forms of marketplace. We then focus predominantly on the issues concerned with the way that knowledge is acquired and used in such environments since we believe this is the key differentiator between current grid endeavours and those envisioned for the Semantic Grid.

title: The Semantic Grid: A Future e‐Science Infrastructure
abstract: This paper introduces the Semantic Grid as a transformative e-Science infrastructure designed to bridge the gap between current grid technologies and the aspirational vision of seamless, automated, and flexible global scientific collaboration. Building on the analogy between the Semantic Web and the Web, the Semantic Grid extends traditional grid computing by incorporating advanced knowledge services alongside data and information layers. The proposed conceptual architecture adopts a service-oriented approach, where software agents representing diverse stakeholders provide and consume services within dynamic marketplaces governed by service level agreements. Central to this vision is the acquisition, representation, and use of knowledge to enable personalized, automated support for scientific processes, facilitating richer interactions and more effective resource sharing. The paper outlines key research challenges in realizing this infrastructure, emphasizing the pivotal role of knowledge management in achieving the full potential of e-Science.

title: Advances in Economics and Econometrics: Theory and Applications: Theory and experiment in the analysis of strategic interaction
abstract: Much of economics has to do with the coordination of independent decisions, and such questions with some well-known exceptions are inherently game theoretic. Yet when the Econometric Society held its First World Congress in 1965, economic theory was still almost entirely non-strategic and game theory remained largely a branch of mathematics, whose applications in economics were the work of a few pioneers. As recently as the early 1970s, the profession's view of game-theoretic modeling was typified by Paul Samuelson's customarily vivid phrase, 'the swamp of n-person game theory'; and even students to whom the swamp seemed a fascinating place thought carefully before descending from the high ground of perfect competition and monopoly. The game-theoretic revolution that ensued altered the landscape in ways that would have been difficult to imagine in 1965, adding so much to our understanding that many questions whose strategic aspects once made them seem intractable are now considered fit for textbook treatment. This process was driven by a fruitful dialogue between game theory and economics, in which game theory supplied a rich language for describing strategic interactions and a set of tools for predicting their outcomes, and economics contributed questions and intuitions about strategic behavior

title: Advances in Economics and Econometrics: Theory and Applications: Theory and experiment in the analysis of strategic interaction
abstract: This paper examines the evolving interplay between theory and experiment in the analysis of strategic interaction within economics, highlighting the limitations of relying solely on theoretical models to predict behavior in noncooperative games. Tracing the historical development of game theory from a mathematical curiosity to a central tool in economic analysis, the paper argues that theoretical predictions often depend on strong assumptions that may not hold in practice, necessitating empirical investigation. The discussion reviews leading theoretical frameworks—including traditional noncooperative game theory, cooperative game theory, evolutionary models, and adaptive learning—and assesses their explanatory power in light of experimental evidence. Experimental methods are shown to offer crucial insights by controlling for environmental variables and systematically observing behavior, thereby complementing theory and refining our understanding of strategic decision-making. The paper advocates for a closer dialogue between theorists and experimentalists, emphasizing that a synthesis of theoretical ideas and empirical findings is essential for advancing knowledge about strategic behavior. Theoretical frameworks provide structure for interpreting data, while experiments delineate the boundaries of theoretical applicability and reveal behavioral regularities not captured by existing models. The analysis concludes that progress in understanding strategic interaction depends on integrating theoretical rigor with empirical validation, and outlines directions for future research at this intersection.

title: Economics and the Modern Economic Historian
abstract: I reflect on the role of modern economic history in economics. I document a substantial increase in the percentage of papers devoted to economic history in the top-5 economic journals over the last few decades. I discuss how the study of the past has contributed to economics by providing ground to test economic theory, improve economic policy, understand economic mechanisms, and answer big economic questions. Recent graduates in economic history appear to have roughly similar prospects to those of other economists in the economics job market. I speculate how the increase in availability of high quality micro level historical data, the decline in costs of digitizing data, and the use of computationally intensive methods to convert large-scale qualitative information into quantitative data might transform economic history in the future.

title: Economics and the Modern Economic Historian
abstract: This paper examines the evolving role of economic history within the economics profession, documenting a notable resurgence in the presence of economic history research in top economics journals over recent decades. Drawing on publication trends and job market outcomes, the analysis highlights that economic historians today enjoy professional prospects comparable to those of their peers in other fields. The study argues that historical analysis has become increasingly valued for its contributions to testing economic theories, informing policy, and addressing major economic questions. The paper also explores how advances in data availability, digitization, and computational methods are poised to further transform the field, enabling richer and more rigorous analysis of historical phenomena. Overall, the paper contends that while most economists remain primarily interested in history for its relevance to current issues, the integration of historical perspective is now recognized as essential for a deeper understanding of economic mechanisms and development.

title: Institutions, Entrepreneurship, and Economic Growth: What Do We Know? And What Do We Still Need to Know?
abstract: We review the literature that links institutions, entrepreneurship, and economic growth outcomes, focusing in particular on the empirics of the links between these. Most of this literature has an economics orientation, but we also review relevant literature from other social science and from management research. The review helps identify a number of conceptual, theoretical and empirical gaps, calling for further research. For example, the literature narrowly identifies entrepreneurship with start-ups and self-employment; does not theorize many potentially relevant inter-level links and mechanisms; and suffers from sample limitations, omitted variable biases, causality issues, and response heterogeneity. We argue that theories in management research, such as the resource-based view, transaction cost economics, and strategic entrepreneurship theory, can fill some of the conceptual and theoretical gaps.

title: Institutions, Entrepreneurship, and Economic Growth: What Do We Know? And What Do We Still Need to Know?
abstract: This paper reviews and synthesizes the empirical literature linking institutions, entrepreneurship, and economic growth, highlighting significant conceptual, theoretical, and methodological gaps that persist in current research. The authors note that most studies narrowly define entrepreneurship as start-ups or self-employment and often overlook the roles of established firms and the multilevel mechanisms through which institutions shape entrepreneurial activity and aggregate economic outcomes. The review identifies limitations such as sample constraints, omitted variable bias, causality issues, and response heterogeneity in existing empirical work. The authors argue that integrating management theories—including the resource-based view, transaction cost economics, and strategic entrepreneurship theory—can address these gaps by elucidating how institutions influence the costs of resource assembly and entrepreneurial action under uncertainty. They propose a multilevel framework in which institutional arrangements affect the aggregate elasticity of substitution in an economy, thereby shaping the relationship between entrepreneurship and growth. The paper concludes by calling for more interdisciplinary research to better understand the complex pathways linking institutions, entrepreneurship, and economic performance.

title: Regression Discontinuity Designs in Economics
abstract: This paper provides an introduction and “user guide” to Regression Discontinuity (RD) designs for empirical researchers. It presents the basic theory behind the research design, details when RD is likely to be valid or invalid given economic incentives, explains why it is considered a “quasi-experimental” design, and summarizes different ways (with their advantages and disadvantages) of estimating RD designs and the limitations of interpreting these estimates. Concepts are discussed using examples drawn from the growing body of empirical research using RD. ( JEL C21, C31)

title: Regression Discontinuity Designs in Economics
abstract: This paper offers a comprehensive introduction to regression discontinuity (RD) designs, emphasizing their theoretical foundations, practical implementation, and growing importance in empirical economics. The authors review the origins and evolution of RD designs, highlighting their appeal as a quasi-experimental method that can yield credible causal inferences when treatment assignment is determined by a threshold rule. Key issues addressed include the conditions under which RD designs are valid or invalid, particularly the necessity that individuals cannot precisely manipulate the assignment variable near the cutoff. The paper discusses methodological approaches for estimating RD effects, including both parametric and non-parametric techniques, and outlines best practices for graphical presentation and validity testing. Drawing on examples from recent economic research, the authors illustrate the versatility of RD designs across diverse applications and provide practical guidance for researchers seeking to apply this method. The review clarifies common misconceptions and synthesizes current knowledge, establishing RD designs as a central tool in the empirical economist’s toolkit.

title: Technology and Economic Theory
abstract: Technology and technological change play a central role in economics, whether in the theory of resource allocation or in the theory of growth and development. Yet the nature of technology is largely ignored in economic theory, it being considered sufficient to treat technology as a constraint on productive opportunities. This short essay delves a little deeper into the nature of technology and the material, energy and information transformation processes that it represents. A deeper understanding of technology leads to a deeper understanding of the main currents of technological advance and to the reasons why the development of technology and its application are so uneven over time and place.

title: Technology and Economic Theory
abstract: This paper explores the complex relationship between technology and economic theory, emphasizing the central role of technological change in shaping economic growth, competition, and the structure of firms. It critically examines how economists conceptualize technology, highlighting the limitations of traditional production function approaches that treat technology as an unexplained constraint or a simple menu of inputs and outputs. Drawing on historical perspectives from Smith, Marshall, and Schumpeter, as well as modern evolutionary economics, the paper argues that technology is inseparable from human agency and organizational structures. It advocates for a broader understanding of technology that encompasses not only codified knowledge and physical artifacts but also the organization and management of production systems. By analyzing the architecture of technological systems and the division of labor, the paper situates its discussion within both classical and contemporary traditions, ultimately calling for a more nuanced integration of technological complexity into economic theory.

title: The economics of animal health and production.
abstract: During the last 200 years, there has been massive socio-economic change through industrial and agricultural revolutions. This change has been associated with rapid increases in human and domestic livestock populations, and a movement of people from rural to urban areas. More than half the people in the world now live in urban environments where they have bet- ter access to work, but limited or no access to land and livestock to produce food. This implies that a majority of people are dependent on others for raw, semi-processed and processed food products. The efficient functioning of the livestock sector, encompassing all facets of input sup- ply, production, processing and marketing, has become a critical issue for guaranteeing: ● that sufficient livestock products are available at affordable prices – food security; and ● that the livestock products are safe to eat – food safety. Within the livestock sector, the livestock producers and business people involved in input supply and output processing and marketing need to be able to plan, make a profit and have a sustainable livelihood. The State also plays a critical role in facilitating how the livestock sec- tor functions and develops in order to satisfy society’s needs. Therefore, both the private and public sectors require economic theory and tools to understand the drivers of change for the livestock sector, and how to assess the impact of future actions and investments.

title: The economics of animal health and production.
abstract: This study evaluates the potential of mass drug administration (MDA) with moxidectin to accelerate the elimination of onchocerciasis in Africa compared to the current standard of ivermectin. Using the stochastic, individual-based EPIONCHO-IBM model, the research simulates various scenarios across a range of endemicity levels, treatment frequencies, and coverage/adherence rates. Results indicate that biannual moxidectin MDA could halve the time required to achieve elimination of transmission (EoT) in mesoendemic areas and may be essential for achieving EoT in hyperendemic regions. The findings highlight significant limitations of annual ivermectin MDA in high-transmission settings and underscore the need for improved data on repeated moxidectin efficacy, individual response variability, effects on parasite development, and adherence patterns to refine projections. The study supports consideration of moxidectin as a key strategy to meet World Health Organization 2030 targets for onchocerciasis elimination, particularly where current interventions are insufficient.

title: The Economics of Property Rights: Towards a Theory of Comparative Systems
abstract: To understand recent developments in Eastern Europe requires a method of analysis that is capable of internalizing into a theoretical framework (i) the logical premises deduced from the costs of transactions and incentive structures generated by various institutions and (ii) the evidence for refutable implications of those premises. The economics of property rights is such a theory. It expands the scope of the ability of economic analysis to explain a wide range of institutional structures and provides empirical corroboration of its logical implications. The economics of property rights is, then, an effective scholarly instrument that offers more significant understanding of the three current issues in the area of comparative economic studies: (i) evaluating the performance of alternative institutional arrangements, (ii) explaining the failure of socialist institutions in Eastern Europe, and (iii) identifying the costs (political as well as economic) of institutional reforms in that part of the world. In that sense, the book is both timely and relevant. In the late 1980s East Europeans crossed the threshold of fear and forced their leaders to abandon Marxism. With that theory of history dead and buried, the cost of current sacrifices in the pursuit of socialism has risen relative to the present value of its expected future benefits.

title: The Economics of Property Rights: Towards a Theory of Comparative Systems
abstract: This book develops a comparative theory of economic systems by analyzing the central role of property rights in shaping institutional structures, incentives, and economic performance. Drawing on historical, philosophical, and sociological perspectives, it contrasts the evolution and functioning of private-property, free-market capitalism with state-owned, centrally planned Soviet-type economies. The study examines how property rights influence economic behavior, production efficiency, innovation, and the organization of firms under capitalism, while exploring the implications of state ownership, economic planning, and political monopoly in socialist systems. Through detailed case studies of the Soviet Union and Eastern European reforms, the work highlights the impact of institutional arrangements on transaction costs, resource allocation, and quality of life. Ultimately, it argues that differences in property rights regimes are fundamental to understanding the dynamics and outcomes of alternative economic systems.

title: The Economics of Smoking
abstract: While the tobacco industry is among the most substantial and successful economic enterprises, tobacco consumption kills more people than any other product. Economic analysis of tobacco product markets, particularly for cigarettes, has contributed considerable insight to debates about the industry's importance and appropriate public policy roles in grappling with health consequences of tobacco. The most significant example is the rapidly expanding and increasingly sophisticated body of research on the effects of price increases on cigarette consumption. Because excise tax is a component of price, the resultant literature has been prominent in legislative debates about taxation as a tool to discourage smoking, and has contributed theory and empirical evidence to the growing interest in modeling demand for addictive products. This chapter examines the research and several equity and efficiency concerns accompanying cigarette taxation debates. It includes economic analysis of other tobacco control policies, such as advertising restrictions, prominent in tobacco control debates. Research addressing the validity of tobacco-industry arguments that its contributions to employment, tax revenues, and trade balances are vital to economic health in states and nations is also considered, as it is the industry's principal weapon in the battle against policy measures to reduce tobacco consumption.

title: The Economics of Smoking
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the economics of smoking, focusing on the interplay between tobacco consumption, pricing, taxation, and public health outcomes. It reviews empirical and theoretical research on the price elasticity of demand for cigarettes and other tobacco products, including conventional econometric studies and models of addiction. The paper examines the effects of excise taxation on consumption, equity, efficiency, and smuggling, as well as the broader social costs associated with smoking. It also explores the impact of advertising, promotion, and various tobacco control policies—such as health information campaigns, restrictions on smoking in public places, and limits on youth access—on tobacco demand. In addition, the paper assesses the macroeconomic significance of the tobacco industry, including its contributions to employment and government revenues, and evaluates agricultural policies affecting tobacco production. While primarily drawing on U.S. data and literature, the analysis highlights generalizable economic principles relevant to global tobacco control debates. The findings underscore the central role of economic tools in shaping effective tobacco policy aimed at reducing smoking prevalence and its associated health burdens.

title: The Virtues and Vices of Equilibrium and the Future of Financial Economics
abstract: The use of equilibrium models in economics springs from the desire for parsimonious models of economic phenomena that take human reasoning into account. This approach has been the cornerstone of modern economic theory. We explain why this is so, extolling the virtues of equilibrium theory; then we present a critique and describe why this approach is inherently limited, and why economics needs to move in new directions if it is to continue to make progress. We stress that this shouldn't be a question of dogma, but should be resolved empirically. There are situations where equilibrium models provide useful predictions and there are situations where they can never provide useful predictions. There are also many situations where the jury is still out, i.e., where so far they fail to provide a good description of the world, but where proper extensions might change this. Our goal is to convince the skeptics that equilibrium models can be useful, but also to make traditional economists more aware of the limitations of equilibrium models. We sketch some alternative approaches and discuss why they should play an important role in future research in economics.

title: The Virtues and Vices of Equilibrium and the Future of Financial Economics
abstract: This paper critically examines the central role of equilibrium models in financial economics, highlighting both their strengths in providing parsimonious, structured explanations of market behavior and their inherent limitations in capturing complex, real-world phenomena. Drawing on perspectives from both economics and physics, the authors discuss the foundational assumptions of equilibrium theory—such as rational expectations, market clearing, and agent optimization—and assess their empirical validity. While equilibrium models have been instrumental in shaping economic thought and practice, especially in contexts like risk management and arbitrage, the paper argues that their predictive power is often constrained by unrealistic assumptions about agent rationality and information. The authors review empirical evidence for and against equilibrium approaches and illustrate cases where non-equilibrium dynamics—such as power laws, market crises, and heterogeneous agent interactions—are more relevant. The paper advocates for a pluralistic approach to financial economics, integrating alternative methodologies including agent-based modeling, behavioral finance, bounded rationality, and insights from biology and complex systems. Ultimately, the authors call for an empirically grounded reassessment of equilibrium’s place in economic theory and encourage the development of models that better reflect the adaptive, evolving nature of real financial markets.

title: Authentic Assessment and Pedagogical Strategies in Higher Education
abstract: Problem statement: Researchers have noted that there is a mismatch between curriculum content and assessment practices in higher education. At the moment, the focus is still on the assessment of learning and not much on assessment for learning. Therefore, this study was conducted to examine the implementation of authentic assessment in higher education in Malaysia. Approach: The study employed a qualitative research method and involved the use of instruments such as interviews, document analysis and unobtrusive classroom observations to collect the relevant data in the classrooms of a three-credit hour course from a Masters degree programme. The total population consisted of 2 lecturers and 20 students from the two selected intact TSL 752 classes. Results: In this study, researchers identified different types of authentic assessment with the suitability to certain pedagogical strategies, their effects on students' learning and the appropriate procedures of conducting authentic assessments. The findings indicated that alternative and authentic assessment have more acceptance from students and should therefore be viewed as an alternative to traditional standardized assessment. Conclusion/Recommendations: The study identified that assessment strategies should be closely related to teaching and learning. Assessing authentic performances should become integral parts of the instructional cycle and feedback provided by the lecturer and peers should be formative in order to help the students assess their strengths and weaknesses, identifying areas of needed growth and mobilizing current capacity.

title: Authentic Assessment and Pedagogical Strategies in Higher Education
abstract: This study investigates the implementation of authentic assessment and its alignment with pedagogical strategies in higher education in Malaysia. Employing a qualitative research design, data were collected through interviews, document analysis, and classroom observations involving two lecturers and twenty students from a postgraduate course. The findings reveal that various forms of authentic assessment, when integrated with suitable pedagogical approaches, enhance student engagement, promote deeper learning, and are generally preferred over traditional standardized assessments. The study underscores the importance of aligning assessment methods with instructional practices and recommends that authentic assessment be embedded as a formative process within the instructional cycle. Providing timely feedback from both lecturers and peers is highlighted as essential for supporting students’ self-assessment, identifying learning needs, and fostering continuous improvement. The results suggest that adopting authentic assessment practices can better prepare students for real-world challenges and lifelong learning.

title: Design Thinking in Pedagogy
abstract: The twenty-first century has brought lots of challenges for people in all spheres, including education. In the new context, traditional approaches often seem ineffective and therefore new tools and methods have to be applied. An alternative approach that might be useful in the given context is design thinking – the approach that originated in architecture, design and art, and nowadays is applied in many fields. It is a human-centered problem-solving approach that may be used in the teaching/learning process to develop twenty-first century skills and enhance creativity and innovation. This paper introduces readers to the origin of design thinking, its attributes and processes as well as its application in pedagogy.

title: Design Thinking in Pedagogy
abstract: This paper explores the integration of design thinking into pedagogy as a response to the complex challenges faced by education in the twenty-first century. Design thinking, originating from architecture, design, and art, is presented as a human-centered, problem-solving approach that fosters creativity, innovation, and the development of essential twenty-first-century skills. The paper examines the origins and theoretical foundations of design thinking, highlighting its evolution and key characteristics such as ambiguity, collaboration, empathy, and iterative processes. It discusses how design thinking complements traditional scientific reasoning by emphasizing abductive logic and solution-based approaches to 'wicked problems'—complex issues with no definitive solutions. The application of design thinking in educational contexts is analyzed, with attention to its potential for enhancing critical thinking, creativity, teamwork, and adaptability among learners. The paper concludes by offering insights into how educators can cultivate design thinking skills within teaching and learning processes to better prepare students for an unpredictable and rapidly changing world.

title: Entrepreneurship education pedagogy: teacher-student-centred paradox
abstract: The purpose of this paper is to answer the research question: “Do different pedagogies used in teaching entrepreneurship education influence individual skill development, which then in turn translates into a likelihood of entrepreneurial implementation intention?” Design/methodology/approach The number of total participants for the quasi-experiment was 308 undergraduate students in Malaysia, in which pre- and post-test (n=203) and control (n=105) groups are included. Students who enroled in the entrepreneurship course were randomly allocated into a class employing teacher-centred pedagogy or student-centred pedagogy. Learning outcomes are measured by objective and subjective measures. Findings Both pedagogical approaches had a positive effect on the development of the learning outcomes. However, the students who learned using the teacher-centred approach statistically developed a higher level of objective and subjective learning outcomes compared to the students who learned using the student-centred approach. The findings also suggest that the relationship between entrepreneurship education and entrepreneurial intention mediates by learned skills. Originality/value The quasi-experimental design greatly improves the ability to make accurate claims about the impact of entrepreneurial education on entrepreneurship-related outcomes. Further, the study uses the implementation intention strategy in measuring the entrepreneurial intention. Thus, the study strongly supports for the view that implementation intention improves predictive validity of the behavioural intention within the framework of theory of planned behaviour by setting out in advance when, where, and how the goal will be achieved.

title: Entrepreneurship education pedagogy: teacher-student-centred paradox
abstract: This study investigates the impact of teacher-centred versus student-centred pedagogies in entrepreneurship education on undergraduate skill development and entrepreneurial intention within Malaysian higher education. Employing a quasi-experimental design with 308 participants, students were randomly assigned to either teacher-centred or student-centred entrepreneurship courses, with learning outcomes assessed through both objective (exam scores) and subjective (self-reported) measures. Findings reveal that while both pedagogical approaches positively influence skill acquisition and entrepreneurial intention, the teacher-centred approach yields significantly higher objective and subjective learning outcomes. Furthermore, the relationship between entrepreneurship education and entrepreneurial intention is mediated by the skills learned. By integrating implementation intention strategies and robust experimental controls, this research enhances the methodological rigor of entrepreneurship education studies and demonstrates that pedagogical delivery methods critically shape educational effectiveness and entrepreneurial outcomes.

title: Evaluating an English Language Teacher Education Program through Peacock's Model
abstract: The main aim of this study is to draw attention to the importance of program evaluation for teacher education programs and to reveal the pre-service English teacher education program components that are in need of improvement or maintenance both from teachers' and students' perspectives by using Peacock's (2009) recent evaluation model in a Turkish university context. The study is based on the data collected from teachers and fourth year student teachers who have had experience with the new teacher education program initiated by Higher Education Council (HEC) in 2006-2007 academic year. The data collected by means of questionnaires and interviews revealed that although participating teachers and student teachers have similar views about some program components, they hold different ideas about the balance among linguistic and pedagogic competences in the program. While teachers believe that the program does not suffice to improve student teachers' linguistic competence, student teachers think that the pedagogic side of the program needs to be improved.

title: Evaluating an English Language Teacher Education Program through Peacock's Model
abstract: This study evaluates a pre-service English language teacher education program at a Turkish university using Peacock’s (2009) model to identify areas for improvement and maintenance from both teacher and student perspectives. Data were collected through questionnaires and interviews with program instructors and fourth-year student teachers who experienced the curriculum introduced by the Higher Education Council in 2006-2007. Findings indicate that while both groups share similar views on certain program components, teachers perceive a lack of emphasis on developing linguistic competence, whereas student teachers highlight the need for stronger pedagogic training. The results underscore the importance of systematic program evaluation in teacher education and suggest targeted enhancements to better balance linguistic and pedagogic elements, contributing to ongoing professionalization in English language teaching.

title: From telecollaboration to virtual exchange: state-of-the‑art and the role of UNICollaboration in moving forward
abstract: Telecollaboration, or ‘virtual exchange’, are terms used to refer to the engagement of groups of learners in online intercultural interactions and collaboration projects with partners from other cultural contexts or geographical locations as an integrated part of their educational programmes. In recent years, approaches to virtual exchange have evolved in different contexts and different areas of education, and these approaches have had, at times, very diverse organisational structures and pedagogical objectives.
