This article provides an overview of the different models and approaches to virtual exchange which are currently being used in higher education contexts. It also provides a short historical review of the major developments and trends in virtual exchange to date and describes the origins of the UNICollaboration organisation and the rationale behind this journal.

title: From telecollaboration to virtual exchange: state-of-the‑art and the role of UNICollaboration in moving forward
abstract: This article examines the evolution of telecollaboration, now increasingly termed virtual exchange, as a pedagogically structured approach to online intercultural interaction and collaboration in education. It provides a comprehensive overview of the diverse models and terminologies that have emerged across disciplines, highlighting both the adaptability and challenges resulting from this heterogeneity. The paper traces the historical development of virtual exchange, analyzes key trends and barriers to broader implementation, and discusses the need for unified terminology to facilitate understanding and dissemination among educators and policymakers. The role of the UNICollaboration organization is explored as a cross-disciplinary platform aimed at consolidating research, fostering collaboration, and advancing the field of virtual exchange in higher education. The article concludes by emphasizing the importance of interdisciplinary approaches and coordinated efforts to address ongoing challenges and maximize the educational benefits of virtual exchange initiatives.

title: Nursing students’ experiences of a pedagogical transition from campus learning to distance learning using digital tools
abstract: The use of distance education using digital tools in higher education has increased over the last decade, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic. Therefore, this study aimed to describe and evaluate nursing students’ experiences of the pedagogical transition from traditional campus based learning to distance learning using digital tools. Methods The nursing course Symptom and signs of illness underwent a transition from campus based education to distance learning using digital tools because of the COVID-19 pandemic. This pedagogical transition in teaching was evaluated using both quantitative and qualitative data analysis. Focus group interviews ( n = 9) were analysed using qualitative content analysis to explore students’ experiences of the pedagogical transition and to construct a web-based questionnaire. The questionnaire comprised 14 items, including two open-ended questions. The questionnaire was delivered to all course participants and responses were obtained from 96 of 132 students (73%). Questionnaire data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and comments from the open-ended questions were used as quotes to highlight the quantitative data. Results The analysis of the focus group interviews extracted three main dimensions: didactic aspects of digital teaching , study environment , and students’ own resources. Social interaction was an overall theme included in all three dimensions. Data from the questionnaire showed that a majority of students preferred campus based education and experienced deterioration in all investigated dimensions after the pedagogical transition. However, approximately one-third of the students appeared to prefer distance learning using digital tools. Conclusions The main finding was that the pedagogical transition to distance education reduced the possibility for students’ social interactions in their learning process. This negatively affected several aspects of their experience of distance learning using digital tools, such as reduced motivation. However, the heterogeneity in the responses suggested that a blended learning approach may offer pedagogical benefits while maintaining an advantageous level of social interaction.

title: Nursing students’ experiences of a pedagogical transition from campus learning to distance learning using digital tools
abstract: This study explores nursing students’ experiences during the rapid pedagogical transition from traditional campus-based learning to distance learning using digital tools, prompted by the COVID-19 pandemic. Employing a mixed-methods approach, researchers conducted focus group interviews to identify key themes and developed a web-based questionnaire completed by 96 out of 132 students. Qualitative analysis revealed three main dimensions affecting students’ experiences: didactic aspects of digital teaching, the study environment, and students’ personal resources, with social interaction emerging as a central theme across all dimensions. Quantitative findings indicated that most students preferred campus-based education and perceived a decline in motivation and learning quality following the transition to distance learning, largely due to reduced opportunities for social interaction. Nevertheless, approximately one-third of students favored distance learning with digital tools. The study concludes that diminished social interaction negatively impacted the overall learning experience but suggests that a blended learning approach could balance pedagogical effectiveness with the benefits of interpersonal engagement in nursing education.

title: Open education and critical pedagogy
abstract: This paper argues for a revaluation of the potential of open education to support more critical forms of pedagogy. Section 1 examines contemporary discourses around open education, offering a commentary on the perception of openness as both a disruptive force in education, and a potential solution to contemporary challenges. Section 2 examines the implications of the lack of consensus around what it means to be open, focusing on the example of commercial and proprietary claims to openness commonly known as ‘openwashing’. Section 3 uses Raymond's influential essay on open source software ‘The Cathedral and the Bazaar’ as a framework for thinking through these issues, and about alternative power structures in open education. In Section 4, an explicit link is drawn between more equal and democratic power structures and the possibility for developing pedagogies which are critical and reflexive, providing examples which show how certain interpretations of openness can raise opportunities to support critical approaches to pedagogy.

title: Open education and critical pedagogy
abstract: This paper critically examines the intersection of open education and critical pedagogy, arguing that open educational practices and resources have significant but under-theorized potential to foster more democratic, reflexive, and critical forms of learning. Through discourse analysis of contemporary narratives around openness—particularly the rise of MOOCs and OER—the paper highlights how open education is often framed as a disruptive force capable of addressing crises in traditional educational models. However, it also interrogates the ambiguity and contested meanings of “openness,” drawing attention to practices such as “openwashing” where commercial interests co-opt the rhetoric of openness without enacting its transformative possibilities. Using Raymond’s “The Cathedral and the Bazaar” as a conceptual lens, the paper explores alternative power structures within open education and considers how these may support or hinder critical pedagogical aims. Ultimately, it contends that genuine openness—grounded in transparency, collaboration, and equitable participation—can create conditions for critical pedagogy by challenging dominant power relations and enabling learners to engage deeply with questions of knowledge, justice, and social transformation.

title: Participatory technologies, pedagogy 2.0 and information literacy
abstract: This paper seeks to explore the impact participatory technologies have had on education and the information environment in which students operate. It seeks to define a pedagogical approach that will capitalize on the benefits of participatory technologies in the classroom and applies this “pedagogy 2.0” to information literacy instruction.Design/methodology/approach – A thorough literature review was conducted on the use of participatory technologies in education as well as theories related to collaborative learning. This review formed the basis of the proposed pedagogy 2.0 model.Findings – Web 2.0 and the growth in use of participatory technologies has had a tremendous impact on the information environment. Instructors seeking to take advantage of participatory technologies in the classroom should also consider altering the classroom learning environment to one that embraces social constructivist and connectivist pedagogies. Changes in the information environment also require a corresponding sh...

title: Participatory technologies, pedagogy 2.0 and information literacy
abstract: This paper examines the transformative impact of participatory technologies and Web 2.0 on education and the information landscape, focusing on their implications for information literacy instruction. Through a comprehensive literature review, the study explores how participatory technologies have shifted the roles of learners and instructors, enabling students to become both consumers and producers of information while challenging traditional notions of authority and expertise. The paper proposes a “pedagogy 2.0” model grounded in social constructivist and connectivist theories, advocating for instructional approaches that leverage collaborative learning and reflective engagement. It argues that these pedagogical shifts are essential for making information literacy instruction relevant and effective in an environment characterized by information abundance, rapid change, and evolving credibility standards. The article bridges educational research on participatory pedagogies with library science literature, offering practical strategies for educators to enhance student learning and adapt information literacy teaching to the realities of the contemporary digital environment.

title: Pedagogic partnership in higher education: encountering emotion in learning and enhancing student wellbeing
abstract: Despite emotion being recognized as fundamental to learning, the affective aspects of learning have often been side-lined in higher education. In the context of rising student wellbeing challenges, exploring ways of supporting students and their emotions in learning is increasingly significant. Pedagogic partnerships have the potential to help students to recognize and work with their emotions in their learning in a positive manner. As such, pedagogic partnerships offer opportunities to promote resilience and enhance student wellbeing. In this paper, we develop partnership research in three ways by: 1) considering the ways in which pedagogic partnership may support students to encounter emotions and empower them to develop resilience, leading to positive wellbeing; 2) exploring how this process might be achieved in the disciplinary context of geography; and 3) developing an evidence-based model to summarize the potential effect of pedagogic partnership in enhancing student wellbeing. We draw upon two case studies of student-faculty and student-student pedagogic partnership within geography curricula in order to evidence that emotional awareness in learning comes through the joys and struggles of working in partnership. We argue that pedagogic partnership may be developed to support the wellbeing of modern-day higher education communities.
venue: Journal of Geography in Higher Education

title: Pedagogic partnership in higher education: encountering emotion in learning and enhancing student wellbeing
abstract: This paper explores the role of pedagogic partnership in higher education as a means to engage with student emotion in learning and enhance student wellbeing. Recognizing that affective dimensions are often overlooked despite their fundamental importance, the authors examine how collaborative partnerships between students and faculty, as well as among students, can foster emotional awareness, resilience, and positive wellbeing outcomes. Drawing on two case studies within geography curricula, the research demonstrates that encountering and working through emotions in partnership settings supports transformative learning and academic resilience. The paper further develops an evidence-based model illustrating the mechanisms by which pedagogic partnership can enhance wellbeing, and offers practical guidance for faculty to navigate the emotional aspects of teaching. The findings highlight the need to integrate affective and cognitive domains in higher education, positioning pedagogic partnership as a key strategy for supporting student wellbeing in contemporary academic environments.
venue: Journal of Geography in Higher Education

title: Personalisation in educational technology: the absence of underlying pedagogies
abstract: Personalization is one of the recurring themes in education and has occupied a large amount of specialised literature, since its appearance in the 1960s. A systematic exploration of the literature of the last 55 years (1960–2015) is presented and is intended to analyse which educational perspective underlies the customized environments or experiences proposed in the educational technology that is addressed in the literature. It is important to understand that this analysis is a very relevant challenge, if we want to understand what pedagogical approaches have been continuously developed and how and why we should consider their future. The results show a complete centralisation of experiences in technological developments, the majority of them focussed in Higher Education, as well as a lack of an explicit pedagogical perspective in the experiences analysed, especially those with greater impact. It also shows a shortage of in-house pedagogical material – developed in the light of this research, that evolves and makes an impact on the educational landscape.
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education

title: Personalisation in educational technology: the absence of underlying pedagogies
abstract: This study systematically reviews 55 years of literature on personalisation in educational technology to examine the extent to which pedagogical perspectives underpin technology-enhanced adaptive learning environments, particularly in higher education. The analysis reveals that while technological innovation and the promise of personalised learning have been persistent themes, there is a striking absence of explicit pedagogical frameworks guiding these developments. Most implementations focus on technological capabilities rather than educational theory, resulting in a lack of coherent epistemological and psychological foundations. The findings highlight a critical gap between the rhetoric of personalisation and its practical realisation, with few examples of didactic material or instructional design grounded in robust pedagogical models. The paper calls for a reorientation towards integrating educational theory into the design and evaluation of personalised learning technologies to ensure meaningful and transformative learning experiences.
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education

title: The effect of games and simulations on higher education: a systematic literature review
abstract: The focus of higher education institutions is the preparation of future professionals. To achieve this aim, innovative teaching methods are often deployed, including games and simulations, which form the subject of this paper. As the field of digital games and simulations is ever maturing, this paper attempts to systematically review the literature relevant to games and simulation pedagogy in higher education. Two researchers collaborate to apply a qualitative method, coding and synthesizing the results using multiple criteria. The main objective is to study the impact of games and simulations with regard to achieving specific learning objectives. On balance, results indicate that games and/or simulations have a positive impact on learning goals. The researchers identify three learning outcomes when integrating games into the learning process: cognitive, behavioural, and affective. As a final step, the authors consolidate evidence for the benefit of academics and practitioners in higher education interested in the efficient use of games and simulations for pedagogical purposes. Such evidence also provides potential options and pathways for future research.
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education

title: The effect of games and simulations on higher education: a systematic literature review
abstract: This systematic literature review investigates the impact of games and simulations on higher education, aiming to synthesize existing research across a broad spectrum of academic disciplines. By analyzing qualitative data from multiple studies, the review identifies how games and simulations contribute to achieving cognitive, behavioral, and affective learning outcomes. The findings indicate that these interactive tools generally have a positive effect on student engagement, motivation, and performance, though their effectiveness varies depending on implementation and context. The review highlights the lack of standardized frameworks and clear policy guidelines for integrating games and simulations into curricula, emphasizing the need for educators to make informed decisions based on pedagogical goals. The study concludes by offering evidence-based recommendations for academics and practitioners seeking to leverage games and simulations in higher education and outlines directions for future research to address existing gaps in practice and policy.
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education

title: The Past, Present, and Future of Media Literacy Education
abstract: Media literacy education in the United States is actively focused on the instructional methods and pedagogy of media literacy, integrating theoretical and critical frameworks rising from constructivist learning theory, media studies and cultural studies scholarship. This work has arisen from a legacy of media and technology use in education throughout the 20th century and the emergence of cross-disciplinary work at the intersections of scholarly work in media studies and education. Reflecting the emergence of a common ground for the field, the Core Principles of Media Literacy Education in the United States was created by a team of scholars and practitioners in 2007. This work reconciles the “protectionist” and “empowerment” wings of the media literacy education community and attempts to counter various misunderstandings among non-specialists. Two issues are identified for their potential to impact the future of the field: (1) media literacy’s relationship to the integration of educational technology into the K-12 curriculum and (2) the relationship between media literacy education and the humanities, arts, and sciences.

title: The Past, Present, and Future of Media Literacy Education
abstract: This paper examines the evolution of media literacy education in the United States, tracing its historical roots from early 20th-century visual education movements to its current status as a cross-disciplinary field integrating constructivist learning theory, media studies, and cultural studies. The authors highlight the development of core principles that reconcile protectionist and empowerment approaches, reflecting a maturing consensus among scholars and practitioners. The analysis addresses persistent challenges, such as the fragmentation of the field and tensions between educational and commercial interests. Looking forward, the paper identifies two critical issues shaping the future of media literacy education: its relationship with educational technology integration in K-12 curricula and its connections to the humanities, arts, and sciences. By situating media literacy as both a critical citizenship practice and a transcurricular endeavor, the paper underscores its ongoing relevance in fostering communication, creativity, collaboration, and critical thinking skills in response to evolving media landscapes.

title: The Role of Teachers in Task-Based Language Education
abstract: Both in the research literature on tasks and second language learning and in the pedagogical literature on task-based language teaching (TBLT), the role of the teacher has received scant attention. In this article, the role of the teacher in TBLT is approached from three perspectives: (a) the teacher as mediator of the students’ language development, contributing to the effectiveness of TBLT as a pedagogical approach to second language education; (b) the teacher as a key figure in the implementation of TBLT, and thus as a change agent in the innovation of second language education; and (c) the teacher as researcher, and thus as an active contributor to the development and further refinement of TBLT as a researched pedagogy.

title: The Role of Teachers in Task-Based Language Education
abstract: This article critically examines the often-overlooked role of teachers in task-based language teaching (TBLT), arguing that teachers are central to the effectiveness, implementation, and ongoing development of TBLT. Drawing on empirical research and pedagogical literature, the paper explores three key perspectives: teachers as mediators of students’ language development, as change agents in the adoption and adaptation of TBLT, and as researchers contributing to its refinement. The analysis highlights the limitations of viewing TBLT as solely learner-centered and emphasizes the necessity of teacher involvement for overcoming learning obstacles, providing scaffolding, and ensuring meaningful engagement with tasks. The article also reviews frameworks describing effective teacher behaviors—such as the “7 C’s”—and discusses how these can enhance student learning outcomes within TBLT. Finally, it underscores the importance of involving teachers in classroom-based research to bridge gaps between theory and practice, ultimately advocating for a more nuanced understanding of teachers’ multifaceted roles in task-based language education.

title: ‘You have to find your slant, your groove:’ one physical education teacher's efforts to employ transformative pedagogy
abstract: Teaching for social good and inequity has been presented as needed in sport pedagogy research. However, very little is known how transformative pedagogical practices that teach for social good are implemented and sustained at the elementary level. Purpose: This digital ethnographic study sought to describe one elementary school physical education (PE) teacher's attempt to employ transformative pedagogy (TP). Method: Cochran-Smith's [1998. “Teaching for Social Change: Toward a Grounded Theory of Teacher Education.” In The International Handbook of Educational Change, edited by A. Hargreaves, A. Lieberman, M. Fullan, and D. Hopkins, 916–952. Netherlands: Kluwer Academic Publishers, 2004. Walking the Road: Race, Diversity, and Social Justice in Teacher Education. New York: Teachers College Press] pedagogical principles for social justice education (SJE) drove our data collection and analysis. Seven qualitative methods were employed to collect data about Harry's pedagogies, organizational structures, and the content he taught. These were formal and informal interviews, conversations, short films, document collection, social media accounts, and an electronic journal. Data were analyzed using both inductive and deductive methods [Patton 2015. Qualitative Research and Evaluation Methods. 4th ed. Thousand Oaks: Sage]. Findings: Harry's TP and the factors that facilitated and limited his practice were uncovered within five main themes: (a) creating communities of learners through restorative practice principles, (b) building on what students bring to school with them for a democratic curriculum, (c) teaching skills, bridging gaps, and the affective component, (d), working with communities in-between social justice illiteracy, and (e) utilizing diverse forms of assessment. Conclusion: We confirmed that there is no best way to teach social justice through PE and that TP must be individual to the teacher. In addition, this study highlighted methods and pedagogies by which teachers could engage in TP. Finally, the study's findings implied how teacher educators might go about working with both preservice and inservice PE teachers with the goal that they focus on facilitating social justice through their pedagogical approach.

title: ‘You have to find your slant, your groove:’ one physical education teacher's efforts to employ transformative pedagogy
abstract: This digital ethnographic study explores the efforts of an elementary school physical education teacher, Harry, to implement transformative pedagogy (TP) aimed at promoting social justice within his teaching practice. Guided by Cochran-Smith’s pedagogical principles for social justice education, the research employed seven qualitative methods—including interviews, observations, document analysis, and digital artifacts—to examine Harry’s pedagogical approaches, curricular content, and organizational structures. The findings reveal five central themes: fostering communities of learners through restorative practices; leveraging students’ backgrounds for a democratic curriculum; integrating skill development with affective learning; navigating challenges related to social justice literacy; and employing diverse assessment strategies. The study highlights both the facilitators and barriers Harry encountered in enacting TP, emphasizing that transformative approaches must be individualized and context-specific rather than prescriptive. Implications are discussed for teacher educators seeking to support both preservice and inservice physical education teachers in adopting pedagogies that foreground equity and social justice.

title: An efficient recombination system for chromosome engineering in Escherichia coli.
abstract: A recombination system has been developed for efficient chromosome engineering in Escherichia coli by using electroporated linear DNA. A defective lambda prophage supplies functions that protect and recombine an electroporated linear DNA substrate in the bacterial cell. The use of recombination eliminates the requirement for standard cloning as all novel joints are engineered by chemical synthesis in vitro and the linear DNA is efficiently recombined into place in vivo. The technology and manipulations required are simple and straightforward. A temperature-dependent repressor tightly controls prophage expression, and, thus, recombination functions can be transiently supplied by shifting cultures to 42 degrees C for 15 min. The efficient prophage recombination system does not require host RecA function and depends primarily on Exo, Beta, and Gam functions expressed from the defective lambda prophage. The defective prophage can be moved to other strains and can be easily removed from any strain. Gene disruptions and modifications of both the bacterial chromosome and bacterial plasmids are possible. This system will be especially useful for the engineering of large bacterial plasmids such as those from bacterial artificial chromosome libraries.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: An efficient recombination system for chromosome engineering in Escherichia coli.
abstract: We describe the development of an efficient recombination system for chromosome engineering in Escherichia coli that utilizes a defective lambda prophage to supply Exo, Beta, and Gam functions, enabling the protection and recombination of electroporated linear DNA substrates. This system is tightly regulated by a temperature-sensitive repressor, allowing transient induction of recombination functions by a short heat shock. Unlike traditional cloning methods, this approach eliminates the need for restriction enzymes and ligation by engineering novel DNA junctions in vitro and facilitating their direct integration in vivo using short homology arms as brief as 30–50 base pairs. The recombination process is independent of host RecA function and is applicable to both chromosomal and plasmid modifications, including large constructs such as bacterial artificial chromosomes. The defective prophage can be easily transferred to or removed from various E. coli strains, providing flexibility for diverse genetic manipulations. This system streamlines genetic engineering in E. coli, offering a rapid, simple, and versatile tool for constructing targeted genomic alterations and advancing recombinant DNA technologies.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: Engineering and the Problem of Moral Overload
abstract: When thinking about ethics, technology is often only mentioned as the source of our problems, not as a potential solution to our moral dilemmas. When thinking about technology, ethics is often only mentioned as a constraint on developments, not as a source and spring of innovation. In this paper, we argue that ethics can be the source of technological development rather than just a constraint and technological progress can create moral progress rather than just moral problems. We show this by an analysis of how technology can contribute to the solution of so-called moral overload or moral dilemmas. Such dilemmas typically create a moral residue that is the basis of a second-order principle that tells us to reshape the world so that we can meet all our moral obligations. We can do so, among other things, through guided technological innovation.

title: Engineering and the Problem of Moral Overload
abstract: This paper challenges the conventional view that technology is primarily a source of ethical problems and that ethics merely constrains technological development. Instead, it argues that ethical considerations can drive technological innovation and that engineering can be a means to resolve moral dilemmas, particularly those arising from moral overload—situations where conflicting obligations cannot all be fulfilled. The authors analyze the structure of moral overload and moral dilemmas, highlighting the concept of moral residue, which motivates efforts to reshape the world so that all value commitments can be met. They contend that guided technological innovation can expand the set of feasible options, thereby reducing or eliminating moral overload and its associated psychological burdens. By framing engineering as a proactive force for moral progress, the paper emphasizes the responsibility of engineers not only to navigate existing ethical conflicts but also to prevent morally dilemmatic situations through creative technical solutions. This perspective positions engineering as integral to both addressing and preempting ethical challenges, illustrating how technological progress can contribute directly to moral advancement.

title: Engineering BioBrick vectors from BioBrick parts
abstract: The underlying goal of synthetic biology is to make the process of engineering biological systems easier. Recent work has focused on defining and developing standard biological parts. The technical standard that has gained the most traction in the synthetic biology community is the BioBrick standard for physical composition of genetic parts. Parts that conform to the BioBrick assembly standard are BioBrick standard biological parts. To date, over 2,000 BioBrick parts have been contributed to, and are available from, the Registry of Standard Biological Parts.ResultsHere we extended the same advantages of BioBrick standard biological parts to the plasmid-based vectors that are used to provide and propagate BioBrick parts. We developed a process for engineering BioBrick vectors from BioBrick parts. We designed a new set of BioBrick parts that encode many useful vector functions. We combined the new parts to make a BioBrick base vector that facilitates BioBrick vector construction. We demonstrated the utility of the process by constructing seven new BioBrick vectors. We also successfully used the resulting vectors to assemble and propagate other BioBrick standard biological parts.ConclusionWe extended the principles of part reuse and standardization to BioBrick vectors. As a result, myriad new BioBrick vectors can be readily produced from all existing and newly designed BioBrick parts. We invite the synthetic biology community to (1) use the process to make and share new BioBrick vectors; (2) expand the current collection of BioBrick vector parts; and (3) characterize and improve the available collection of BioBrick vector parts.

title: Engineering BioBrick vectors from BioBrick parts
abstract: Synthetic biology seeks to streamline the engineering of biological systems through standardized biological parts, with the BioBrick standard emerging as a widely adopted framework for genetic part assembly. However, plasmid vectors used to propagate BioBrick parts have remained ad hoc and non-standardized, limiting modularity and reuse. In this work, we present a methodology for engineering BioBrick vectors from BioBrick parts by designing a new set of standardized vector components and introducing a BioBrick base vector that facilitates rapid construction of diverse vectors. Using this approach, we assembled seven new BioBrick vectors and demonstrated their effectiveness in propagating and assembling BioBrick standard biological parts. Our process extends the principles of standardization and part reuse to vector design, enabling the synthetic biology community to efficiently generate, share, and improve an expanded repertoire of BioBrick-compatible vectors. This advancement supports more robust, scalable, and collaborative genetic engineering efforts.

title: Engineering complex tissues.
abstract: This article summarizes the views expressed at the third session of the workshop 'Tissue Engineering--The Next Generation,' which was devoted to the engineering of complex tissue structures. Antonios Mikos described the engineering of complex oral and craniofacial tissues as a 'guided interplay' between biomaterial scaffolds, growth factors, and local cell populations toward the restoration of the original architecture and function of complex tissues. Susan Herring, reviewing osteogenesis and vasculogenesis, explained that the vascular arrangement precedes and dictates the architecture of the new bone, and proposed that engineering of osseous tissues might benefit from preconstruction of an appropriate vasculature. Jennifer Elisseeff explored the formation of complex tissue structures based on the example of stratified cartilage engineered using stem cells and hydrogels. Helen Lu discussed engineering of tissue interfaces, a problem critical for biological fixation of tendons and ligaments, and the development of a new generation of fixation devices. Rita Kandel discussed the challenges related to the re-creation of the cartilage-bone interface, in the context of tissue engineered joint repair. Frederick Schoen emphasized, in the context of heart valve engineering, the need for including the requirements derived from 'adult biology' of tissue remodeling and establishing reliable early predictors of success or failure of tissue engineered implants. Mehmet Toner presented a review of biopreservation techniques and stressed that a new breakthrough in this field may be necessary to meet all the needs of tissue engineering. David Mooney described systems providing temporal and spatial regulation of growth factor availability, which may find utility in virtually all tissue engineering and regeneration applications, including directed in vitro and in vivo vascularization of tissues. Anthony Atala offered a clinician's perspective for functional tissue regeneration, and discussed new biomaterials that can be used to develop new regenerative technologies.

title: Engineering complex tissues.
abstract: Engineering complex tissues represents a significant challenge in tissue engineering, requiring the integration of biomaterial scaffolds, growth factors, and cell populations to restore native architecture and function. This paper summarizes key perspectives from leading researchers on strategies for regenerating complex oral, craniofacial, osseous, cartilage, and cardiovascular tissues. Advances discussed include the design of injectable scaffolds with appropriate mechanical and degradation properties, the importance of pre-vascularization for bone engineering, stem cell-based approaches for stratified cartilage, and novel solutions for tissue interfaces critical to tendon, ligament, and joint repair. The need for biomaterials that support selective cell adhesion and controlled growth factor delivery is emphasized, as is the development of biopreservation techniques to extend the viability of engineered grafts. Clinical considerations highlight the translation of these technologies into functional regenerative therapies. The article concludes that overcoming challenges related to vascularization, interface engineering, scaffold design, and preservation will be essential for the next generation of tissue engineering solutions targeting complex tissue structures.

title: Engineering optimisation by cuckoo search
abstract: A new metaheuristic optimisation algorithm, called Cuckoo Search (CS), was developed recently by Yang and Deb (2009). This paper presents a more extensive comparison study using some standard test functions and newly designed stochastic test functions. We then apply the CS algorithm to solve engineering design optimisation problems, including the design of springs and welded beam structures. The optimal solutions obtained by CS are far better than the best solutions obtained by an efficient particle swarm optimiser. We will discuss the unique search features used in CS and the implications for further research.
venue: Int. J. Math. Model. Numer. Optimisation

title: Engineering optimisation by cuckoo search
abstract: This paper introduces the Cuckoo Search (CS) algorithm, a novel metaheuristic inspired by the brood parasitism of certain cuckoo species and the efficiency of Lévy flight-based random walks. The CS algorithm is designed to address highly nonlinear and multimodal engineering optimisation problems that are challenging for traditional local search methods. The study provides an in-depth comparison of CS with established algorithms such as particle swarm optimisation (PSO), using both standard and newly developed stochastic test functions. Results demonstrate that CS consistently achieves superior optimal solutions, particularly in complex engineering design tasks like spring and welded beam structure optimisation. The paper also discusses the unique intensification and diversification mechanisms of CS, highlighting its robustness, parameter insensitivity, and potential for further research in global optimisation applications.
venue: Int. J. Math. Model. Numer. Optimisation

title: Genetic Engineering
abstract: The application of genetic-based biotechnology to modify the characteristics of an organism by cutting, splicing, and transferring genetic materials, especially DNA, from one or more species of organism.

title: Genetic Engineering
abstract: Genetic engineering refers to the deliberate modification of an organism’s genetic material using biotechnological techniques, particularly the cutting, splicing, and transfer of DNA between species. This process enables the introduction of new traits or the enhancement of existing characteristics in a wide range of organisms, including plants, animals, and microorganisms. The field has significant implications for medicine, agriculture, and industry by enabling the development of genetically modified organisms with desirable properties such as disease resistance, improved yield, or novel functionalities. As a rapidly evolving area of research, genetic engineering continues to raise important ethical, regulatory, and safety considerations that are central to its application and public acceptance.

title: Modern control engineering
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive overview of modern control engineering, covering fundamental concepts, mathematical modeling, and analytical techniques essential for the design and analysis of control systems. It introduces control system types, contrasts open-loop and closed-loop configurations, and explores Laplace transform methods for solving linear differential equations. The work details the modeling of dynamic systems—including mechanical, electrical, fluid, and thermal domains—using both transfer function and state-space approaches, with practical applications demonstrated through MATLAB. Key topics include transient and steady-state response analyses, stability criteria such as Routh's and Nyquist's methods, root-locus and frequency-response techniques, and compensation strategies for system performance enhancement. Advanced subjects address PID controller design, tuning methodologies, two-degrees-of-freedom control systems, and optimal state-space control including pole placement and observer design. The paper emphasizes computational tools for analysis and synthesis, providing a foundational resource for students and practitioners in modern automatic control engineering.

title: Polymeric nanofibers in tissue engineering.
abstract: Polymeric nanofibers can be produced using methods such as electrospinning, phase separation, and self-assembly, and the fiber composition, diameter, alignment, degradation, and mechanical properties can be tailored to the intended application. Nanofibers possess unique advantages for tissue engineering. The small diameter closely matches that of extracellular matrix fibers, and the relatively large surface area is beneficial for cell attachment and bioactive factor loading. This review will update the reader on the aspects of nanofiber fabrication and characterization important to tissue engineering, including control of porous structure, cell infiltration, and fiber degradation. Bioactive factor loading will be discussed with specific relevance to tissue engineering. Finally, applications of polymeric nanofibers in the fields of bone, cartilage, ligament and tendon, cardiovascular, and neural tissue engineering will be reviewed.

title: Polymeric nanofibers in tissue engineering.
abstract: Polymeric nanofibers have emerged as versatile scaffolds in tissue engineering due to their structural similarity to extracellular matrix components, high surface area for cell attachment, and capacity for bioactive factor delivery. This review examines the primary fabrication methods—electrospinning, phase separation, and self-assembly—highlighting how each technique influences fiber diameter, alignment, porosity, mechanical properties, and degradation profiles. The ability to tailor these characteristics enables the design of scaffolds optimized for specific tissue engineering applications. The review also discusses strategies for incorporating bioactive molecules into nanofibers to enhance cellular responses and tissue regeneration. Applications in bone, cartilage, ligament and tendon, cardiovascular, and neural tissue engineering are explored, demonstrating the broad utility of polymeric nanofibers. Overall, advances in nanofiber fabrication and functionalization continue to expand their potential as biomimetic scaffolds for regenerative medicine.

title: Preliminary Guidelines for Empirical Research in Software Engineering
abstract: Empirical software engineering research needs research guidelines to improve the research and reporting processes. We propose a preliminary set of research guidelines aimed at stimulating discussion among software researchers. They are based on a review of research guidelines developed for medical researchers and on our own experience in doing and reviewing software engineering research. The guidelines are intended to assist researchers, reviewers, and meta-analysts in designing, conducting, and evaluating empirical studies. Editorial boards of software engineering journals may wish to use our recommendations as a basis for developing guidelines for reviewers and for framing policies for dealing with the design, data collection, and analysis and reporting of empirical studies.

title: Preliminary Guidelines for Empirical Research in Software Engineering
abstract: Empirical research in software engineering often suffers from methodological and statistical shortcomings, limiting the reliability and impact of its findings. This paper proposes a preliminary set of guidelines for conducting and reporting empirical studies in software engineering, drawing on established practices from medical research and the authors’ extensive experience. The guidelines are designed to assist researchers, reviewers, and meta-analysts in improving study design, data collection, analysis, and reporting. By highlighting common pitfalls and adapting quality criteria from other disciplines, the paper aims to stimulate discussion within the software engineering community and encourage the adoption of standards that enhance research quality. The authors advocate for broader debate and refinement of these guidelines to support the development of specialized recommendations for different types of empirical studies.

title: Recent advances in 3D printing of biomaterials
abstract: 3D Printing promises to produce complex biomedical devices according to computer design using patient-specific anatomical data. Since its initial use as pre-surgical visualization models and tooling molds, 3D Printing has slowly evolved to create one-of-a-kind devices, implants, scaffolds for tissue engineering, diagnostic platforms, and drug delivery systems. Fueled by the recent explosion in public interest and access to affordable printers, there is renewed interest to combine stem cells with custom 3D scaffolds for personalized regenerative medicine. Before 3D Printing can be used routinely for the regeneration of complex tissues (e.g. bone, cartilage, muscles, vessels, nerves in the craniomaxillofacial complex), and complex organs with intricate 3D microarchitecture (e.g. liver, lymphoid organs), several technological limitations must be addressed. In this review, the major materials and technology advances within the last five years for each of the common 3D Printing technologies (Three Dimensional Printing, Fused Deposition Modeling, Selective Laser Sintering, Stereolithography, and 3D Plotting/Direct-Write/Bioprinting) are described. Examples are highlighted to illustrate progress of each technology in tissue engineering, and key limitations are identified to motivate future research and advance this fascinating field of advanced manufacturing.

title: Recent advances in 3D printing of biomaterials
abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) printing has emerged as a transformative technology in the fabrication of complex biomedical devices, enabling the creation of patient-specific implants, tissue engineering scaffolds, diagnostic platforms, and drug delivery systems. This review examines recent advances in 3D printing of biomaterials, focusing on developments over the past five years across major solid freeform fabrication (SFF) technologies including Three Dimensional Printing, Fused Deposition Modeling, Selective Laser Sintering, Stereolithography, and 3D Plotting/Direct-Write/Bioprinting. The integration of computer-aided design with advanced imaging techniques has facilitated precise control over macro-, micro-, and nano-architectures, allowing for customization based on individual anatomical data. Despite significant progress in machine resolution and accessibility—driven by both industrial and consumer-grade printers—challenges remain in expanding the range of printable biomaterials and optimizing processes for clinical applications. This review highlights key technological innovations, showcases representative examples in tissue engineering, and discusses persistent limitations that must be addressed to fully realize the potential of 3D printing in regenerative medicine and complex organ reconstruction.

title: Sampling in software engineering research: a critical review and guidelines
abstract: Representative sampling appears rare in empirical software engineering research. Not all studies need representative samples, but a general lack of representative sampling undermines a scientific field. This article therefore reports a critical review of the state of sampling in recent, high-quality software engineering research. The key findings are: (1) random sampling is rare; (2) sophisticated sampling strategies are very rare; (3) sampling, representativeness and randomness often appear misunderstood. These findings suggest that software engineering research has a generalizability crisis. To address these problems, this paper synthesizes existing knowledge of sampling into a succinct primer and proposes extensive guidelines for improving the conduct, presentation and evaluation of sampling in software engineering research. It is further recommended that while researchers should strive for more representative samples, disparaging non-probability sampling is generally capricious and particularly misguided for predominately qualitative research.

title: Sampling in software engineering research: a critical review and guidelines
abstract: This paper critically examines the state of sampling practices in empirical software engineering research, revealing that representative and random sampling are infrequently employed and often misunderstood, leading to concerns about the generalizability of research findings. Through a comprehensive review of recent high-quality studies, the authors identify a widespread reliance on convenience and non-probability sampling strategies, with limited use of more sophisticated or probabilistic methods. The paper synthesizes existing knowledge into an accessible primer on sampling concepts and techniques tailored to software engineering, highlighting the importance of appropriate sampling for both positivist and interpretivist research paradigms. Extensive guidelines are proposed to improve the design, reporting, and evaluation of sampling in future studies, emphasizing that while striving for representativeness is important, non-probability sampling remains valuable—especially in qualitative contexts—and should not be dismissed outright. The work aims to foster methodological rigor and consensus in the field by clarifying common misconceptions and offering practical recommendations for researchers.

title: Semiotic Engineering Methods for Scientific Research in HCI
abstract: Semiotic engineering was originally proposed as a semiotic approach to designing user interface languages. Over the years, with research done at the Department of Informatics of the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro, it evolved into a semiotic theory of human-computer interaction (HCI). It views HCI as computer-mediated communication between designers and users at interaction time. The system speaks for its designers in various types of conversations specified at design time. These conversations communicate the designers' understanding of who the users are, what they know the users want or need to do, in which preferred ways, and why. The designers' message to users includes even the interactive language in which users will have to communicate back with the system in order to achieve their specific goals. Hence, the process is, in fact, one of communication about communication, or metacommunication. Semiotic engineering has two methods to evaluate the quality of metacommunication in HCI: the semiotic inspection method (SIM) and the communicability evaluation method (CEM). Up to now, they have been mainly used and discussed in technical contexts, focusing on how to detect problems and how to improve the metacommunication of specific systems. In this book, Clarisse de Souza and Carla Leito discuss how SIM and CEM, which are both qualitative methods, can also be used in scientific contexts to generate new knowledge about HCI. The discussion goes into deep considerations about scientific methodology, calling the reader's attention to the essence of qualitative methods in research and the kinds of results they can produce. To illustrate their points, the authors present an extensive case study with a free open-source digital audio editor called Audacity. They show how the results obtained with a triangulation of SIM and CEM point at new research avenues not only for semiotic engineering and HCI but also for other areas of computer science such as software engineering and programming. Table of Contents: Introduction / Essence of Semiotic Engineering / Semiotic Engineering Methods / Case Study with Audacity / Lessons Learned with Semiotic Engineering Methods / The Near Future of Semiotic Engineering
venue: Semiotic Engineering Methods for Scientific Research in HCI

title: Semiotic Engineering Methods for Scientific Research in HCI
abstract: This paper presents semiotic engineering as a distinctive theoretical and methodological framework for scientific research in human–computer interaction (HCI), emphasizing its view of HCI as computer-mediated communication between designers and users. The authors detail the evolution of semiotic engineering from a focus on user interface language design to a comprehensive theory that models systems as proxies for designers, communicating their intentions, assumptions, and understanding of users through interface elements. Two qualitative methods—the Semiotic Inspection Method (SIM) and the Communicability Evaluation Method (CEM)—are described and positioned as tools not only for technical evaluation but also for generating new scientific knowledge about HCI. Through an extensive case study involving the Audacity audio editor, the paper demonstrates how triangulation of SIM and CEM yields insights into system communicability and opens new research avenues in HCI and related fields. The work underscores the value of qualitative approaches in advancing HCI theory and practice, advocating for a shift in perspective that foregrounds metacommunication between designers and users as central to interaction design.
venue: Semiotic Engineering Methods for Scientific Research in HCI

title: Service Systems Engineering
abstract: Service systems engineering (SSE) focuses on the systematic design and development of service systems. Guided by a value proposition, service systems enable value co-creation through a configuration of actors and resources (often including a service architecture, technology, information, and physical artifacts), therefore constituting complex socio-technical systems. IS research can play a leading role in understanding and developing service systems. SSE calls for research leading to actionable design theories, methods and approaches for systematically designing, developing and piloting service systems, based upon understanding the underlying principles of service systems. Three major challenges have been identified: engineering service architectures, engineering service systems interactions, and engineering resource mobilization, i.e. extending the access to and use of resources by means of IT. Researching SSE is challenging. Assessing the models, methods, or artifacts of SSE often requires embedded research within existing or even novel service systems. Consequently, approaches such as piloting IT-based innovations, design research or action research are the most promising for SSE research. As an integrative discipline, IS is in a unique position to spearhead the efforts in advancing the architecture, interaction, and resource base of service systems with evidence-based design.

title: Service Systems Engineering
abstract: Service systems engineering (SSE) emerges as a critical field for future information systems research, addressing the complex socio-technical nature of service systems that underpin value co-creation in contemporary society. This paper highlights the paradigm shift toward service logic, emphasizing collaboration and contextualization as central to value creation and underscoring the pivotal role of information systems in enabling these processes. SSE is positioned as a response to the limitations of traditional service engineering by advocating for evidence-based design knowledge that systematically addresses the architecture, interactions, and resource mobilization within service systems. The authors identify key research challenges, including engineering service architectures for novel value propositions, enhancing interactions among networked actors, and mobilizing diverse resources to support dynamic and multi-sided value creation. By leveraging the integrative capabilities of information systems research, SSE aims to develop actionable frameworks and methodologies for designing, developing, and piloting innovative service systems across various domains. The paper calls for trans-disciplinary efforts to advance the theoretical foundations and practical approaches necessary for engineering adaptable, collaborative, and context-sensitive service systems in an increasingly digitalized world.

title: Tissue engineering of articular cartilage with biomimetic zones.
abstract: Articular cartilage damage is a persistent and increasing problem with the aging population, and treatments to achieve biological repair or restoration remain a challenge. Cartilage tissue engineering approaches have been investigated for over 20 years, but have yet to achieve the consistency and effectiveness for widespread clinical use. One of the potential reasons for this is that the engineered tissues do not have or establish the normal zonal organization of cells and extracellular matrix that appears critical for normal tissue function. A number of approaches are being taken currently to engineer tissue that more closely mimics the organization of native articular cartilage. This review focuses on the zonal organization of native articular cartilage, strategies being used to develop such organization, the reorganization that occurs after culture or implantation, and future prospects for the tissue engineering of articular cartilage with biomimetic zones.

title: Tissue engineering of articular cartilage with biomimetic zones.
abstract: Articular cartilage damage presents significant clinical challenges due to the tissue’s limited self-repair capacity and the shortcomings of current treatments such as joint replacement. Traditional tissue engineering strategies have not achieved consistent clinical success, in part because engineered constructs often lack the complex zonal organization of native cartilage, which is critical for its mechanical and biological function. This review examines the hierarchical structure of articular cartilage, focusing on its distinct superficial, middle, and deep zones characterized by specific variations in extracellular matrix composition and cellular phenotype. It discusses current approaches to recapitulate these biomimetic zones in engineered tissues, including strategies to induce zonal organization during in vitro culture and the remodeling that occurs post-implantation. The review highlights advances in identifying zone-specific markers and materials, as well as the challenges that remain in replicating native tissue architecture and function. Future directions are proposed for developing tissue-engineered articular cartilage with biomimetic zonal organization to achieve durable, functional repair and restoration in clinical applications.

title: Acid rain and air pollution: 50 years of progress in environmental science and policy
abstract: Because of its serious large-scale effects on ecosystems and its transboundary nature, acid rain received for a few decades at the end of the last century wide scientific and public interest, leading to coordinated policy actions in Europe and North America. Through these actions, in particular those under the UNECE Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution, air emissions were substantially reduced, and ecosystem impacts decreased. Widespread scientific research, long-term monitoring, and integrated assessment modelling formed the basis for the policy agreements. In this paper, which is based on an international symposium organised to commemorate 50 years of successful integration of air pollution research and policy, we briefly describe the scientific findings that provided the foundation for the policy development. We also discuss important characteristics of the science–policy interactions, such as the critical loads concept and the large-scale ecosystem field studies. Finally, acid rain and air pollution are set in the context of future societal developments and needs, e.g. the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals. We also highlight the need to maintain and develop supporting scientific infrastructures.

title: Acid rain and air pollution: 50 years of progress in environmental science and policy
abstract: Over the past fifty years, acid rain has evolved from a largely unrecognized phenomenon to a central focus of international environmental science and policy. This review traces the historical development of acid rain research, beginning with early observations in Europe and North America, and highlights the pivotal role of scientific discoveries in driving policy responses such as the UNECE Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution. The integration of long-term monitoring, critical loads concepts, and integrated assessment modeling provided a robust foundation for international agreements that have led to significant reductions in emissions of sulphur dioxide and other pollutants, resulting in measurable ecosystem recovery. The paper examines key milestones in science-policy interactions, underscores the importance of sustained scientific infrastructure, and situates acid rain within broader environmental challenges including climate change and the UN Sustainable Development Goals. Lessons learned from five decades of coordinated action offer valuable insights for addressing current and future transboundary air pollution issues.

title: A procedure for evaluating environmental impact
abstract: Man cannot survive on this planet without utilizing its natural resources prudently. Every human action affects the world around us in some degree and the full effect is difficult to assess because of complex relations among living and nonliving things. Under the circumstances one can neither expect to restore the entire past nor preserve the entire present for future generations. However all can and should strive for proper balance between resource development and maintenance of pleasant surroundings. The Environmental Policy Act of 1969 and the reports on environmental assessment that i t requires are aimed at insuping such a balanced approach. To be effective we must provide a system for relating large numbers of actions and environmental factors and for placing value judgments on impacts which are difficult to quantify. A t my request the Geological Survey has developed an information matrix system that is described and modeled in this Circular. It is published with the thought that it will serve as a useful guide for environmental impact reporting and as a systematic reference. Those who share with us the desire to retain or improve the quality of our environment will recognize that this report is a sincere but still preliminary effort to fill an interim need. We hope that suggestions from others will improve this framework. ' This report contains a procedure that may assist in developing uniform environmental impact statements. The Department of the Interior and the Council on Environmental Quality will appreciate comments on the procedure here proposed. The heart of the system is a matrix which is general enough to be used as a reference checklist o r a reminder of the full range of actions and impacts on the environment that may relate to proposed actions. The marked matrix also serves as a n abstract of the text of the environmental assessment to enable the many reviewers of impact reports to determine quickly what are considered to be the significant impacts and their relative importance a s evaluated by the origina. tors of the impact report.
