title: A procedure for evaluating environmental impact
abstract: This paper presents a systematic procedure for evaluating the environmental impact of proposed actions, developed in response to the requirements of the Environmental Policy Act of 1969. The core of the method is a generalized matrix that serves as both a comprehensive checklist and an analytical tool for assessing the magnitude and importance of potential impacts across various environmental factors. The procedure guides users through a sequence of steps, including defining project objectives, analyzing technological alternatives, characterizing the existing environment, detailing proposed actions, and evaluating impacts for each alternative. Emphasis is placed on interdisciplinary collaboration, objective analysis of impact magnitude, and value-based judgments regarding significance. The approach facilitates transparent and consistent preparation of environmental impact statements and supports informed decision-making by providing a structured framework for comparing alternatives and justifying recommendations. This matrix-based system is intended as a practical interim guide for agencies and practitioners tasked with environmental assessments, pending further refinement through broader application and feedback.

title: Beamline 10.3.2 at ALS: a hard X-ray microprobe for environmental and materials sciences.
abstract: Beamline 10.3.2 at the ALS is a bend-magnet line designed mostly for work on environmental problems involving heavy-metal speciation and location. It offers a unique combination of X-ray fluorescence mapping, X-ray microspectroscopy and micro-X-ray diffraction. The optics allow the user to trade spot size for flux in a size range of 5-17 microm in an energy range of 3-17 keV. The focusing uses a Kirkpatrick-Baez mirror pair to image a variable-size virtual source onto the sample. Thus, the user can reduce the effective size of the source, thereby reducing the spot size on the sample, at the cost of flux. This decoupling from the actual source also allows for some independence from source motion. The X-ray fluorescence mapping is performed with a continuously scanning stage which avoids the time overhead incurred by step-and-repeat mapping schemes. The special features of this beamline are described, and some scientific results shown.

title: Beamline 10.3.2 at ALS: a hard X-ray microprobe for environmental and materials sciences.
abstract: Beamline 10.3.2 at the Advanced Light Source (ALS) is a hard X-ray microprobe specifically designed to address challenges in environmental and materials sciences, particularly for the spatially resolved analysis of heavy-metal speciation and distribution. The beamline integrates X-ray fluorescence (XRF) mapping, X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), and micro-X-ray diffraction (XRD) within a flexible optical system that allows users to trade spot size for flux in the 5–17 μm range across energies from 3 to 17 keV. A Kirkpatrick–Baez mirror pair images a variable-size virtual source onto the sample, enabling precise adjustment of spatial resolution and minimizing the impact of source motion. The system’s monochromatic beam and continuously scanning stage facilitate efficient, high-contrast XRF mapping, while integrated control and data acquisition systems streamline transitions between characterization modes. This combination of techniques provides complementary information on elemental distribution, chemical state, and crystalline structure, supporting advanced studies of heterogeneous natural and synthetic materials. Key features, operational specifications, and representative scientific results are presented to illustrate the beamline’s capabilities in addressing complex analytical problems in environmental geochemistry and materials research.

title: Between activism and science: Grassroots concepts for sustainability coined by Environmental Justice Organizations
abstract: In their own battles and strategy meetings since the early 1980s, EJOs (environmental justice organizations) and their networks have introduced several concepts to political ecology that have also been taken up by academics and policy makers. In this paper, we explain the contexts in which such notions have arisen, providing definitions of a wide array of concepts and slogans related to environmental inequities and sustainability, and explore the connections and relations between them. These concepts include: environmental justice, ecological debt, popular epidemiology, environmental racism, climate justice, environmentalism of the poor, water justice, biopiracy, food sovereignty, 'green deserts', 'peasant agriculture cools downs the Earth', land grabbing, Ogonization and Yasunization, resource caps, corporate accountability, ecocide, and indigenous territorial rights, among others. We examine how activists have coined these notions and built demands around them, and how academic research has in turn further applied them and supplied other related concepts, working in a mutually reinforcing way with EJOs. We argue that these processes and dynamics build an activist-led and co-produced social sustainability science, furthering both academic scholarship and activism on environmental justice. Keywords: Political ecology, environmental justice organizations, environmentalism of the poor, ecological debt, activist knowledge

title: Between activism and science: Grassroots concepts for sustainability coined by Environmental Justice Organizations
abstract: This paper examines the emergence and evolution of key sustainability concepts developed by Environmental Justice Organizations (EJOs) since the early 1980s, highlighting their dual role as both activists and contributors to political ecology. Drawing on collaborative research projects and case studies, the authors trace how EJOs have coined and popularized terms such as environmental justice, ecological debt, popular epidemiology, environmental racism, climate justice, food sovereignty, and others, which have subsequently influenced academic research and policy discourse. The analysis explores the contexts in which these grassroots concepts arose, their definitions, and the interconnections among them, demonstrating a dynamic process of mutual reinforcement between activism and scholarship. The paper argues that this iterative exchange has led to the co-production of a social science of sustainability rooted in activist knowledge, advancing both theoretical understanding and practical action for environmental justice.

title: Building optimism at the environmental science-policy-practice interface through the study of bright spots
abstract: Effectively translating scientific knowledge into policy and practice is essential for helping humanity navigate contemporary environmental challenges. The likelihood of achieving this can be increased through the study of bright spots—instances where science has successfully influenced policy and practice—and the sense of optimism that this can inspire.

title: Building optimism at the environmental science-policy-practice interface through the study of bright spots
abstract: Effectively bridging the gap between environmental science, policy, and practice is critical for addressing contemporary environmental challenges, yet efforts to integrate scientific knowledge into decision-making often focus on barriers and failures, perpetuating a narrative of pessimism. This paper argues for a paradigm shift towards studying 'bright spots'—instances where science has successfully influenced policy and practice—to foster optimism and inspire action among scientists and decision-makers. Drawing on examples from environmental management and fisheries, the authors demonstrate how documenting and analyzing these successes can reveal key principles, such as building trusted relationships, co-developing research questions, and maintaining ongoing stakeholder engagement. The cultivation of optimism, informed by lessons from psychology and organizational behavior, is shown to enhance individual resilience, team collaboration, creativity, and innovation—factors essential for overcoming entrenched institutional barriers and achieving sustainability goals. Ultimately, the systematic study of bright spots offers a constructive approach to strengthening the science-policy-practice interface and promoting evidence-informed environmental decision-making.

title: Challenges of unculturable bacteria: environmental perspectives
abstract: Environmental biotechnology offers several promising techniques for the rehabilitation of polluted environments. The modern industrialized world presents novel challenges to the environmental sciences, requiring a constant development and deepening of knowledge to enable the characterization of novel pollutants and a better understanding of the bioremediation strategies as well as their limiting factors. The success of bioremediation depends heavily on the survival and activities of indigenous microbial communities and their interaction with introduced microorganisms. The majority of natural microbiomes remain uncultivated; therefore, further investigations focusing on their intrinsic functions in ecosystems are needed. In this review, we aimed to provide (a) a comprehensive overview of the presence of viable but nonculturable bacteria and yet-to-be-cultivated cells in nature and their diverse awakening strategies in response to, among other factors, signalling extracellular metabolites (autoinducers, resuscitation promoting factors, and siderophores); (b) an outline of the trends in isolating unculturable bacteria; and (c) the potential applications of these hidden players in rehabilitation processes.
venue: Reviews in Environmental Science and Bio\/technology

title: Challenges of unculturable bacteria: environmental perspectives
abstract: Unculturable bacteria represent a significant challenge in environmental microbiology due to their vast diversity and the limitations of traditional culture-dependent techniques, which capture only a small fraction of microbial life. This review examines the prevalence and ecological roles of viable but nonculturable (VBNC) bacteria in natural environments, emphasizing their adaptive strategies for survival under adverse conditions and their potential for awakening in response to specific environmental signals. The paper discusses recent advances in culture-independent molecular methods, such as metagenomics and other omics technologies, which have expanded our understanding of unculturable microbial communities and their metabolic capabilities. Furthermore, it highlights the implications of unculturable bacteria for bioremediation, noting that the effectiveness of environmental rehabilitation often depends on the activity of these hidden microbial players. The review also addresses current trends in isolating previously uncultured bacteria and explores their potential applications in environmental biotechnology, particularly for pollutant degradation and ecosystem restoration. Overall, the paper underscores the need for continued research into the physiology, genetics, and ecological functions of unculturable bacteria to fully exploit their potential in sustainable environmental management.
venue: Reviews in Environmental Science and Bio\/technology

title: Completing the Link between Exposure Science and Toxicology for Improved Environmental Health Decision Making: The Aggregate Exposure Pathway Framework.
abstract: Driven by major scientific advances in analytical methods, biomonitoring, computation, and a newly articulated vision for a greater impact in public health, the field of exposure science is undergoing a rapid transition from a field of observation to a field of prediction. Deployment of an organizational and predictive framework for exposure science analogous to the 'systems approaches' used in the biological sciences is a necessary step in this evolution. Here we propose the aggregate exposure pathway (AEP) concept as the natural and complementary companion in the exposure sciences to the adverse outcome pathway (AOP) concept in the toxicological sciences. Aggregate exposure pathways offer an intuitive framework to organize exposure data within individual units of prediction common to the field, setting the stage for exposure forecasting. Looking farther ahead, we envision direct linkages between aggregate exposure pathways and adverse outcome pathways, completing the source to outcome continuum for more meaningful integration of exposure assessment and hazard identification. Together, the two frameworks form and inform a decision-making framework with the flexibility for risk-based, hazard-based, or exposure-based decision making.

title: Completing the Link between Exposure Science and Toxicology for Improved Environmental Health Decision Making: The Aggregate Exposure Pathway Framework.
abstract: The Aggregate Exposure Pathway (AEP) framework is proposed as an organizational and predictive structure to bridge exposure science and toxicology, analogous to the Adverse Outcome Pathway (AOP) framework in toxicology. Driven by advances in analytical methods, biomonitoring, and computational tools, exposure science is transitioning toward a predictive discipline capable of forecasting exposures and informing public health decisions. The AEP concept systematically organizes exposure data from source to internal target site, facilitating integration with AOPs and enabling a comprehensive source-to-outcome continuum. This linkage enhances the ability to assess risks, identify hazards, and inform regulatory decisions using risk-based, hazard-based, or exposure-based approaches. Adoption of the AEP framework is expected to improve the efficiency and impact of environmental health decision making by providing a structured means to connect exposure assessment with toxicological outcomes.

title: Emerging trends in geospatial artificial intelligence (geoAI): potential applications for environmental epidemiology
abstract: Geospatial artificial intelligence (geoAI) is an emerging scientific discipline that combines innovations in spatial science, artificial intelligence methods in machine learning (e.g., deep learning), data mining, and high-performance computing to extract knowledge from spatial big data. In environmental epidemiology, exposure modeling is a commonly used approach to conduct exposure assessment to determine the distribution of exposures in study populations. geoAI technologies provide important advantages for exposure modeling in environmental epidemiology, including the ability to incorporate large amounts of big spatial and temporal data in a variety of formats; computational efficiency; flexibility in algorithms and workflows to accommodate relevant characteristics of spatial (environmental) processes including spatial nonstationarity; and scalability to model other environmental exposures across different geographic areas. The objectives of this commentary are to provide an overview of key concepts surrounding the evolving and interdisciplinary field of geoAI including spatial data science, machine learning, deep learning, and data mining; recent geoAI applications in research; and potential future directions for geoAI in environmental epidemiology.

title: Emerging trends in geospatial artificial intelligence (geoAI): potential applications for environmental epidemiology
abstract: Geospatial artificial intelligence (geoAI) is an emerging interdisciplinary field that integrates spatial science, machine learning, deep learning, data mining, and high-performance computing to extract knowledge from spatial big data. This commentary explores the evolving landscape of geoAI and its transformative potential for environmental epidemiology, particularly in exposure modeling. By leveraging vast and diverse spatial and temporal datasets, geoAI offers enhanced computational efficiency, flexible algorithms to address spatial nonstationarity, and scalability for modeling environmental exposures across different regions. The paper reviews key concepts in spatial data science and recent advances in geoAI technologies, highlighting applications such as remote sensing image classification and predictive modeling. It also discusses challenges related to spatial data integration and synthesis, as well as the opportunities presented by volunteered geographic information and remote sensing. The commentary concludes by outlining future directions for geoAI in environmental epidemiology, emphasizing its promise for more accurate exposure assessment and improved understanding of environment-disease relationships.

title: From Bioavailability Science to Regulation of Organic Chemicals.
abstract: The bioavailability of organic chemicals in soil and sediment is an important area of scientific investigation for environmental scientists, although this area of study remains only partially recognized by regulators and industries working in the environmental sector. Regulators have recently started to consider bioavailability within retrospective risk assessment frameworks for organic chemicals; by doing so, realistic decision-making with regard to polluted environments can be achieved, rather than relying on the traditional approach of using total-extractable concentrations. However, implementation remains difficult because scientific developments on bioavailability are not always translated into ready-to-use approaches for regulators. Similarly, bioavailability remains largely unexplored within prospective regulatory frameworks that address the approval and regulation of organic chemicals. This article discusses bioavailability concepts and methods, as well as possible pathways for the implementation of bioavailability into risk assessment and regulation; in addition, this article offers a simple, pragmatic and justifiable approach for use within retrospective and prospective risk assessment.

title: From Bioavailability Science to Regulation of Organic Chemicals.
abstract: The bioavailability of organic chemicals in soils and sediments is a critical factor influencing environmental risk assessment, yet its integration into regulatory frameworks remains limited. This paper reviews the current state of bioavailability science, highlighting conceptual advances, measurement methodologies, and the challenges of translating scientific knowledge into practical regulatory tools. The authors discuss the distinction between total extractable concentrations and bioavailable fractions, emphasizing that reliance on the former can lead to overly conservative and sometimes unrealistic risk assessments. Recent developments in retrospective and prospective risk assessment frameworks are examined, including emerging methods such as passive sampling and biologically relevant extraction techniques. The paper proposes a pragmatic approach for incorporating bioavailability into both retrospective and prospective regulatory contexts, aiming to improve decision-making and site-specific management of organic chemical contamination. Enhanced collaboration among scientists, regulators, and industry is identified as essential for advancing the implementation of bioavailability concepts in environmental regulation.

title: Livestock production: recent trends, future prospects
abstract: The livestock sector globally is highly dynamic. In developing countries, it is evolving in response to rapidly increasing demand for livestock products. In developed countries, demand for livestock products is stagnating, while many production systems are increasing their efficiency and environmental sustainability. Historical changes in the demand for livestock products have been largely driven by human population growth, income growth and urbanization and the production response in different livestock systems has been associated with science and technology as well as increases in animal numbers. In the future, production will increasingly be affected by competition for natural resources, particularly land and water, competition between food and feed and by the need to operate in a carbon-constrained economy. Developments in breeding, nutrition and animal health will continue to contribute to increasing potential production and further efficiency and genetic gains. Livestock production is likely to be increasingly affected by carbon constraints and environmental and animal welfare legislation. Demand for livestock products in the future could be heavily moderated by socio-economic factors such as human health concerns and changing socio-cultural values. There is considerable uncertainty as to how these factors will play out in different regions of the world in the coming decades.
venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences

title: Livestock production: recent trends, future prospects
abstract: The global livestock sector is undergoing significant transformation, with developing countries experiencing rapid growth in demand for animal products due to population increases, urbanization, and rising incomes, while developed countries face stagnating demand but improvements in production efficiency and sustainability. This review synthesizes recent trends in livestock production, highlighting the expansion of intensive and extensive systems, advances in genetics, nutrition, and animal health, and the sector’s growing economic and social importance, particularly for smallholder farmers. Future prospects are shaped by challenges such as competition for land and water, climate change, carbon constraints, evolving socio-cultural values, and regulatory pressures related to environment and animal welfare. The outlook for livestock production is marked by considerable uncertainty, with potential disruptions from emerging technologies and shifting consumer preferences likely to influence both production systems and global consumption patterns in the coming decades.
venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences

title: Pollution Comes Home and Gets Personal: Women's Experience of Household Chemical Exposure∗
abstract: We report on interviews conducted with participants in a novel study about environmental chemicals in body fluids and household air and dust. Interviews reveal how personal and collective environmental history influence the interpretation of exposure data, and how participants fashion an emergent understanding of environmental health problems from the articulation of science and experience. To the illness experience literature, we contribute a framework for analyzing a new category of embodied narratives—“exposure experience”—that examines the mediating role of science. We update social scientific knowledge about social responses to toxic chemicals during a period in which science alters public understanding of chemical pollution. This article is among the first published accounts of participants' responses to learning personal exposure data, research identified as critical to environmental science and public health. Our findings raise the importance of reporting even uncertain science and underscore the value of a community-based reporting strategy.
venue: Journal of Health and Social Behavior

title: Pollution Comes Home and Gets Personal: Women's Experience of Household Chemical Exposure∗
abstract: This study explores how women interpret and respond to personal data on household chemical exposures, drawing on interviews with participants in a community-based biomonitoring project that measured environmental chemicals in body fluids and household environments. The research reveals that women's understanding of exposure is shaped by both personal and collective environmental histories, as well as by the interplay between scientific information and lived experience. The findings introduce the concept of 'exposure experience' as a new category of embodied health narrative, highlighting the mediating role of science in shaping perceptions of risk and responsibility. By analyzing participants' reactions to learning their own exposure results—often in the context of scientific uncertainty—the study underscores the importance of transparent reporting and community engagement strategies. This work extends the illness experience literature by documenting how science-driven knowledge about ubiquitous, everyday chemical exposures transforms public awareness and responses to environmental health risks within domestic spaces.
venue: Journal of Health and Social Behavior

title: Projected Marine Heatwaves in the 21st Century and the Potential for Ecological Impact
abstract: This research was supported by the Australian Research Council grants CE170100023 and FT170100106, Natural Environment Research Council International Opportunity Fund NE/N00678X/1, National Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada Discovery Grant RGPIN-2018-05255, and Brian Mason (Impacts of an unprecedented marine heatwave). This project was partially supported through funding from the Earth Systems and Climate Change Hub of the Australian Government's National Environmental Science Program.

title: Projected Marine Heatwaves in the 21st Century and the Potential for Ecological Impact
abstract: Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are increasingly frequent and intense extreme events with profound ecological and socioeconomic consequences. Using daily sea surface temperature outputs from six CMIP5 global climate models, this study projects changes in MHW characteristics under two greenhouse gas emission scenarios (RCP4.5 and RCP8.5) through 2100. Results indicate a significant acceleration in both the intensity and annual count of MHW days, with many ocean regions projected to experience near-permanent MHW conditions by the late 21st century, particularly under high emissions. The emergence of these trends from natural variability is evident within the first half of the century, underscoring the strong influence of anthropogenic forcing. The projected escalation in MHW exposure is expected to cause widespread, persistent, and potentially irreversible impacts on marine ecosystems, threatening biodiversity, foundational habitats, and ecosystem services globally. These findings highlight the urgent need for mitigation and adaptation strategies to address the escalating risks posed by marine heatwaves in a warming world.

title: Recent advances in quantitative LA-ICP-MS analysis: challenges and solutions in the life sciences and environmental chemistry
abstract: Laser ablation–inductively coupled plasma–mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS) is a widely accepted method for direct sampling of solid materials for trace elemental analysis. The number of reported applications is high and the application range is broad; besides geochemistry, LA-ICP-MS is mostly used in environmental chemistry and the life sciences. This review focuses on the application of LA-ICP-MS for quantification of trace elements in environmental, biological, and medical samples. The fundamental problems of LA-ICP-MS, such as sample-dependent ablation behavior and elemental fractionation, can be even more pronounced in environmental and life science applications as a result of the large variety of sample types and conditions. Besides variations in composition, the range of available sample states is highly diverse, including powders (e.g., soil samples, fly ash), hard tissues (e.g., bones, teeth), soft tissues (e.g., plants, tissue thin-cuts), or liquid samples (e.g., whole blood). Within this article, quantification approaches that have been proposed in the past are critically discussed and compared regarding the results obtained in the applications described. Although a large variety of sample types is discussed within this article, the quantification approaches used are similar for many analytical questions and have only been adapted to the specific questions. Nevertheless, none of them has proven to be a universally applicable method.

title: Recent advances in quantitative LA-ICP-MS analysis: challenges and solutions in the life sciences and environmental chemistry
abstract: Laser ablation–inductively coupled plasma–mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS) has emerged as a powerful tool for direct, quantitative trace elemental analysis of solid samples in the life sciences and environmental chemistry. However, its broader application is hindered by challenges such as elemental fractionation and matrix effects, which are exacerbated by the diversity of sample types and matrices encountered in these fields. This review critically examines recent advances in quantitative LA-ICP-MS analysis, focusing on strategies to overcome these limitations. It discusses traditional quantification approaches—including external calibration with certified reference materials, matrix-matched standards, and internal standard correction—as well as novel developments such as thin-film coatings and quasi-simultaneous measurement techniques. The capabilities and limitations of each method are compared with respect to their suitability for different sample types and analytical questions. Despite significant progress in instrumentation and methodology, no universally applicable quantification strategy has been established, underscoring the need for continued innovation tailored to the specific challenges of biological and environmental samples.

title: Rhetorical Variation across Research Article Abstracts in Environmental Science and Applied Linguistics
abstract: Abstract is of a pivotal genre in scientific communication, assisting not only highly selective readers with judgment of the pertinent articles but also researchers in disseminating new knowledge and intellectual discoveries. Difficult yet challenging, however, is the task of writing effective abstracts particularly among non-English speaking scholars. This study reports on the identification of moves and co-existing linguistic features commonly used in environmental science and applied linguistics research article abstracts. 200 research article abstracts published during the years of 2010-2013 were analyzed with reference to Hyland’s analytical framework. The two-tier analysis reveals a typical rhetorical structure including a cluster of linguistic features associated with certain pieces of information presented in each particular move, elucidating how research article abstracts in both fields are conventionally constructed. With the presence of all five moves, the structures of I-P-M-Pr-C and P-M-Pr-C were most prevalent among the corpus of environmental science and applied linguistics, respectively. All of the moves, except for Introduction move, were conventional across the two disciplines. Pedagogical implications of the findings are useful particularly for academic reading and writing instruction, enabling language teachers to empower their learners with strategies that contribute to the enhancement of success for publishing in scholarly leading publication.

title: Rhetorical Variation across Research Article Abstracts in Environmental Science and Applied Linguistics
abstract: This study investigates rhetorical variation in research article abstracts from environmental science and applied linguistics by analyzing 200 abstracts published between 2010 and 2013 using Hyland’s five-move analytical framework. The analysis identifies typical move structures and associated linguistic features in each discipline, revealing that environmental science abstracts most commonly follow the I-P-M-Pr-C (Introduction, Purpose, Method, Product, Conclusion) structure, while applied linguistics abstracts predominantly use the P-M-Pr-C (Purpose, Method, Product, Conclusion) pattern. All moves except the Introduction were conventional across both disciplines. The findings highlight both shared and distinct rhetorical conventions shaped by disciplinary norms, offering practical implications for academic writing instruction and supporting non-native English speakers in producing effective abstracts for scholarly publication.

title: Science friction: Data, metadata, and collaboration
abstract: When scientists from two or more disciplines work together on related problems, they often face what we call ‘science friction’. As science becomes more data-driven, collaborative, and interdisciplinary, demand increases for interoperability among data, tools, and services. Metadata – usually viewed simply as ‘data about data’, describing objects such as books, journal articles, or datasets – serve key roles in interoperability. Yet we find that metadata may be a source of friction between scientific collaborators, impeding data sharing. We propose an alternative view of metadata, focusing on its role in an ephemeral process of scientific communication, rather than as an enduring outcome or product. We report examples of highly useful, yet ad hoc, incomplete, loosely structured, and mutable, descriptions of data found in our ethnographic studies of several large projects in the environmental sciences. Based on this evidence, we argue that while metadata products can be powerful resources, usually they must be supplemented with metadata processes. Metadata-as-process suggests the very large role of the ad hoc, the incomplete, and the unfinished in everyday scientific work.

title: Science friction: Data, metadata, and collaboration
abstract: As scientific research becomes increasingly data-driven and interdisciplinary, collaboration across fields often encounters “science friction”—the challenges arising from the movement of data and metadata between diverse domains. This paper examines how metadata, typically conceived as stable descriptors facilitating data interoperability, can instead become sources of friction that impede data sharing and collaborative work. Drawing on ethnographic studies of large environmental science projects, the authors argue that metadata should be understood not only as products but also as dynamic processes embedded in scientific communication. The findings reveal that ad hoc, incomplete, and mutable metadata practices are integral to everyday scientific work, highlighting the limitations of standardized metadata frameworks. The paper advocates for a process-oriented approach to metadata that acknowledges the essential role of informal and evolving practices in enabling effective interdisciplinary collaboration and data exchange.

title: The Number of Scholarly Documents on the Public Web
abstract: The number of scholarly documents available on the web is estimated using capture/recapture methods by studying the coverage of two major academic search engines: Google Scholar and Microsoft Academic Search. Our estimates show that at least 114 million English-language scholarly documents are accessible on the web, of which Google Scholar has nearly 100 million. Of these, we estimate that at least 27 million (24%) are freely available since they do not require a subscription or payment of any kind. In addition, at a finer scale, we also estimate the number of scholarly documents on the web for fifteen fields: Agricultural Science, Arts and Humanities, Biology, Chemistry, Computer Science, Economics and Business, Engineering, Environmental Sciences, Geosciences, Material Science, Mathematics, Medicine, Physics, Social Sciences, and Multidisciplinary, as defined by Microsoft Academic Search. In addition, we show that among these fields the percentage of documents defined as freely available varies significantly, i.e., from 12 to 50%.

title: The Number of Scholarly Documents on the Public Web
abstract: This study estimates the number of English-language scholarly documents accessible on the public web by applying capture-recapture statistical methods to the coverage of Google Scholar and Microsoft Academic Search. Through systematic sampling and overlap analysis of citation data across fifteen academic fields, the research finds that at least 114 million scholarly documents are available online, with Google Scholar indexing nearly 100 million of these. Approximately 24% (27 million) of the documents are freely accessible without subscription or payment, though this proportion varies widely by discipline, ranging from 12% to 50%. The findings highlight both the vast scale and disciplinary variation in the accessibility of scholarly literature on the public web, providing a quantitative foundation for understanding the reach and limitations of major academic search engines.

title: Traditional Ecological Knowledge in Environmental Assessment and Management
abstract: It is now a policy requirement that 'traditional ecological knowledge' (TEK) be incorporated into environmental assessment and resource management in the North. However, there is little common understanding about what TEK is, and no guidance on how to implement the policy in public arenas where knowledge claims must be tested. The problems are inconsistent and unclear definitions of TEK, and insufficient attention to appropriate methods of organizing and presenting it for assessment and management purposes. TEK can be classified as knowledge about the environment, knowledge about the use of the environment, values about the environment, and the knowledge system itself. All categories are required for environmental assessment, but each must be presented and examined differently. TEK and 'Western' science provide partially different information, based on different sets of observations and procedures, and sometimes on different knowledge claims. It is important that TEK be comprehensible and testable as a knowledge claim in public reviews, and usable for ongoing public monitoring and co-management processes. To this end, certain procedures are recommended for recording, organizing, and presenting TEK, with particular emphasis on the need to differentiate between observation and inference or association. Documenting TEK as recommended usually requires trained intermediaries, but they in turn require the support and cooperation of those who have TEK. One consequence is that it is often both impractical and inappropriate to require development proponents to incorporate TEK into their environmental impact statements. However, the environmental assessment process must facilitate the use of TEK in the public review phase.

title: Traditional Ecological Knowledge in Environmental Assessment and Management
abstract: This paper examines the integration of traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) into environmental assessment and resource management in northern Canada, highlighting current policy requirements and the challenges associated with their implementation. The lack of clear definitions and practical guidance for incorporating TEK in public decision-making processes has led to confusion among regulators, proponents, and stakeholders. TEK is categorized as knowledge about the environment, its use, associated values, and the knowledge system itself, each requiring distinct approaches for effective assessment and management. The paper argues that TEK and Western science offer complementary but distinct information based on different observations and methodologies. For TEK to be credible and useful in public reviews and ongoing co-management, it must be organized, documented, and presented in ways that differentiate between observation and inference. This process typically requires trained intermediaries who collaborate closely with knowledge holders. The paper concludes that while it may not always be feasible or appropriate for development proponents to include TEK in environmental impact statements, environmental assessment processes must facilitate its use during public review phases to ensure meaningful participation and informed decision-making.

title: Why we need to focus on developing ethical, responsible, and trustworthy artificial intelligence approaches for environmental science
abstract: Given the growing use of Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods across all aspects of environmental sciences, it is imperative that we initiate a discussion about the ethical and responsible use of AI. In fact, much can be learned from other domains where AI was introduced, often with the best of intentions, yet often led to unintended societal consequences, such as hard coding racial bias in the criminal justice system or increasing economic inequality through the financial system. A common misconception is that the environmental sciences are immune to such unintended consequences when AI is being used, as most data come from observations, and AI algorithms are based on mathematical formulas, which are often seen as objective. In this article, we argue the opposite can be the case. Using specific examples, we demonstrate many ways in which the use of AI can introduce similar consequences in the environmental sciences. This article will stimulate discussion and research efforts in this direction. As a community, we should avoid repeating any foreseeable mistakes made in other domains through the introduction of AI. In fact, with proper precautions, AI can be a great tool to help reduce climate and environmental injustice. We primarily focus on weather and climate examples but the conclusions apply broadly across the environmental sciences.

title: Why we need to focus on developing ethical, responsible, and trustworthy artificial intelligence approaches for environmental science
abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) into environmental science offers significant opportunities for improved prediction and decision-making but also raises critical concerns about ethical, responsible, and trustworthy deployment. This position paper argues that environmental sciences are not immune to the unintended societal consequences observed in other domains where AI has perpetuated bias and injustice. Through specific examples, the authors illustrate how issues such as biased training data, lack of geo-diversity, inappropriate model use, and insufficient transparency can undermine the reliability and fairness of AI applications in weather, climate, and broader environmental contexts. The paper emphasizes the need for the environmental science community to proactively address these challenges by adopting ethical frameworks, ensuring diverse and representative data, and fostering inclusive practices. By learning from past mistakes in other fields and prioritizing environmental justice, AI can become a powerful tool for advancing sustainability and equity. The discussion aims to stimulate further research and community engagement to guide the responsible development and application of AI across environmental sciences.

title: Accelerating materials discovery using artificial intelligence, high performance computing and robotics
abstract: New tools enable new ways of working, and materials science is no exception. In materials discovery, traditional manual, serial, and human-intensive work is being augmented by automated, parallel, and iterative processes driven by Artificial Intelligence (AI), simulation and experimental automation. In this perspective, we describe how these new capabilities enable the acceleration and enrichment of each stage of the discovery cycle. We show, using the example of the development of a novel chemically amplified photoresist, how these technologies’ impacts are amplified when they are used in concert with each other as powerful, heterogeneous workflows.

title: Accelerating materials discovery using artificial intelligence, high performance computing and robotics
abstract: The accelerating demands for rapid materials discovery, driven by global challenges such as pandemics and climate change, necessitate a transformation in scientific workflows. This perspective explores how the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), high performance computing (HPC), and robotics is reshaping the materials discovery cycle by enabling automated, parallel, and iterative processes that augment traditional human-intensive approaches. We discuss enabling technologies for extracting and structuring unstructured technical data, such as the IBM DeepSearch platform, which leverages advanced natural language processing and knowledge graph construction to facilitate large-scale data ingestion and querying. Additionally, we examine the role of AI-driven simulations in overcoming limitations of sparse experimental data and computational bottlenecks, highlighting advances in machine-learned potentials and predictive modeling. Through a case study on the development of sustainable photoacid generators for photoresists, we demonstrate how these heterogeneous technologies, when orchestrated in concert, create powerful closed-loop workflows that accelerate hypothesis generation, experimentation, and knowledge extraction. The paper concludes by identifying ongoing challenges in data access, entity resolution, and complex querying, underscoring the need for continued innovation to fully realize the potential of AI, HPC, and robotics in materials science.

title: A strategy to apply machine learning to small datasets in materials science
abstract: There is growing interest in applying machine learning techniques in the research of materials science. However, although it is recognized that materials datasets are typically smaller and sometimes more diverse compared to other fields, the influence of availability of materials data on training machine learning models has not yet been studied, which prevents the possibility to establish accurate predictive rules using small materials datasets. Here we analyzed the fundamental interplay between the availability of materials data and the predictive capability of machine learning models. Instead of affecting the model precision directly, the effect of data size is mediated by the degree of freedom (DoF) of model, resulting in the phenomenon of association between precision and DoF. The appearance of precision–DoF association signals the issue of underfitting and is characterized by large bias of prediction, which consequently restricts the accurate prediction in unknown domains. We proposed to incorporate the crude estimation of property in the feature space to establish ML models using small sized materials data, which increases the accuracy of prediction without the cost of higher DoF. In three case studies of predicting the band gap of binary semiconductors, lattice thermal conductivity, and elastic properties of zeolites, the integration of crude estimation effectively boosted the predictive capability of machine learning models to state-of-art levels, demonstrating the generality of the proposed strategy to construct accurate machine learning models using small materials dataset.MACHINE LEARNING: Dealing with small datasetsMachine learning can be useful for materials prediction if crude estimations of the outcome are integrated in the code. Machine learning has been attracting tremendous attention lately due to its predictive power; evidence suggests it is directly proportional to the size of the available datasets. Machine learning can be useful in predicting new materials and novel properties, but materials sets tend to be smaller and more diverse than other fields. Ying Zhang and Chen Ling from the Toyota Research Institute of North America report that these small datasets affect the freedom of the algorithms and thus limit their predictive capabilities. In order to counterbalance the effect, they suggest introducing in the code crude estimations of the targeted property, obtained by other means.

title: A strategy to apply machine learning to small datasets in materials science
abstract: The application of machine learning (ML) in materials science is often constrained by the limited size and diversity of available datasets, impeding the development of accurate predictive models. This study systematically investigates the relationship between dataset size, model degree of freedom (DoF), and predictive precision in ML models for materials properties. We demonstrate that the effect of data size on prediction accuracy is mediated through model DoF, with increased precision typically requiring higher DoF, which can lead to underfitting and large prediction bias when data are scarce. To address this challenge, we propose incorporating crude estimations of target properties into the feature space, enabling more accurate predictions without increasing model complexity. Through case studies on band gap prediction in binary semiconductors, lattice thermal conductivity, and elastic properties of zeolites, we show that this strategy significantly enhances ML model performance using small datasets, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy. Our findings provide a generalizable approach for constructing robust ML models in materials science where data availability is limited.

title: Big data and machine learning for materials science
abstract: Herein, we review aspects of leading-edge research and innovation in materials science that exploit big data and machine learning (ML), two computer science concepts that combine to yield computational intelligence. ML can accelerate the solution of intricate chemical problems and even solve problems that otherwise would not be tractable. However, the potential benefits of ML come at the cost of big data production; that is, the algorithms demand large volumes of data of various natures and from different sources, from material properties to sensor data. In the survey, we propose a roadmap for future developments with emphasis on computer-aided discovery of new materials and analysis of chemical sensing compounds, both prominent research fields for ML in the context of materials science. In addition to providing an overview of recent advances, we elaborate upon the conceptual and practical limitations of big data and ML applied to materials science, outlining processes, discussing pitfalls, and reviewing cases of success and failure.

title: Big data and machine learning for materials science
abstract: This review examines the transformative impact of big data and machine learning (ML) on materials science, highlighting how these computational approaches are accelerating materials discovery and the analysis of chemical sensing compounds. The integration of big data and ML enables the handling and interpretation of vast, complex datasets, facilitating the identification of novel materials and the elucidation of their properties. The paper discusses the conceptual underpinnings of big data, including its defining characteristics and challenges related to data curation, infrastructure, and machine readability. It also explores recent advances in ML methodologies—such as deep learning and evolutionary algorithms—and their applications in materials informatics, from high-throughput screening to sensor network analysis. Emphasis is placed on the synergistic relationship between data generation and algorithmic innovation, as well as the limitations and pitfalls encountered in practice. The authors propose a roadmap for future research that leverages these technologies for computer-aided materials design while addressing ongoing challenges in data management, interpretability, and ethical considerations.

title: Biostimulants in Plant Science: A Global Perspective
abstract: This review presents a comprehensive and systematic study of the field of plant biostimulants and considers the fundamental and innovative principles underlying this technology. The elucidation of the biological basis of biostimulant function is a prerequisite for the development of science-based biostimulant industry and sound regulations governing these compounds. The task of defining the biological basis of biostimulants as a class of compounds, however, is made more complex by the diverse sources of biostimulants present in the market, which include bacteria, fungi, seaweeds, higher plants, animals and humate-containing raw materials, and the wide diversity of industrial processes utilized in their preparation. To distinguish biostimulants from the existing legislative product categories we propose the following definition of a biostimulant as “a formulated product of biological origin that improves plant productivity as a consequence of the novel or emergent properties of the complex of constituents, and not as a sole consequence of the presence of known essential plant nutrients, plant growth regulators, or plant protective compounds.” The definition provided here is important as it emphasizes the principle that biological function can be positively modulated through application of molecules, or mixtures of molecules, for which an explicit mode of action has not been defined. Given the difficulty in determining a “mode of action” for a biostimulant, and recognizing the need for the market in biostimulants to attain legitimacy, we suggest that the focus of biostimulant research and validation should be upon proof of efficacy and safety and the determination of a broad mechanism of action, without a requirement for the determination of a specific mode of action. While there is a clear commercial imperative to rationalize biostimulants as a discrete class of products, there is also a compelling biological case for the science-based development of, and experimentation with biostimulants in the expectation that this may lead to the identification of novel biological molecules and phenomenon, pathways and processes, that would not have been discovered if the category of biostimulants did not exist, or was not considered legitimate.

title: Biostimulants in Plant Science: A Global Perspective
abstract: This review provides a comprehensive global analysis of plant biostimulants, examining their diverse origins, mechanisms of action, and roles in enhancing plant productivity and stress resilience. The paper traces the historical development of biostimulant science, clarifies conceptual definitions to distinguish biostimulants from fertilizers, plant growth regulators, and protective compounds, and highlights the challenges posed by their complex compositions and undefined modes of action. Emphasizing the importance of efficacy and safety validation over precise mechanistic elucidation, the authors advocate for a science-based framework for biostimulant classification, regulation, and application. The review synthesizes methodological advances, including chemical characterization, agronomic trials, and -omics technologies, and underscores the potential of biostimulants to uncover novel biological pathways and contribute to sustainable agricultural innovation.

title: Phase-Field Methods in Materials Science and Engineering
abstract: This comprehensive and self-contained, one-stop source discusses phase-field methodology in a fundamental way, explaining complex mathematical and numerical techniques for solving phase-field and related continuum-field models. It also presents techniques used to model various phenomena in a detailed, step-by-step way, such that readers can carry out their own code developments.Features many examples of how the methods explained can be used in materials science and engineering applications.Visit the following page and click on 'Examples' to find a file with codes: http://www.wiley-vch.de/publish/en/books/bySubjectEE00/ISBN3-527-40747-2/?sID=82ekfegtfqadsjnpdnh0rpvkh3

title: Phase-Field Methods in Materials Science and Engineering
abstract: Phase-field methods have emerged as a powerful computational approach in materials science and engineering, enabling the simulation and prediction of complex microstructural evolution processes. This paper reviews the fundamental principles of phase-field modeling, its mathematical formulation, and its application to a wide range of materials phenomena including solidification, grain growth, phase transformations, and fracture. We discuss advances in numerical techniques that enhance the accuracy and efficiency of phase-field simulations, as well as the integration of phase-field models with experimental data and other computational methods such as molecular dynamics and finite element analysis. Case studies highlight the role of phase-field methods in guiding materials design and optimizing processing parameters. The paper concludes by outlining current challenges and future directions, emphasizing the potential of phase-field approaches to accelerate innovation in materials discovery and engineering applications.

title: Recent advances and applications of deep learning methods in materials science
abstract: Deep learning (DL) is one of the fastest-growing topics in materials data science, with rapidly emerging applications spanning atomistic, image-based, spectral, and textual data modalities. DL allows analysis of unstructured data and automated identification of features. The recent development of large materials databases has fueled the application of DL methods in atomistic prediction in particular. In contrast, advances in image and spectral data have largely leveraged synthetic data enabled by high-quality forward models as well as by generative unsupervised DL methods. In this article, we present a high-level overview of deep learning methods followed by a detailed discussion of recent developments of deep learning in atomistic simulation, materials imaging, spectral analysis, and natural language processing. For each modality we discuss applications involving both theoretical and experimental data, typical modeling approaches with their strengths and limitations, and relevant publicly available software and datasets. We conclude the review with a discussion of recent cross-cutting work related to uncertainty quantification in this field and a brief perspective on limitations, challenges, and potential growth areas for DL methods in materials science.

title: Recent advances and applications of deep learning methods in materials science
abstract: Deep learning (DL) has rapidly emerged as a transformative approach in materials science, enabling automated analysis and feature extraction from diverse data modalities including atomistic, image-based, spectral, and textual datasets. This review provides a comprehensive overview of fundamental DL concepts and highlights recent advances in applying DL methods to atomistic simulations, materials imaging, spectral analysis, and natural language processing within materials research. We examine the integration of large-scale materials databases, the use of synthetic data and generative models, and the adoption of advanced modeling techniques such as transfer learning and active learning to address challenges posed by limited data. The strengths and limitations of DL approaches are discussed for both theoretical and experimental applications, alongside an assessment of available software tools and datasets. The review concludes with insights into ongoing efforts in uncertainty quantification, interpretability, and the future potential for DL to accelerate discovery and innovation in materials science.

title: Searching for materials with high refractive index and wide band gap: A first-principles high-throughput study
abstract: Materials combining both a high refractive index and a wide band gap are of great interest for optoelectronic and sensor applications. However, these two properties are typically described by an inverse correlation with high refractive index appearing in small gap materials and vice-versa. Here, we conduct a first-principles high-throughput study on more than 4000 semiconductors (with a special focus on oxides). Our data confirm the general inverse trend between refractive index and band gap but interesting outliers are also identified. The data are then analyzed through a simple model involving two main descriptors: the average optical gap and the effective frequency. The former can be determined directly from the electronic structure of the compounds, but the latter cannot. This calls for further analysis in order to obtain a predictive model. Nonetheless, it turns out that the negative effect of a large band gap on the refractive index can counterbalanced in two ways: (i) by limiting the difference between the direct band gap and the average optical gap which can be realized by a narrow distribution in energy of the optical transitions and (ii) by increasing the effective frequency which can be achieved through either a high number of transitions from the top of the valence band to the bottom of the conduction or a high average probability for these transitions. Focusing on oxides, we use our data to investigate how the chemistry influences this inverse relationship and rationalize why certain classes of materials would perform better. Our findings can be used to search for new compounds in many optical applications both in the linear and non-linear regime (waveguides, optical modulators, laser, frequency converter, etc.).

title: Searching for materials with high refractive index and wide band gap: A first-principles high-throughput study
abstract: We present a first-principles high-throughput study of over 4000 semiconductors, with a focus on oxides, to identify materials that simultaneously exhibit a high refractive index and a wide band gap—properties critical for advanced optoelectronic and photonic applications. Our comprehensive dataset confirms the well-known inverse correlation between refractive index and band gap but also reveals notable outliers that defy this trend. By analyzing the results with a simple two-descriptor model based on the average optical gap and effective frequency, we elucidate key factors that enable certain materials to achieve both desirable properties. Specifically, we show that minimizing the energy difference between direct band gap and average optical gap, as well as maximizing the number or probability of optical transitions, can counterbalance the inverse relationship. Focusing on oxides, we further explore how chemical composition influences this interplay and highlight promising material classes for future exploration. Our findings provide valuable guidelines for the targeted discovery of new materials for both linear and nonlinear optical devices.

title: Spin Ice State in Frustrated Magnetic Pyrochlore Materials
abstract: A frustrated system is one whose symmetry precludes the possibility that every pairwise interaction (“bond”) in the system can be satisfied at the same time. Such systems are common in all areas of physical and biological science. In the most extreme cases, they can have a disordered ground state with “macroscopic” degeneracy; that is, one that comprises a huge number of equivalent states of the same energy. Pauling's description of the low-temperature proton disorder in water ice was perhaps the first recognition of this phenomenon and remains the paradigm. In recent years, a new class of magnetic substance has been characterized, in which the disorder of the magnetic moments at low temperatures is precisely analogous to the proton disorder in water ice. These substances, known as spin ice materials, are perhaps the “cleanest” examples of such highly frustrated systems yet discovered. They offer an unparalleled opportunity for the study of frustration in magnetic systems at both an experimental and a theoretical level. This article describes the essential physics of spin ice, as it is currently understood, and identifies new avenues for future research on related materials and models.

title: Spin Ice State in Frustrated Magnetic Pyrochlore Materials
abstract: Spin ice materials, exemplified by rare earth pyrochlores such as Ho2Ti2O7 and Dy2Ti2O7, represent a class of frustrated magnetic systems in which the local arrangement of magnetic moments mimics the proton disorder found in water ice. In these systems, geometric constraints imposed by the corner-sharing tetrahedral lattice prevent simultaneous minimization of all pairwise interactions, resulting in a macroscopically degenerate ground state characterized by residual entropy analogous to that predicted by Pauling for water ice. The discovery of spin ice has provided a unique platform for investigating the consequences of frustration in three-dimensional magnets, enabling direct experimental and theoretical exploration of phenomena such as zero-point entropy, emergent excitations, and collective dynamics. This article reviews the essential physics underlying spin ice behavior, highlights key experimental observations and theoretical models, and discusses new directions for research in frustrated magnetism and related materials.

title: The Martini Model in Materials Science
abstract: The Martini model, a coarse‐grained force field initially developed with biomolecular simulations in mind, has found an increasing number of applications in the field of soft materials science. The model's underlying building block principle does not pose restrictions on its application beyond biomolecular systems. Here, the main applications to date of the Martini model in materials science are highlighted, and a perspective for the future developments in this field is given, particularly in light of recent developments such as the new version of the model, Martini 3.

title: The Martini Model in Materials Science
abstract: The Martini model is a widely used coarse-grained force field that enables efficient molecular dynamics simulations by grouping atoms into representative beads, thereby extending accessible length and time scales while retaining essential chemical specificity. Originally developed for biomolecular systems, the Martini model’s modular building-block approach and extensive parameter library have facilitated its adoption in materials science, including the simulation of polymers, nanoparticle–polymer composites, organic electronic materials, ion-conducting materials, and self-assembled supramolecular systems. This perspective reviews the parametrization strategies tailored for material systems, highlights key application areas, and discusses the advantages of Martini—such as near-atomic resolution and broad chemical compatibility—over more generic coarse-grained models. The paper also outlines recent developments, including the release of Martini 3 and new tools for polymer structure generation and constant pH simulations, and provides an outlook on future directions for expanding the Martini model’s role in advancing materials science research.

title: A Research Agenda to Underpin Malaria Eradication
abstract: Pedro Alonso and colleagues introduce the Malaria Eradication Research Agenda (malERA) initiative and the set of articles published in this PLoS Medicine Supplement that distill the research questions key to malaria eradication.

title: A Research Agenda to Underpin Malaria Eradication
abstract: Malaria eradication remains a formidable global health challenge, despite significant progress in control efforts and increased investment over the past decade. This review outlines the limitations of current tools and strategies, emphasizing that while aggressive scale-up can achieve elimination in some regions, global eradication is not attainable with existing knowledge and interventions. The heterogeneity of malaria transmission, diversity of Plasmodium species and vectors, operational constraints, and emerging drug and insecticide resistance underscore the need for a comprehensive research agenda. The Malaria Eradication Research Agenda (malERA) is proposed to address key knowledge gaps and guide the development of new tools, strategies, and interventions aimed at reducing malaria transmission to zero. Success will require sustained commitment from local communities, policymakers, researchers—particularly those from endemic regions—and ongoing investment in both biomedical and social sciences. This agenda represents a paradigm shift from morbidity reduction to interruption of transmission and ultimate parasite eradication.

title: Classification, Ontology, and Precision Medicine.
abstract: Precision medicine aims to stratify patients for improved diagnosis and treatment by leveraging increasingly complex and heterogeneous clinical and molecular data. However, the integration and analysis of such data are hindered by limitations in electronic health records, inconsistent data standards, and insufficient semantic interoperability. This review examines the role of ontologies—systematic, computational representations of knowledge—in enabling precise patient classification by providing standardized semantics and logical relationships among biomedical concepts. Ontologies facilitate the integration of diverse data sources, support computational reasoning, and enhance the extraction of clinically relevant information from structured and unstructured data. By bridging basic science and clinical domains, ontologies empower translational research and enable more nuanced disease classification, ultimately advancing the goals of precision medicine through improved diagnostic accuracy, care management, and discovery of novel therapeutic insights.

title: CLINICAL CHEMISTRY IN PRACTICAL MEDICINE
abstract: This paper reviews four significant texts in the field of clinical chemistry and laboratory medicine, evaluating their contributions to practical medical education and laboratory practice. The second edition of 'Practical Clinical Biochemistry' by Varley is commended for its comprehensive methods, new chapters, and improved guidance on accuracy control, though it retains some outdated techniques and typographical errors. The fifth edition of 'Clinical Chemistry in Practical Medicine' by Stewart and Dunlop is recognized for its enduring value, updated content, and clarity in most areas, despite some inconsistencies in chapter quality and terminology that may confuse readers. 'Principles of Biological Microtechnique' by Baker is described as a critical and stimulating review focused on fixation and staining, with a strong zoological orientation that may limit its utility for pathologists but remains valuable for broader histological study. The revised 'Absorption Spectrophotometry' by Lothian is praised for its comprehensive overview of principles, applications, and instrumentation in spectrophotometry, making it a recommended resource for those seeking foundational knowledge, although it does not explore topics in depth. Collectively, these works are assessed for their relevance, accuracy, accessibility, and practical utility in advancing clinical chemistry as applied to medical practice.

title: CONSORT 2010 Statement: updated guidelines for reporting parallel group randomised trials
abstract: The CONSORT statement is used worldwide to improve the reporting of randomised controlled trials. Kenneth Schulz and colleagues describe the latest version, CONSORT 2010, which updates the reporting guideline based on new methodological evidence and accumulating experience.To encourage dissemination of the CONSORT 2010 Statement, this article is freely accessible on bmj.com and will also be published in the Lancet, Obstetrics and Gynecology, PLoS Medicine, Annals of Internal Medicine, Open Medicine, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, BMC Medicine, and Trials.

title: CONSORT 2010 Statement: updated guidelines for reporting parallel group randomised trials
abstract: The CONSORT 2010 Statement provides updated, evidence-based guidelines for reporting parallel group randomised controlled trials, aiming to enhance the clarity, completeness, and transparency of trial reports. Building on previous versions and incorporating new methodological research and accumulated experience, CONSORT 2010 offers a 25-item checklist and flow diagram to guide authors in reporting essential aspects of trial design, conduct, analysis, and interpretation. The revision process involved extensive consultation with a diverse group of experts and led to evolutionary changes that address persistent inadequacies in trial reporting. While focused on individually randomised, two-group parallel trials, the guidelines are broadly applicable and supported by numerous journals and editorial organizations worldwide. The CONSORT initiative continues to evolve in response to emerging evidence and serves as a model for other reporting guidelines, ultimately aiming to improve the quality of published research and facilitate critical appraisal by readers, editors, and reviewers.

title: Definition of Health 2.0 and Medicine 2.0: A Systematic Review
abstract: During the last decade, the Internet has become increasingly popular and is now an important part of our daily life. When new “Web 2.0” technologies are used in health care, the terms “Health 2.0' or 'Medicine 2.0” may be used. Objective The objective was to identify unique definitions of Health 2.0/Medicine 2.0 and recurrent topics within the definitions. Methods A systematic literature review of electronic databases (PubMed, Scopus, CINAHL) and gray literature on the Internet using the search engines Google, Bing, and Yahoo was performed to find unique definitions of Health 2.0/Medicine 2.0. We assessed all literature, extracted unique definitions, and selected recurrent topics by using the constant comparison method. Results We found a total of 1937 articles, 533 in scientific databases and 1404 in the gray literature. We selected 46 unique definitions for further analysis and identified 7 main topics. Conclusions Health 2.0/Medicine 2.0 are still developing areas. Many articles concerning this subject were found, primarily on the Internet. However, there is still no general consensus regarding the definition of Health 2.0/Medicine 2.0. We hope that this study will contribute to building the concept of Health 2.0/Medicine 2.0 and facilitate discussion and further research.

title: Definition of Health 2.0 and Medicine 2.0: A Systematic Review
abstract: This systematic review aimed to identify unique definitions and recurrent topics associated with the terms Health 2.0 and Medicine 2.0, which describe the application of Web 2.0 technologies in health care. A comprehensive search of scientific databases (PubMed, Scopus, CINAHL) and gray literature using major search engines yielded 1937 articles, from which 46 unique definitions were extracted and analyzed using the constant comparison method. Seven main topics emerged from these definitions, reflecting the evolving nature of Health 2.0 and Medicine 2.0 concepts. The findings reveal significant variability and lack of consensus in definitions, highlighting the need for further conceptual development to support research and practice in this area. This review contributes to clarifying the terminology and encourages ongoing discussion about the scope and meaning of Health 2.0 and Medicine 2.0.

title: Digital medicine and the curse of dimensionality
abstract: Digital health data are multimodal and high-dimensional. A patient’s health state can be characterized by a multitude of signals including medical imaging, clinical variables, genome sequencing, conversations between clinicians and patients, and continuous signals from wearables, among others. This high volume, personalized data stream aggregated over patients’ lives has spurred interest in developing new artificial intelligence (AI) models for higher-precision diagnosis, prognosis, and tracking. While the promise of these algorithms is undeniable, their dissemination and adoption have been slow, owing partially to unpredictable AI model performance once deployed in the real world. We posit that one of the rate-limiting factors in developing algorithms that generalize to real-world scenarios is the very attribute that makes the data exciting—their high-dimensional nature. This paper considers how the large number of features in vast digital health data can challenge the development of robust AI models—a phenomenon known as “the curse of dimensionality” in statistical learning theory. We provide an overview of the curse of dimensionality in the context of digital health, demonstrate how it can negatively impact out-of-sample performance, and highlight important considerations for researchers and algorithm designers.

title: Digital medicine and the curse of dimensionality
abstract: Digital health data are characterized by their high dimensionality and multimodal nature, encompassing diverse sources such as imaging, genomics, wearable sensors, and speech. While these rich datasets hold promise for advancing precision medicine through artificial intelligence (AI), the development and deployment of robust AI models are hindered by the curse of dimensionality—a phenomenon where the number of features vastly exceeds the available sample size. This imbalance leads to 'blind spots' in the feature space, resulting in unreliable model performance estimates and poor generalizability to real-world scenarios. Using examples from speech-based digital biomarker discovery, this perspective highlights how small sample sizes combined with high-dimensional data exacerbate overfitting and misestimation of model accuracy. The paper underscores the need for careful consideration of dimensionality in digital medicine research and offers guidance for algorithm designers to mitigate these challenges, ultimately aiming to improve the translation of AI innovations into clinical practice.

title: European Respiratory Society
abstract: The mission of the European Respiratory Society (ERS) is to advance respiratory medicine by stimulating and coordinating the actions of its members, in order to achieve the highest possible medical, paramedical and social standards in the treatment of respiratory disease in Europe. The society’s 2005 congress had approximately 16 000 registered participants from 100 countries and with over 110 scientific and clinical sessions, the congress was Europe’s largest annual scientific gathering in respiratory medicine.

title: European Respiratory Society
abstract: This report summarizes key findings and discussions from the 15th Annual Congress of the European Respiratory Society, held in Copenhagen in September 2005, which brought together approximately 16,000 participants from 100 countries. The congress highlighted the urgent need for increased governmental funding for lung health, given the rising burden and economic impact of respiratory diseases in Europe. Evidence presented underscored the benefits of public smoking bans and smoking cessation programs in improving respiratory health and reducing disease incidence, particularly COPD and asthma. Advances in the management of severe persistent allergic asthma were discussed, notably the long-term efficacy and safety of omalizumab, a monoclonal antibody targeting IgE, which significantly improves asthma control and quality of life. Ongoing threats from emerging respiratory infectious agents such as SARS and avian influenza were reviewed, emphasizing the necessity for vigilance, early diagnosis, and pandemic preparedness. The introduction of improved inhaler technologies, such as the Respimat Soft Mist Inhaler, demonstrated enhanced patient outcomes and ease of use in asthma and COPD management. Overall, the congress reinforced the importance of coordinated research, policy action, and innovation to address current and future challenges in respiratory medicine.

title: Evidence based medicine: a movement in crisis?
abstract: Trisha Greenhalgh and colleagues argue that, although evidence based medicine has had many benefits, it has also had some negative unintended consequences.
