They offer a preliminary agenda for the movement’s renaissance, refocusing on providing useable evidence that can be combined with context and professional expertise so that individual patients get optimal treatment

title: Evidence based medicine: a movement in crisis?
abstract: Evidence-based medicine (EBM) has transformed clinical practice by promoting the use of high-quality research evidence alongside clinical expertise and patient values, resulting in notable improvements in care and outcomes. However, this essay argues that EBM now faces a crisis marked by the distortion of its principles by vested interests, an overwhelming volume of guidelines, marginal clinical gains, overreliance on algorithmic decision-making, and poor applicability to patients with multimorbidity. The authors highlight how industry influence shapes research agendas and outcomes, how guideline proliferation impedes practical use, and how rigid adherence to protocols can undermine individualized care. They contend that EBM has drifted from its original patient-centered ethos toward a managerial, population-focused approach that often neglects the complexities of real-world clinical decision-making. To address these challenges, the authors propose a renaissance for EBM that prioritizes usable evidence integrated with professional judgment and patient context, aiming to restore optimal, individualized care as the movement’s core objective.

title: Improving Health Care Globally: A Critical Review of the Necessity of Family Medicine Research and Recommendations to Build Research Capacity
abstract: An invitational conference led by the World Organization of Family Doctors (Wonca) involving selected delegates from 34 countries was held in Kingston, Ontario, Canada, March 8 to12, 2003. The conference theme was “Improving Health Globally: The Necessity of Family Medicine Research.” Guiding conference discussions was the value that to improve health care worldwide, strong, evidence-based primary care is indispensable. Eight papers reviewed before the meeting formed the basic material from which the conference developed 9 recommendations. Wonca, as an international body of family medicine, was regarded as particularly suited to pursue these conference recommendations: Research achievements in family medicine should be displayed to policy makers, health (insurance) authorities, and academic leaders in a systematic way. In all countries, sentinel practice systems should be developed to provide surveillance reports on illness and diseases that have the greatest impact on the population’s health and wellness in the community. A clearinghouse should be organized to provide a central repository of knowledge about family medicine research expertise, training, and mentoring. National research institutes and university departments of family medicine with a research mission should be developed. Practice-based research networks should be developed around the world. Family medicine research journals, conferences, and Web sites should be strengthened to disseminate research findings internationally, and their use coordinated. Improved representation of family medicine research journals in databases, such as Index Medicus, should be pursued. Funding of international collaborative research in family medicine should be facilitated. International ethical guidelines, with an international ethical review process, should be developed in particular for participatory (action) research, where researchers work in partnership with communities. When implementing these recommendations, the specific needs and implications for developing countries should be addressed. The Wonca executive committee has reviewed these recommendations and the supporting rationale for each. They plan to follow the recommendations, but to do so will require the support and cooperation of many individuals, organizations, and national governments around the world.

title: Improving Health Care Globally: A Critical Review of the Necessity of Family Medicine Research and Recommendations to Build Research Capacity
abstract: This paper critically reviews the necessity of family medicine research in improving global health care and presents recommendations to build research capacity worldwide. Drawing on the proceedings of an international conference organized by the World Organization of Family Doctors (Wonca) with delegates from 34 countries, the paper underscores the essential role of evidence-based primary care and family medicine in delivering accessible, equitable, and effective health services. The conference identified key challenges, including limited recognition of family medicine research, insufficient infrastructure, and barriers to knowledge dissemination. Through collaborative discussions and review of eight foundational papers, participants formulated nine strategic recommendations: systematically showcasing research achievements to policymakers, developing sentinel practice systems for community health surveillance, establishing a central clearinghouse for research expertise and training, creating national research institutes and university departments with a research focus, expanding practice-based research networks globally, strengthening dissemination channels such as journals and conferences, facilitating funding for international collaborative studies, developing international ethical guidelines for participatory research, and addressing the specific needs of developing countries. The paper concludes that implementing these recommendations requires coordinated efforts among individuals, organizations, and governments to strengthen the global impact of family medicine research and ultimately improve health outcomes.

title: Medicine sellers and malaria treatment in sub-Saharan Africa: what do they do and how can their practice be improved?
abstract: Medicine sellers are widely used for fever and malaria treatment in sub-Saharan Africa, but concerns surround the appropriateness of drugs and information provided. Because there is increasing interest in improving their services, we reviewed the literature on their characteristics and interventions to improve their malaria-related practices. Sixteen interventions were identified, involving a mixture of training/capacity building, demand generation, quality assurance, and creating an enabling environment. Although evidence is insufficient to prove which approaches are superior, tentative conclusions were possible. Interventions increased rates of appropriate treatment, and medicine sellers were willing to participate. Features of successful interventions included a comprehensive situation analysis of the legal and market environment; buy-in from medicine sellers, community members and government; use of a combination of approaches; and maintenance of training and supervision. Interventions must be adapted to include artemisinin-based combination therapies, and their sustainability and potential to operate at a national level should be further explored.
venue: American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene

title: Medicine sellers and malaria treatment in sub-Saharan Africa: what do they do and how can their practice be improved?
abstract: Medicine sellers are a primary source of malaria treatment in sub-Saharan Africa, offering accessible and affordable care but often providing inappropriate drugs and advice. This review synthesizes literature on the characteristics and operations of medicine sellers and evaluates interventions aimed at improving their malaria-related practices. Sixteen interventions were identified, employing strategies such as training, demand generation, quality assurance, and environmental support. Evidence suggests these interventions can enhance appropriate treatment rates and that medicine sellers are receptive to participation. Key factors for success include thorough situation analysis, stakeholder engagement, multifaceted approaches, and ongoing training and supervision. However, evidence remains insufficient to determine the most effective strategies, and interventions must adapt to incorporate artemisinin-based combination therapies. Further research is needed to assess sustainability and scalability at the national level.
venue: American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene

title: Mitigating bias in machine learning for medicine
abstract: Several sources of bias can affect the performance of machine learning systems used in medicine and potentially impact clinical care. Here, we discuss solutions to mitigate bias across the different development steps of machine learning-based systems for medical applications. Vokinger et al. discuss potential sources of bias in machine learning systems used in medicine. The authors propose solutions to mitigate bias across the different stages of model development, from data collection and preparation to model evaluation and application.

title: Mitigating bias in machine learning for medicine
abstract: Machine learning (ML) systems hold significant promise for improving medical care but are vulnerable to bias at multiple stages of development, potentially leading to systematic errors and health disparities. This paper examines sources of bias arising during data collection, model development, evaluation, and deployment in clinical practice. It highlights how non-representative training data, algorithmic design choices, and domain shifts can disproportionately impact underrepresented patient groups. The authors propose a range of mitigation strategies, including assembling diverse datasets, applying mathematical de-biasing techniques, employing interpretability and explainability tools during model evaluation, and implementing ongoing monitoring after deployment. Regulatory frameworks such as FDA guidelines and reporting checklists like PROBAST are discussed as mechanisms to support transparency and accountability. The paper emphasizes the need for continuous vigilance and adaptation to ensure ML-based medical systems deliver equitable and reliable outcomes across diverse patient populations.

title: Molecular Biology, Nucleic Acids, and the Future of Medicine
abstract: It seems particularly fitting, in this symposium, to try to assess the prob able and possible impact of molecular biology and its important com ponent, the structure and function of nucleic acids, on the future of medicine. Although I attempt specific predictions with considerable trepi dation, not being qualified in either fortunetelling or medicine, I do so in the firm belief that the findings and concepts of molecular biology will play a leading role in the future of medicine. Medicine, after all, primarily involves the application of biological concepts and understanding to the health and welfare of man.

title: Molecular Biology, Nucleic Acids, and the Future of Medicine
abstract: This paper explores the transformative impact of molecular biology and nucleic acid research on the future of medicine, focusing on key problem areas such as viral diseases, hereditary metabolic disorders, developmental defects, and cancer. It discusses the anticipated advancements in understanding and controlling viral infections through immunological and chemical means, the identification and management of genetic metabolic disorders via improved diagnostic and therapeutic approaches, and the prevention or correction of developmental abnormalities through insights into gene regulation. The paper also highlights the promise of molecular biology in elucidating the causes of cancer and developing effective preventive and curative strategies. Central to these advances is the elucidation of DNA structure and function, particularly its role in heredity, replication, mutation, and protein synthesis. The discussion includes recent findings on DNA circularity, strandedness, and their implications for replication, repair, and transcription, as well as the molecular interactions of antibiotics with nucleic acids. The author concludes that the exponential growth of knowledge in molecular biology will continue to drive significant medical progress, provided broader societal challenges such as population growth are addressed.

title: PEG Hydrogels for the Controlled Release of Biomolecules in Regenerative Medicine
abstract: Polyethylene glycol (PEG) hydrogels are widely used in a variety of biomedical applications, including matrices for controlled release of biomolecules and scaffolds for regenerative medicine. The design, fabrication, and characterization of PEG hydrogels rely on the understanding of fundamental gelation kinetics as well as the purpose of the application. This review article will focus on different polymerization mechanisms of PEG-based hydrogels and the importance of these biocompatible hydrogels in regenerative medicine applications. Furthermore, the design criteria that are important in maintaining the availability and stability of the biomolecules as well as the mechanisms for loading of biomolecules within PEG hydrogels will also be discussed. Finally, we overview and provide a perspective on some of the emerging novel design and applications of PEG hydrogel systems, including the spatiotemporal-controlled delivery of biomolecules, hybrid hydrogels, and PEG hydrogels designed for controlled stem cell differentiation.

title: PEG Hydrogels for the Controlled Release of Biomolecules in Regenerative Medicine
abstract: Polyethylene glycol (PEG) hydrogels have emerged as versatile platforms for the controlled release of biomolecules in regenerative medicine due to their tunable physicochemical properties and excellent biocompatibility. This review examines the fundamental gelation mechanisms of PEG hydrogels, including chain-growth, step-growth, and mixed-mode polymerizations, and discusses how these influence network structure, degradation, and release kinetics. Critical design considerations such as gel crosslinking density, incorporation of functional moieties, and strategies for loading and preserving bioactive molecules are addressed in the context of optimizing therapeutic efficacy and minimizing adverse reactions. The article highlights advances in spatiotemporal control of biomolecule delivery, hybrid hydrogel systems, and PEG-based matrices engineered to direct stem cell fate. By integrating recent developments with established principles, this review provides a comprehensive perspective on the current challenges and future directions for PEG hydrogels in facilitating targeted, sustained delivery of therapeutics for tissue regeneration.

title: Predicting the Future - Big Data, Machine Learning, and Clinical Medicine.
abstract: The algorithms of machine learning, which can sift through vast numbers of variables looking for combinations that reliably predict outcomes, will improve prognosis, displace much of the work of radiologists and anatomical pathologists, and improve diagnostic accuracy.

title: Predicting the Future - Big Data, Machine Learning, and Clinical Medicine.
abstract: This paper examines the transformative potential of big data and machine learning in clinical medicine, arguing that the true value lies not in data accumulation but in the development and application of advanced algorithms. Unlike traditional expert systems that encode established medical knowledge, machine learning algorithms learn predictive rules directly from vast and complex datasets, enabling nuanced prognostication, image interpretation, and diagnostic support. The authors discuss key challenges, including overfitting, data quality, and the limitations of causal inference, emphasizing the need for rigorous validation and high-quality input data. They predict that machine learning will soon enhance prognosis accuracy, automate image-based specialties such as radiology and pathology, and gradually improve diagnostic precision, although progress in diagnosis will be slower due to data and methodological constraints. Ultimately, the integration of machine learning into clinical practice promises to reshape medical decision-making, with patients standing to benefit most from these advances.

title: Stem cell paracrine actions and tissue regeneration.
abstract: Stem cells have emerged as a key element of regenerative medicine therapies due to their inherent ability to differentiate into a variety of cell phenotypes, thereby providing numerous potential cell therapies to treat an array of degenerative diseases and traumatic injuries. A recent paradigm shift has emerged suggesting that the beneficial effects of stem cells may not be restricted to cell restoration alone, but also due to their transient paracrine actions. Stem cells can secrete potent combinations of trophic factors that modulate the molecular composition of the environment to evoke responses from resident cells. Based on this new insight, current research directions include efforts to elucidate, augment and harness stem cell paracrine mechanisms for tissue regeneration. This article discusses the existing studies on stem/progenitor cell trophic factor production, implications for tissue regeneration and cancer therapies, and development of novel strategies to use stem cell paracrine delivery for regenerative medicine.

title: Stem cell paracrine actions and tissue regeneration.
abstract: Stem cells are central to regenerative medicine due to their ability to differentiate into diverse cell types, but emerging evidence highlights the significance of their paracrine actions—secretion of bioactive factors that influence the tissue microenvironment and modulate resident cell behavior. This review synthesizes current understanding of stem and progenitor cell trophic factor production, emphasizing their roles in promoting cell proliferation, cytoprotection, angiogenesis, immunomodulation, and extracellular matrix remodeling. The paracrine mechanisms of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), in particular, are explored with respect to immune modulation and support of hematopoiesis, as well as implications for tissue repair and cancer therapy. Advances in genomic and proteomic profiling have elucidated the spectrum of cytokines, growth factors, and other molecules secreted by various stem cell populations, informing strategies to harness these effects for therapeutic purposes. The article discusses methods to augment and direct stem cell paracrine actions, positioning stem/progenitor cells as complex biological delivery vehicles for regenerative applications. Understanding and manipulating these paracrine pathways hold promise for enhancing tissue regeneration and developing novel treatments for degenerative diseases and immune-related disorders.

title: TCMSP: a database of systems pharmacology for drug discovery from herbal medicines
abstract: BackgroundModern medicine often clashes with traditional medicine such as Chinese herbal medicine because of the little understanding of the underlying mechanisms of action of the herbs. In an effort to promote integration of both sides and to accelerate the drug discovery from herbal medicines, an efficient systems pharmacology platform that represents ideal information convergence of pharmacochemistry, ADME properties, drug-likeness, drug targets, associated diseases and interaction networks, are urgently needed.DescriptionThe traditional Chinese medicine systems pharmacology database and analysis platform (TCMSP) was built based on the framework of systems pharmacology for herbal medicines. It consists of all the 499 Chinese herbs registered in the Chinese pharmacopoeia with 29,384 ingredients, 3,311 targets and 837 associated diseases. Twelve important ADME-related properties like human oral bioavailability, half-life, drug-likeness, Caco-2 permeability, blood-brain barrier and Lipinski’s rule of five are provided for drug screening and evaluation. TCMSP also provides drug targets and diseases of each active compound, which can automatically establish the compound-target and target-disease networks that let users view and analyze the drug action mechanisms. It is designed to fuel the development of herbal medicines and to promote integration of modern medicine and traditional medicine for drug discovery and development.ConclusionsThe particular strengths of TCMSP are the composition of the large number of herbal entries, and the ability to identify drug-target networks and drug-disease networks, which will help revealing the mechanisms of action of Chinese herbs, uncovering the nature of TCM theory and developing new herb-oriented drugs. TCMSP is freely available at http://sm.nwsuaf.edu.cn/lsp/tcmsp.php.

title: TCMSP: a database of systems pharmacology for drug discovery from herbal medicines
abstract: TCMSP is an integrative systems pharmacology database and analysis platform designed to facilitate drug discovery from traditional Chinese herbal medicines. It encompasses comprehensive data on 499 herbs from the Chinese pharmacopoeia, including 29,384 ingredients, 3,311 targets, and 837 associated diseases. The database incorporates twelve key ADME-related properties for each compound, enabling effective screening and evaluation of drug-likeness and pharmacokinetic profiles. TCMSP also establishes compound-target and target-disease interaction networks, providing tools for network visualization and analysis to elucidate mechanisms of action and support the development of new herb-derived drugs. By integrating large-scale chemical, pharmacological, and disease association data with user-friendly analytical tools, TCMSP serves as a valuable resource for researchers aiming to bridge traditional herbal medicine with modern drug discovery approaches. The database is freely accessible online.

title: THE APPLICATIONS OF INTERNATIONAL CLASSIFICATION OF FUNCTIONING, DISABILITY AND HEALTH (ICF) BY WORLD HEALTH ORGANIZATION(WHO) IN REHABILITATION MEDICINE PRACTICE
abstract: Rehabilitation Medicine is dedicated to optimise patients function and health in the most comprehensive manner. ICF, the latest International Classification by World Health Organization (WHO) is a conceptual framework for the assessment of functioning, disability and health. The purpose of this paper is to describe the applications of ICF in Rehabilitation Medicine practice in the Medical Rehabilitation Unit, University of Malaya Medical Centre (UMMC), Kuala Lumpur. Issues: ICF consists of body function, structure, activity, participation and environmental factor. ICF categories are exhaustive, but are not practical to be used entirely and not applicable in clinical practice on their own. How is ICF used from the clinical perspective? It has to be adapted to make it usable. In Rehabilitation Medicine settings, the following are ways ICF is applied in clinical practice: research in terms of validating the use of available ICF Core Sets and development of new ICF Core Set; clinical practice based on the ICF-based sheet; and educational tools. Conclusion: The practice of Rehabilitation Medicine is in line and compatible with the concept of ICF and can serve as a new important language that can improve the practice of Rehabilitation Medicine. It can be a universal language in functioning, disability and health and can improve understanding in addressing issues on disability within the medical community, improve multi professionals’ communication among patients, healthcare providers and stakeholders.

title: THE APPLICATIONS OF INTERNATIONAL CLASSIFICATION OF FUNCTIONING, DISABILITY AND HEALTH (ICF) BY WORLD HEALTH ORGANIZATION(WHO) IN REHABILITATION MEDICINE PRACTICE
abstract: The International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) by the World Health Organization provides a comprehensive framework for understanding and assessing health, functioning, and disability. This paper explores the practical applications of ICF in rehabilitation medicine at the University of Malaya Medical Centre, Kuala Lumpur. It discusses how ICF’s multidimensional model—encompassing body functions, structures, activities, participation, and environmental factors—aligns with the holistic goals of rehabilitation medicine. The paper highlights the adaptation of ICF through the use of Core Sets tailored for specific health conditions to enhance feasibility in clinical practice, research, and education. Ongoing initiatives include the validation of existing Core Sets and the development of new ones for conditions prevalent in rehabilitation settings. The integration of ICF fosters improved communication among healthcare professionals, patients, and stakeholders by providing a standardized language for describing health and disability. Ultimately, the adoption of ICF enhances patient-centered care, supports interdisciplinary collaboration, and contributes to better health outcomes in rehabilitation medicine.

title: The quest for modernisation of traditional Chinese medicine
abstract: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) is an integral part of mainstream medicine in China. Due to its worldwide use, potential impact on healthcare and opportunities for new drug development, TCM is also of great international interest. Recently, a new era for modernisation of TCM was launched with the successful completion of the Good Practice in Traditional Chinese Medicine Research in the Post-genomic Era (GP-TCM) project, the European Union’s Seventh Framework Programme (FP7) coordination action on TCM research. This 3.5-year project that involved inputs from over 200 scientists resulted in the production of 20 editorials and in-depth reviews on different aspects of TCM that were published in a special issue of Journal of Ethnopharmacology (2012; volume 140, issue 3). In this narrative review, we aim to summarise the findings of the FP7 GP-TCM project and highlight the relevance of TCM to modern medicine within a historical and international context. Advances in TCM research since the 1950s can be characterised into three phases: Phase I (1950s-1970s) was fundamental for developing TCM higher education, research and hospital networks in China; Phase II (1980s-2000s) was critical for developing legal, economic and scientific foundations and international networks for TCM; and Phase III (2011 onwards) is concentrating on consolidating the scientific basis and clinical practice of TCM through interdisciplinary, interregional and intersectoral collaborations. Taking into account the quality and safety requirements newly imposed by a globalised market, we especially highlight the scientific evidence behind TCM, update the most important milestones and pitfalls, and propose integrity, integration and innovation as key principles for further modernisation of TCM. These principles will serve as foundations for further research and development of TCM, and for its future integration into tomorrow’s medicine.

title: The quest for modernisation of traditional Chinese medicine
abstract: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) has evolved from an ancient, experience-based system into a globally significant component of healthcare, prompting increasing efforts toward its modernisation. This review synthesises the historical trajectory and recent advancements in TCM, with particular emphasis on the outcomes of the European Union’s FP7 GP-TCM project, which fostered international collaboration and set new standards for TCM research. The modernisation process is delineated into three phases: foundational development of education and infrastructure in China (1950s–1970s), establishment of legal, scientific, and international frameworks (1980s–2000s), and current consolidation of scientific evidence and clinical practice through interdisciplinary and cross-sectoral partnerships (2011 onwards). Key milestones include the integration of TCM into mainstream healthcare, landmark drug discoveries such as artemisinin, and the expansion of research networks worldwide. The review highlights ongoing challenges related to quality control, safety, and scientific validation in a globalised context. It proposes integrity, integration, and innovation as guiding principles for future research and development, aiming to further bridge traditional practices with modern medical science and facilitate the integration of TCM into contemporary healthcare systems.

title: The Smartphone in Medicine: A Review of Current and Potential Use Among Physicians and Students
abstract: Advancements in technology have always had major impacts in medicine. The smartphone is one of the most ubiquitous and dynamic trends in communication, in which one’s mobile phone can also be used for communicating via email, performing Internet searches, and using specific applications. The smartphone is one of the fastest growing sectors in the technology industry, and its impact in medicine has already been significant. Objective To provide a comprehensive and up-to-date summary of the role of the smartphone in medicine by highlighting the ways in which it can enhance continuing medical education, patient care, and communication. We also examine the evidence base for this technology. Methods We conducted a review of all published uses of the smartphone that could be applicable to the field of medicine and medical education with the exclusion of only surgical-related uses. Results In the 60 studies that were identified, we found many uses for the smartphone in medicine; however, we also found that very few high-quality studies exist to help us understand how best to use this technology. Conclusions While the smartphone’s role in medicine and education appears promising and exciting, more high-quality studies are needed to better understand the role it will have in this field. We recommend popular smartphone applications for physicians that are lacking in evidence and discuss future studies to support their use.

title: The Smartphone in Medicine: A Review of Current and Potential Use Among Physicians and Students
abstract: This review examines the current and potential applications of smartphones in medicine, focusing on their use among physicians and medical students. Through a comprehensive literature search of Medline and Scopus databases, 60 relevant studies were identified and analyzed, revealing that smartphones are increasingly integrated into patient care, monitoring, medical education, communication, and reference tasks. Examples include remote patient monitoring for chronic diseases, rehabilitation support, diagnostic aids, and educational tools. Despite the widespread adoption of smartphones and the proliferation of medical apps, the review highlights a significant lack of high-quality evidence guiding best practices for their use in clinical settings. The authors conclude that while smartphones hold considerable promise for enhancing healthcare delivery and education, further rigorous research is needed to establish their efficacy and inform evidence-based integration into medical practice. Recommendations for useful applications are provided alongside suggestions for future studies to address existing knowledge gaps.

title: Toxicity and Safety Implications of Herbal Medicines Used in Africa
abstract: The use of herbal medicines has seen a great upsurge globally. In developing countries, many patronize them largely due to cultural acceptability, availability and cost. In devel-oped countries, they are used because they are natural and therefore assumed to be safer than allopathic medicines. In recent times, however, there has been a growing concern about their safety. This has created a situation of ambivalence in discussions regarding their use. Some medicinal plants are intrinsically toxic by virtue of their constituents and can cause adverse reactions if inappropriately used. Other factors such as herb-drug interactions, lack of adherence to good manufacturing practice (GMP), poor regulatory measures and adulteration may also lead to adverse events in their use. Many in vivo tests on aqueous extracts largely support the safety of herbal medicines, whereas most in vitro tests on isolated single cells mostly with extracts other than aqueous ones show contrary results and thus continue the debate on herbal medicine safety. It is expected that toxicity studies concerning herbal medicine should reflect their traditional use to allow for rational discussions regarding their safety for their beneficial use. While various attempts continue to establish the safety of vari ous herbal medicines in man, their cautious and responsible use is required.

title: Toxicity and Safety Implications of Herbal Medicines Used in Africa
abstract: The widespread use of herbal medicines in Africa is driven by cultural acceptance, accessibility, affordability, and the limitations of allopathic medicine. Despite their long-standing role in traditional healthcare systems and perceived safety, concerns about the toxicity and safety of these remedies have intensified due to reports of adverse effects, intrinsic toxicity of certain plant constituents, herb-drug interactions, poor manufacturing practices, regulatory gaps, and adulteration. This chapter critically examines the determinants of herbal medicine safety in Africa, reviewing evidence from animal and cellular toxicity studies and highlighting discrepancies between in vivo and in vitro findings. It underscores the importance of aligning toxicity assessments with traditional usage patterns to ensure rational evaluation and safe integration of herbal medicines into healthcare. While scientific validation has confirmed the efficacy and relative safety of many African medicinal plants, ongoing vigilance, responsible use, and strengthened regulatory oversight are essential to mitigate risks and maximize their therapeutic benefits.

title: Why digital medicine depends on interoperability
abstract: Digital data are anticipated to transform medicine. However, most of today’s medical data lack interoperability: hidden in isolated databases, incompatible systems and proprietary software, the data are difficult to exchange, analyze, and interpret. This slows down medical progress, as technologies that rely on these data – artificial intelligence, big data or mobile applications – cannot be used to their full potential. In this article, we argue that interoperability is a prerequisite for the digital innovations envisioned for future medicine. We focus on four areas where interoperable data and IT systems are particularly important: (1) artificial intelligence and big data; (2) medical communication; (3) research; and (4) international cooperation. We discuss how interoperability can facilitate digital transformation in these areas to improve the health and well-being of patients worldwide.

title: Why digital medicine depends on interoperability
abstract: Digital medicine holds significant promise for transforming healthcare through innovations such as artificial intelligence, big data analytics, and mobile health technologies. However, the lack of interoperability among current medical data systems—characterized by isolated databases, incompatible formats, and proprietary software—hampers the effective exchange, analysis, and interpretation of health information. This perspective article argues that interoperability is a foundational requirement for realizing the full potential of digital medicine. The authors provide an overview of interoperability at technical, syntactic, semantic, and organizational levels and highlight its critical role in four key areas: artificial intelligence and big data, medical communication, research, and international cooperation. By enabling seamless data integration and standardized communication across diverse healthcare systems, interoperability facilitates digital transformation and supports improved patient care globally. The article emphasizes the need for international standards, clear medical terminologies, and supportive policies to overcome current barriers and advance digital health innovation.

title: Year in review in Intensive Care Medicine 2012: III. Noninvasive ventilation, monitoring and patient–ventilator interactions, acute respiratory distress syndrome, sedation, paediatrics and miscellanea
abstract: In 2012, the journal published several articles dealing with the use of noninvasive ventilation (NIV) in patients with acute respiratory failure (ARF). Carrillo et al. [1] prospectively evaluated the characteristics and outcomes of 184 patients with severe ARF due to community-acquired pneumonia treated with NIV, and determined the factors predicting NIV failure and mortality. NIV was successful in 63 % of patients. Confirming previous findings, the authors found that patients with “de novo” ARF failed NIV more frequently than those with previous cardiac or other respiratory disease (46 vs. 26 %). Worsening radiologic infiltrate 24 h after admission, maximum Sepsis-Related Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, and higher heart rate and lower PaO2/FiO2 after 1 h of NIV were among the factors predicting NIV failure. NIV failure, maximum SOFA, and older age independently predicted hospital mortality. In patients with de novo ARF only, delayed intubation was consistently associated with a decreased survival. In 13 patients (six with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), Piquilloud et al. [2] compared short-term patient–ventilator interaction during NIV with pressure support (PS) and neurally adjusted ventilatory assist (NAVA). As compared with PS, NAVA improved patient–ventilator synchrony during NIV by reducing trigger delay and severe asynchrony and by abolishing ineffective efforts and both delayed and premature cycling. Vaschetto et al. [3] performed a pilot study to assess the feasibility of using NIV to facilitate discontinuation of invasive mechanical ventilation in patients with resolving hypoxaemic ARF. Twenty patients randomly received immediate NIV after early extubation or conventional weaning. At the end of the study, arterial blood gas, success of extubation, septic complications, ICU length of stay, and mortality were similar, but the number of days without invasive ventilation at day 28 was higher in the NIV group than in the control group. The authors concluded that, in a highly experienced centre, early extubation followed by NIV is feasible and might facilitate liberation from mechanical ventilation in selected patients with hypoxaemic ARF. These findings were discussed in the editorial by Laghi and Fernandez.

title: Year in review in Intensive Care Medicine 2012: III. Noninvasive ventilation, monitoring and patient–ventilator interactions, acute respiratory distress syndrome, sedation, paediatrics and miscellanea
abstract: This review summarizes key advances in intensive care medicine published in 2012, focusing on noninvasive ventilation (NIV), monitoring, patient–ventilator interactions, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), sedation, paediatrics, and related topics. Studies highlighted the predictors of NIV success and failure in acute respiratory failure, the benefits of neurally adjusted ventilatory assist for patient–ventilator synchrony, and the feasibility of early extubation followed by NIV in selected hypoxaemic patients. Research on pediatric NIV interfaces emphasized the importance of individualized mask selection based on age and disease. Bench studies addressed the need for standardized evaluation criteria for NIV equipment. Biomarker studies identified NT-proBNP as a predictor of post-extubation respiratory distress, supporting its role in guiding prophylactic NIV use. Advances in monitoring included ultrasonographic assessment of diaphragmatic function, noninvasive work of breathing prediction using neural networks, and validation of automated algorithms for detecting ineffective respiratory efforts. Technological innovations such as adaptive support ventilation and speaking valves were evaluated for safety and their impact on patient outcomes. Overall, these developments reflect ongoing efforts to optimize respiratory support, monitoring, and patient care strategies in the intensive care setting.

title: ALICE: Physics Performance Report, Volume II
abstract: ALICE is a general-purpose heavy-ion experiment designed to study the physics of strongly interacting matter and the quark–gluon plasma in nucleus–nucleus collisions at the LHC. It currently involves more than 900 physicists and senior engineers, from both the nuclear and high-energy physics sectors, from over 90 institutions in about 30 countries.The ALICE detector is designed to cope with the highest particle multiplicities above those anticipated for Pb–Pb collisions (dNch/dy up to 8000) and it will be operational at the start-up of the LHC. In addition to heavy systems, the ALICE Collaboration will study collisions of lower-mass ions, which are a means of varying the energy density, and protons (both pp and pA), which primarily provide reference data for the nucleus–nucleus collisions. In addition, the pp data will allow for a number of genuine pp physics studies.The detailed design of the different detector systems has been laid down in a number of Technical Design Reports issued between mid-1998 and the end of 2004. The experiment is currently under construction and will be ready for data taking with both proton and heavy-ion beams at the start-up of the LHC.Since the comprehensive information on detector and physics performance was last published in the ALICE Technical Proposal in 1996, the detector, as well as simulation, reconstruction and analysis software have undergone significant development. The Physics Performance Report (PPR) provides an updated and comprehensive summary of the performance of the various ALICE subsystems, including updates to the Technical Design Reports, as appropriate.The PPR is divided into two volumes. Volume I, published in 2004 (CERN/LHCC 2003-049, ALICE Collaboration 2004 J. Phys. G: Nucl. Part. Phys. 30 1517–1763), contains in four chapters a short theoretical overview and an extensive reference list concerning the physics topics of interest to ALICE, the experimental conditions at the LHC, a short summary and update of the subsystem designs, and a description of the offline framework and Monte Carlo event generators.The present volume, Volume II, contains the majority of the information relevant to the physics performance in proton–proton, proton–nucleus, and nucleus–nucleus collisions. Following an introductory overview, Chapter 5 describes the combined detector performance and the event reconstruction procedures, based on detailed simulations of the individual subsystems. Chapter 6 describes the analysis and physics reach for a representative sample of physics observables, from global event characteristics to hard processes.

title: ALICE: Physics Performance Report, Volume II
abstract: This report presents a comprehensive assessment of the physics performance of the ALICE experiment at the CERN Large Hadron Collider, focusing on its capabilities for studying the properties of strongly interacting matter at extreme energy densities. Detailed simulations and analyses are used to evaluate the detector’s response, reconstruction algorithms, and expected physics reach for a variety of observables, including hadron production, jet quenching, heavy flavor dynamics, and quark-gluon plasma signatures in heavy-ion collisions. The results demonstrate ALICE’s ability to provide precise measurements of key probes such as identified particles, resonances, and rare signals over a broad kinematic range. The report also discusses systematic uncertainties, background conditions, and strategies for data analysis, establishing a solid foundation for the experiment’s scientific program and its potential to advance understanding of QCD matter under extreme conditions.

title: An invitation to loop quantum gravity
abstract: We describe the basic assumptions and key results of loop quantum gravity, which is a background independent approach to quantum gravity. The emphasis is on the basic physical principles and how one deduces predictions from them, at a level suitable for physicsts in other areas such as string theory, cosmology, particle physics, astrophysics and condensed matter physics. No details are given, but references are provided to guide the interested reader to the literature. The present state of knowledge is summarized in a list of 35 key results on topics including the hamiltonian and path integral quantizations, coupling to matter, extensions to supergravity and higher dimensional theories, as well as applications to black holes, cosmology and Plank scale phenomenology. We describe the near term prospects for observational tests of quantum theories of gravity and the expectations that loop quantum gravity may provide predictions for their outcomes. Finally, we provide answers to frequently asked questions and a list of key open problems.

title: An invitation to loop quantum gravity
abstract: This paper provides an accessible overview of loop quantum gravity (LQG), a background independent approach to quantum gravity grounded solely in the principles of general relativity and quantum mechanics. Emphasizing foundational physical concepts and their implications, the review outlines how LQG constructs a quantum theory of spacetime without assuming a fixed background geometry. Key results are summarized across canonical and path integral quantizations, matter coupling, unification attempts, extensions to supergravity and higher dimensions, and applications to black holes, cosmology, and Planck-scale phenomenology. The current experimental prospects for testing quantum gravity predictions are discussed, alongside answers to common questions and a list of open problems. The aim is to introduce the main ideas, methods, and achievements of LQG to physicists from diverse fields, providing references for further study while highlighting both the successes and ongoing challenges in the theory’s development.

title: A Note on inflation and transPlanckian physics
abstract: In this paper we consider the influence of trans-Planckian physics on the CMBR anisotropies produced by inflation. We consider a simple toy model that allows for analytic calculations and argue on general grounds, based on ambiguities in the choice of vacuum, that effects are expected with a magnitude of the order of $H/\ensuremath{\Lambda},$ where H is the Hubble constant during inflation and \ensuremath{\Lambda} the scale for new physics, e.g., the Planck scale.

title: A Note on inflation and transPlanckian physics
abstract: This paper investigates the potential impact of trans-Planckian physics on the cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR) anisotropies generated during inflation. By employing a simple toy model that permits analytic treatment, the study focuses on ambiguities in the choice of vacuum state at the onset of inflation, particularly when quantum fluctuations originate at scales comparable to or smaller than the Planck length. The analysis demonstrates that reasonable variations in the initial vacuum, such as those motivated by minimum uncertainty or adiabatic arguments, can lead to corrections in the predicted fluctuation spectrum of order H/Λ, where H is the Hubble parameter during inflation and Λ denotes the scale of new physics (e.g., the Planck scale). These findings suggest that trans-Planckian effects could be more significant than previously estimated by some effective field theory approaches, highlighting the sensitivity of inflationary predictions to unknown high-energy physics and underscoring the need for careful consideration of initial state choices in cosmological models.

title: A review of progress in the physics of open quantum systems: theory and experiment
abstract: This report on progress explores recent advances in our theoretical and experimental understanding of the physics of open quantum systems (OQSs). The study of such systems represents a core problem in modern physics that has evolved to assume an unprecedented interdisciplinary character. OQSs consist of some localized, microscopic, region that is coupled to an external environment by means of an appropriate interaction. Examples of such systems may be found in numerous areas of physics, including atomic and nuclear physics, photonics, biophysics, and mesoscopic physics. It is the latter area that provides the main focus of this review, an emphasis that is driven by the capacity that exists to subject mesoscopic devices to unprecedented control. We thus provide a detailed discussion of the behavior of mesoscopic devices (and other OQSs) in terms of the projection-operator formalism, according to which the system under study is considered to be comprised of a localized region (Q), embedded into a well-defined environment (P) of scattering wavefunctions (with Q + P = 1). The Q subspace must be treated using the concepts of non-Hermitian physics, and of particular interest here is: the capacity of the environment to mediate a coupling between the different states of Q; the role played by the presence of exceptional points (EPs) in the spectra of OQSs; the influence of EPs on the rigidity of the wavefunction phases, and; the ability of EPs to initiate a dynamical phase transition (DPT). EPs are singular points in the continuum, at which two resonance states coalesce, that is where they exhibit a non-avoided crossing. DPTs occur when the quantum dynamics of the open system causes transitions between non-analytically connected states, as a function of some external control parameter. Much like conventional phase transitions, the behavior of the system on one side of the DPT does not serve as a reliable indicator of that on the other. In addition to discussing experiments on mesoscopic quantum point contacts that provide evidence of the environmentally-mediated coupling of quantum states, we also review manifestations of DPTs in mesoscopic devices and other systems. These experiments include observations of resonance-trapping behavior in microwave cavities and open quantum dots, phase lapses in tunneling through single-electron transistors, and spin swapping in atomic ensembles. Other possible manifestations of this phenomenon are presented, including various superradiant phenomena in low-dimensional semiconductors. From these discussions a generic picture of OQSs emerges in which the environmentally-mediated coupling between different quantum states plays a critical role in governing the system behavior. The ability to control or manipulate this interaction may even lead to new applications in photonics and electronics.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: A review of progress in the physics of open quantum systems: theory and experiment
abstract: This review presents a comprehensive overview of recent theoretical and experimental developments in the physics of open quantum systems (OQSs), with a particular emphasis on mesoscopic devices. OQSs, characterized by the coupling of a localized quantum region to an external environment, are central to numerous fields including atomic, nuclear, photonic, and mesoscopic physics. The report discusses the projection-operator formalism, which models the system as a non-Hermitian subspace embedded within a continuum of scattering states, highlighting the role of environmentally mediated coupling between quantum states. Key phenomena explored include exceptional points (EPs)—singularities where resonance states coalesce—and their influence on wavefunction phase rigidity and the initiation of dynamical phase transitions (DPTs). Experimental evidence from mesoscopic quantum point contacts, microwave cavities, open quantum dots, single-electron transistors, and atomic ensembles is reviewed, illustrating manifestations of resonance trapping, phase lapses, spin swapping, and superradiant behavior. The findings underscore the critical impact of environmental interactions on quantum state dynamics and suggest that precise control over these couplings may enable novel applications in photonics and electronics.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: B-physics anomalies: a guide to combined explanations
abstract: Motivated by additional experimental hints of Lepton Flavour Universality violation in B decays, both in charged- and in neutral-current processes, we analyse the ingredients necessary to provide a combined description of these phenomena. By means of an Effective Field Theory (EFT) approach, based on the hypothesis of New Physics coupled predominantly to the third generation of left-handed quarks and leptons, we show how this is possible. We demonstrate, in particular, how to solve the problems posed by electroweak precision tests and direct searches with a rather natural choice of model parameters, within the context of a U(2)q ×U(2)ℓ flavour symmetry. We further exemplify the general EFT findings by means of simplified models with explicit mediators in the TeV range: coloured scalar or vector leptoquarks and colour-less vectors. Among these, the case of an SU(2)L-singlet vector leptoquark emerges as a particularly simple and successful framework.

title: B-physics anomalies: a guide to combined explanations
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the observed anomalies in B-meson decays that suggest violations of Lepton Flavour Universality (LFU) in both charged- and neutral-current processes. Employing an Effective Field Theory (EFT) framework with new physics predominantly coupled to third-generation left-handed quarks and leptons, the study systematically explores the minimal set of semi-leptonic operators required to explain the data. The analysis incorporates constraints from electroweak precision tests, high-pT LHC searches, and flavor observables, under the assumption of a minimally broken U(2)q × U(2)ℓ flavor symmetry. The EFT results are further illustrated through simplified models featuring explicit mediators, such as vector and scalar leptoquarks and colorless vectors at the TeV scale. Among these, the SU(2)L-singlet vector leptoquark model emerges as a particularly promising and natural candidate for a unified explanation of both sets of anomalies while remaining consistent with current experimental bounds. The findings offer a guide for constructing viable new physics scenarios addressing B-physics anomalies and highlight key directions for future theoretical and experimental investigations.

title: Biological evolution and statistical physics
abstract: This review is an introduction to theoretical models and mathematical calculations for biological evolution, aimed at physicists. The methods in the field are naturally very similar to those used in statistical physics, although the majority of publications have appeared in biology journals. The review has three parts, which can be read independently. The first part deals with evolution in fitness landscapes and includes Fisher's theorem, adaptive walks, quasispecies models, effects of finite population sizes, and neutral evolution. The second part studies models of coevolution, including evolutionary game theory, kin selection, group selection, sexual selection, speciation, and coevolution of hosts and parasites. The third part discusses models for networks of interacting species and their extinction avalanches. Throughout the review, attention is paid to giving the necessary biological information, and to pointing out the assumptions underlying the models, and their limits of validity.

title: Biological evolution and statistical physics
abstract: This review introduces physicists to the theoretical models and mathematical approaches used to study biological evolution, highlighting the strong parallels with methods from statistical physics. The paper is organized into three independent sections: the first explores evolution on fitness landscapes, covering Fisher’s theorem, adaptive walks, quasispecies models, finite population effects, and neutral evolution; the second examines coevolutionary models, including evolutionary game theory, kin and group selection, sexual selection, speciation, and host-parasite dynamics; the third discusses models of interacting species networks and extinction avalanches. Throughout, the review provides essential biological context, clarifies model assumptions and limitations, and emphasizes the interplay between biological complexity and statistical physics concepts in understanding evolutionary processes.

title: Chapter 5: Physics of energetic ions
abstract: This chapter reviews the progress accomplished since the redaction of the first ITER Physics Basis (1999 Nucl. Fusion 39 2137–664) in the field of energetic ion physics and its possible impact on burning plasma regimes. New schemes to create energetic ions simulating the fusion-produced alphas are introduced, accessing experimental conditions of direct relevance for burning plasmas, in terms of the Alfvénic Mach number and of the normalised pressure gradient of the energetic ions, though orbit characteristics and size cannot always match those of ITER. Based on the experimental and theoretical knowledge of the effects of the toroidal magnetic field ripple on direct fast ion losses, ferritic inserts in ITER are expected to provide a significant reduction of ripple alpha losses in reversed shear configurations. The nonlinear fast ion interaction with kink and tearing modes is qualitatively understood, but quantitative predictions are missing, particularly for the stabilisation of sawteeth by fast particles that can trigger neoclassical tearing modes. A large database on the linear stability properties of the modes interacting with energetic ions, such as the Alfvén eigenmode has been constructed. Comparisons between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements of mode structures and drive/damping rates approach a satisfactory degree of consistency, though systematic measurements and theory comparisons of damping and drive of intermediate and high mode numbers, the most relevant for ITER, still need to be performed. The nonlinear behaviour of Alfvén eigenmodes close to marginal stability is well characterized theoretically and experimentally, which gives the opportunity to extract some information on the particle phase space distribution from the measured instability spectral features. Much less data exists for strongly unstable scenarios, characterised by nonlinear dynamical processes leading to energetic ion redistribution and losses, and identified in nonlinear numerical simulations of Alfvén eigenmodes and energetic particle modes. Comparisons with theoretical and numerical analyses are needed to assess the potential implications of these regimes on burning plasma scenarios, including in the presence of a large number of modes simultaneously driven unstable by the fast ions.

title: Chapter 5: Physics of energetic ions
abstract: This chapter provides a comprehensive review of recent advances in the physics of energetic ions, with a focus on their behavior and impact in burning plasma regimes relevant to ITER and future fusion reactors. It discusses new experimental schemes for generating energetic ions that simulate fusion-born alpha particles, enabling the study of key parameters such as Alfvénic Mach number and normalized pressure gradient under conditions approaching those expected in ITER. The chapter examines the effects of toroidal magnetic field ripple on fast ion losses and highlights the role of ferritic inserts in mitigating these losses in reversed shear configurations. It also addresses the nonlinear interactions between fast ions and magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) modes, noting qualitative understanding but emphasizing the need for improved quantitative predictions, particularly regarding sawtooth stabilization and neoclassical tearing mode triggering by fast particles. A substantial database on the linear stability of Alfvén eigenmodes and other collective modes has been established, with increasing consistency between theoretical models and experimental observations, although further systematic studies are required for higher mode numbers. The nonlinear dynamics of Alfvén eigenmodes near marginal stability are well characterized, offering insights into energetic ion phase space distributions, while data on strongly unstable scenarios remain limited. The chapter concludes that continued integration of experimental results with advanced theoretical and numerical modeling is essential to fully assess the implications of energetic ion physics for burning plasma operation and control in ITER.

title: Deep Learning and Its Application to LHC Physics
abstract: Machine learning has played an important role in the analysis of high-energy physics data for decades. The emergence of deep learning in 2012 allowed for machine learning tools which could adeptly handle higher-dimensional and more complex problems than previously feasible. This review is aimed at the reader who is familiar with high-energy physics but not machine learning. The connections between machine learning and high-energy physics data analysis are explored, followed by an introduction to the core concepts of neural networks, examples of the key results demonstrating the power of deep learning for analysis of LHC data, and discussion of future prospects and concerns.
venue: Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science

title: Deep Learning and Its Application to LHC Physics
abstract: Deep learning has rapidly advanced the analysis capabilities in high-energy physics, particularly at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), by enabling the extraction of complex patterns from high-dimensional data that traditional methods struggle to address. This review introduces the foundational concepts of neural networks and deep learning for physicists, surveys their transformative applications in LHC data analysis—including event selection, jet classification, tracking, and fast simulation—and highlights key breakthroughs where deep learning has surpassed previous approaches. The paper also discusses ongoing challenges such as optimization objectives, interpretability, reliance on simulations, and software infrastructure. Finally, it outlines future prospects for integrating deep learning more deeply into particle physics research, emphasizing its potential to enhance discovery and understanding in the field.
venue: Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science

title: Direct detection of WIMP dark matter: concepts and status
abstract: The existence of dark matter as evidenced by numerous indirect observations is one of the most important indications that there must be physics beyond the Standard Model of particle physics. This article reviews the concepts of direct detection of dark matter in the form of Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs) in ultra-sensitive detectors located in underground laboratories, discusses the expected signatures, detector concepts, and how the stringent low-background requirements are achieved. Finally, it summarizes the current status of the field and provides an outlook on the years to come.
venue: Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics

title: Direct detection of WIMP dark matter: concepts and status
abstract: The direct detection of Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs) as candidates for dark matter is a central challenge in contemporary physics, motivated by extensive astrophysical and cosmological evidence for non-luminous, non-baryonic matter that shapes the structure and evolution of the Universe. This review outlines the theoretical foundations and experimental strategies for WIMP detection, focusing on the operation of ultra-sensitive detectors in underground laboratories designed to observe rare WIMP-nucleus scattering events. Key aspects discussed include the expected interaction signatures, the necessity of stringent background suppression, and the modeling of local dark matter distributions that inform signal predictions. The current status of leading experiments is summarized, highlighting recent results and ongoing advancements in detector technology and analysis techniques. The outlook emphasizes future prospects for improving sensitivity and exploring new parameter spaces, with the ultimate goal of achieving a definitive direct detection of WIMP dark matter.
venue: Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics

title: Double exchange alone does not explain the resistivity of La1-xSrxMnO3.
abstract: The ${\mathrm{La}}_{1\ensuremath{-}x}{\mathrm{Sr}}_{x}{\mathrm{MnO}}_{3}$ system with $0.2\ensuremath{\lesssim}x\ensuremath{\lesssim}0.4$ has traditionally been modeled with a ``double-exchange'' Hamiltonian in which it is assumed that the only relevant physics is the tendency of carrier hopping to line up neighboring spins. We present a solution of the double-exchange model, show it is incompatible with many aspects of the data, and propose that in addition to double-exchange physics a strong electron-phonon interaction arising from the Jahn-Teller splitting of the outer Mn $d$ level plays a crucial role.

title: Double exchange alone does not explain the resistivity of La1-xSrxMnO3.
abstract: We present a comprehensive analysis of the double exchange model as applied to the resistivity of La1-xSrxMnO3 for 0.2 ≲ x ≲ 0.4, demonstrating that this mechanism alone cannot account for key experimental observations. By deriving and solving the double exchange Hamiltonian, we calculate the frequency and temperature dependence of conductivity and show that the predicted energy scales and resistivity behavior are inconsistent with measured values, particularly in terms of transition temperatures and optical conductivity. Our findings indicate that additional physics, specifically strong electron-phonon coupling associated with Jahn-Teller distortions of Mn d-levels, must be included to reconcile theory with experiment. We propose that polaronic effects arising from these interactions play a crucial role in determining transport properties and suggest specific experiments to test this hypothesis.

title: Exciton–polariton condensates
abstract: Recently a new type of system exhibiting spontaneous coherence has emerged—the exciton–polariton condensate. Exciton–polaritons (or polaritons for short) are bosonic quasiparticles that exist inside semiconductor microcavities, consisting of a superposition of an exciton and a cavity photon. Above a threshold density the polaritons macroscopically occupy the same quantum state, forming a condensate. The polaritons have a lifetime that is typically comparable to or shorter than thermalization times, giving them an inherently non-equilibrium nature. Nevertheless, they exhibit many of the features that would be expected of equilibrium Bose–Einstein condensates (BECs). The non-equilibrium nature of the system raises fundamental questions as to what it means for a system to be a BEC, and introduces new physics beyond that seen in other macroscopically coherent systems. In this review we focus on several physical phenomena exhibited by exciton–polariton condensates. In particular, we examine topics such as the difference between a polariton BEC, a polariton laser and a photon laser, as well as physical phenomena such as superfluidity, vortex formation, and Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless and Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer physics. We also discuss the physics and applications of engineered polariton structures. Exciton–polaritons, resulting from the light–matter coupling between an exciton and a photon in a cavity, form Bose–Einstein-like condensates above a critical density. Various aspects of the physics of exciton–polariton condensates are now reviewed.

title: Exciton–polariton condensates
abstract: Exciton-polariton condensates are a novel class of quantum coherent systems formed by bosonic quasiparticles—superpositions of excitons and cavity photons—in semiconductor microcavities. Distinguished by their extremely light effective mass and inherently non-equilibrium dynamics due to short lifetimes, polariton condensates exhibit macroscopic occupation of a single quantum state above a threshold density, analogous to Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC). However, their open-dissipative nature introduces unique physical phenomena and challenges the conventional thermodynamic definition of BEC. This review surveys recent advances in the realization and understanding of exciton-polariton condensates, emphasizing differences between polariton BECs, polariton lasers, and photon lasers, as well as exploring emergent phenomena such as superfluidity, vortex formation, Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transitions, and Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) physics. The discussion also covers engineered polariton structures and their potential applications, highlighting the fundamental and technological significance of these systems in exploring collective coherence and quantum phase transitions in low-dimensional, non-equilibrium environments.

title: Forces inside hadrons: Pressure, surface tension, mechanical radius, and all that
abstract: The physics related to the form factors of the energy–momentum tensor spans a wide spectrum of problems, and includes gravitational physics, hard-exclusive reactions, hadronic decays of heavy quarkonia, and the physics of exotic hadrons described as hadroquarkonia. It also provides access to the “last global unknown property:” the D-term. We review the physics associated with the form factors of the energy–momentum tensor and the D-term, their interpretations in terms of mechanical properties, their applications, and the current experimental status.
venue: International Journal of Modern Physics A

title: Forces inside hadrons: Pressure, surface tension, mechanical radius, and all that
abstract: This paper reviews the mechanical properties of hadrons as encoded in the form factors of the energy-momentum tensor (EMT), with particular emphasis on the D-term, a fundamental but experimentally elusive characteristic alongside mass and spin. The EMT form factors provide insight into the internal distribution of forces, pressure, and surface tension within hadrons, and are accessible through hard exclusive reactions and generalized parton distributions. The review covers the theoretical foundations of the EMT in QCD, definitions and constraints of EMT form factors for hadrons of various spins, and their interpretation in terms of stress tensors and mechanical radii. Applications to phenomena such as hadronic decays, exotic hadrons, and hidden-charm states are discussed, along with recent experimental progress in extracting EMT densities for nucleons and pions. The D-term’s unique sensitivity to strong interaction dynamics is highlighted, distinguishing it from other global observables, and its role in understanding the stability and structure of hadrons is elucidated.
venue: International Journal of Modern Physics A

title: Formulas and Theorems for the Special Functions of Mathematical Physics
abstract: It must be difficult to write a good collection of formulas and theorems; it surely is difficult to review one. This book is not meant for reading: It quotes theorem upon theorem without proof and hardly can hold the interest of any reader. It is not meant to be used that way. Rather, I believe, it is meant to remind one of a formula with which one is already vaguely familiar and give its exact form, including the constants which one is likely to forget.

title: Formulas and Theorems for the Special Functions of Mathematical Physics
abstract: This comprehensive reference presents an extensive compilation of formulas and theorems for the special functions central to mathematical physics, systematically covering the gamma function, hypergeometric and Bessel functions, Legendre functions, orthogonal polynomials, Kummer and Whittaker functions, parabolic cylinder functions, incomplete gamma functions, elliptic integrals and functions, as well as integral transforms and coordinate transformations. Each chapter provides definitions, key properties, recurrence relations, differential equations, integral representations, asymptotic expansions, and interrelations among functions, with formulas organized by increasing complexity to facilitate ease of use. The work incorporates updated material and expanded references to books and monographs, making it an indispensable resource for researchers and practitioners seeking precise results and methodologies in the theory and application of special functions.

title: Geometric phase from Aharonov–Bohm to Pancharatnam–Berry and beyond
abstract: Whenever a quantum system undergoes a cyclic evolution governed by a slow change of parameters, it acquires a phase factor: the geometric phase. Its most common formulations are known as the Aharonov–Bohm phase and the Pancharatnam and Berry phase, but both earlier and later manifestations exist. Although traditionally attributed to the foundations of quantum mechanics, the geometric phase has been generalized and become increasingly influential in many areas from condensed-matter physics and optics to high-energy and particle physics and from fluid mechanics to gravity and cosmology. Interestingly, the geometric phase also offers unique opportunities for quantum information and computation. In this Review, we first introduce the Aharonov–Bohm effect as an important realization of the geometric phase. Then, we discuss in detail the broader meaning, consequences and realizations of the geometric phase, emphasizing the most important mathematical methods and experimental techniques used in the study of the geometric phase, in particular those related to recent works in optics and condensed-matter physics. The geometric phase is a deep and influential concept in modern physics and related sciences. This Review briefly discusses its origin, mathematical formulation and various forms, some of which are topological; then elaborates on contemporary optical and condensed-matter applications. The Aharonov–Bohm phase, acquired by charged particles encircling a confined magnetic flux, is topological, gauge invariant and realistic, highlighting the unique role of electromagnetic potentials in quantum mechanics. The Aharonov–Bohm phase can be seen as a manifestation of Berry’s geometric phase accumulated whenever a quantum system is adiabatically transported around a cyclic circuit on an abstract surface in the parameter space (with additional generalizations to degenerate and open systems, and to non-adiabatic, non-cyclic, non-unitary evolutions). The geometric phase is an example of a holonomy (failure of parallel transport around closed cycles to preserve the geometrical information being transported) and its profound role in physics. The two main types of geometric phase in optics originate from ‘spin redirection’ (when light with a fixed state of polarization is changing direction) and from a slow change in polarization (of light propagating through an anisotropic medium in a fixed direction), giving rise to the Pancharatnam–Berry phase. In condensed-matter physics, the geometric phase manifests itself in the electronic Bloch states, quantum Hall effect, electric polarization, exchange statistics and many other phenomena. The Aharonov–Bohm phase, acquired by charged particles encircling a confined magnetic flux, is topological, gauge invariant and realistic, highlighting the unique role of electromagnetic potentials in quantum mechanics. The Aharonov–Bohm phase can be seen as a manifestation of Berry’s geometric phase accumulated whenever a quantum system is adiabatically transported around a cyclic circuit on an abstract surface in the parameter space (with additional generalizations to degenerate and open systems, and to non-adiabatic, non-cyclic, non-unitary evolutions). The geometric phase is an example of a holonomy (failure of parallel transport around closed cycles to preserve the geometrical information being transported) and its profound role in physics. The two main types of geometric phase in optics originate from ‘spin redirection’ (when light with a fixed state of polarization is changing direction) and from a slow change in polarization (of light propagating through an anisotropic medium in a fixed direction), giving rise to the Pancharatnam–Berry phase. In condensed-matter physics, the geometric phase manifests itself in the electronic Bloch states, quantum Hall effect, electric polarization, exchange statistics and many other phenomena.

title: Geometric phase from Aharonov–Bohm to Pancharatnam–Berry and beyond
abstract: The geometric phase, a fundamental concept in quantum mechanics, arises when a quantum system undergoes a cyclic evolution driven by slow changes in its parameters, resulting in a phase factor dependent solely on the path's geometry. This review traces the development of geometric phase from its early manifestation in the Aharonov–Bohm effect—highlighting the physical significance of electromagnetic potentials and the topological nature of phase acquisition—to its broader generalizations, including the Pancharatnam and Berry phases. We discuss key mathematical frameworks underpinning geometric phases, their realization in various physical systems such as condensed matter, optics, and open quantum systems, and their extensions to non-Abelian and non-Hermitian contexts. Emphasis is placed on recent experimental advances and techniques, particularly in optics and condensed-matter physics, as well as on the role of geometric phase in quantum information science. By synthesizing historical developments, theoretical foundations, and experimental progress, this review underscores the pervasive influence of geometric phase across diverse areas of physics and its continuing relevance in both fundamental research and emerging technologies.

title: Herwig++ physics and manual
abstract: In this paper we describe $\mathsf{Herwig++}$ version 2.2, a general-purpose Monte Carlo event generator for the simulation of hard lepton-lepton and hadron-hadron collisions. A number of important hard scattering processes are available, together with an interface via the Les Houches Accord to specialized matrix element generators for additional processes. The simulation of Beyond the Standard Model (BSM) physics includes a range of models and allows new models to be added by encoding the Feynman rules of the model. The parton-shower approach is used to simulate initial- and final-state QCD radiation, including colour coherence effects, with special emphasis on the correct description of radiation from heavy particles. The underlying event is simulated using an eikonal multiple parton-parton scattering model. The formation of hadrons from the quarks and gluons produced in the parton shower is described using the cluster hadronization model. Hadron decays are simulated using matrix elements, where possible including spin correlations and off-shell effects.

title: Herwig++ physics and manual
abstract: Herwig++ is a general-purpose Monte Carlo event generator designed for the simulation of high-energy lepton-lepton and hadron-hadron collisions, with a particular focus on the accurate modeling of QCD radiation. Building on the legacy of the HERWIG program, Herwig++ introduces a flexible and modular structure that supports a wide range of hard scattering processes, including those beyond the Standard Model through user-defined Feynman rules. The program employs a parton-shower approach to simulate both initial- and final-state QCD radiation, incorporating color coherence and the dead-cone effect for massive particles.
