Underlying event activity is modeled using an eikonal multiple parton scattering framework, while hadronization is described by a cluster model based on non-perturbative gluon splitting. Detailed hadron and tau decays are simulated using matrix elements that account for spin correlations and off-shell effects. This paper provides a comprehensive description of the physics models, algorithms, and code structure implemented in Herwig++ version 2.2, offering guidance for both users and developers in configuring and extending the generator for collider phenomenology studies.

title: Higgs Boson studies at future particle colliders
abstract: This document aims to provide an assessment of the potential of future colliding beam facilities to perform Higgs boson studies. The analysis builds on the submissions made by the proponents of future colliders to the European Strategy Update process, and takes as its point of departure the results expected at the completion of the HL-LHC program. This report presents quantitative results on many aspects of Higgs physics for future collider projects of sufficient maturity using uniform methodologies.

title: Higgs Boson studies at future particle colliders
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive assessment of the capabilities of proposed future particle colliders to advance Higgs boson studies beyond the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) program. Building on input from collider proponents for the European Strategy Update, the analysis systematically compares the projected performance of several collider concepts—including HE-LHC, FCC-ee, FCC-hh, CEPC, ILC, CLIC, and LHeC—using uniform methodologies. Key aspects examined include precision measurements of Higgs couplings to fermions and vector bosons within both the kappa framework and effective field theory approaches, sensitivity to rare and invisible Higgs decays, determination of the Higgs self-coupling, CP properties, mass, and total width. The study also considers theoretical uncertainties and explores the prospects for further improvements with advanced facilities such as muon colliders and multi-TeV electron-positron colliders. The results demonstrate that future colliders can significantly enhance our understanding of the Higgs sector, providing stringent tests of Standard Model predictions and offering powerful probes for new physics scenarios.

title: Information, physics, quantum: the search for links
abstract: This report reviews what quantum physics and information theory have to tell us about the age-old question, How come existence? No escape is evident from four conclusions: (1) The world cannot be a giant machine, ruled by any preestablished continuum physical law. (2) There is no such thing at the microscopic level as space or time or spacetime continuum. (3) The familiar probability function or functional, and wave equation or functional wave equation, of standard quantum theory provide mere continuum idealizations and by reason of this circumstance conceal the information-theoretic source from which they derive. (4) No element in the description of physics shows itself as closer to primordial than the elementary quantum phenomenon, that is, the elementary device-intermediated act of posing a yes-no physical question and eliciting an answer or, in brief, the elementary act of observer-participancy. Otherwise stated, every physical quantity, every it, derives its ultimate significance from bits, binary yes-or-no indications, a conclusion which we epitomize in the phrase, it from bit. Revolution in outlook though Kepler, Newton, and Einstein brought us [1-4], and still more startling the story of life [5-7] that evolution forced upon an unwilling world, the ultimate shock to preconceived ideas lies ahead, be it a decade hence, a century or a millenium. The overarching principle of 20th-century physics, the quantum [8] — and the principle of complementarity [9] that is central idea of the quantum — leaves us no escape, Niels Bohr tells us, [10] from 'a radical revision of our attitude as regards physical reality' and a 'fundamental modification of all ideas regarding the absolute character of physical phenomena.' Transcending Einstein's summons [11] of 1908, 'This quantum business is so incredibly important and difficult that everyone should busy himself with it,' Bohr's modest words direct us to the supreme goal: Deduce the quantum from an understanding of existence. How make headway toward a goal so great against difficulties so large? The search for understanding presents to us three questions, four no's and five clues:

title: Information, physics, quantum: the search for links
abstract: This paper explores the foundational connections between quantum physics and information theory in addressing the question of existence. It argues that the universe cannot be understood as a deterministic machine governed by preexisting physical laws or a spacetime continuum at the microscopic level. Instead, quantum phenomena and the mathematical structures of standard quantum theory are seen as idealizations that obscure their true information-theoretic origins. The central thesis, encapsulated in the phrase 'it from bit,' posits that all physical entities and phenomena ultimately derive from discrete acts of observation—binary yes-or-no questions and their outcomes—making information fundamental to reality. Through examples such as photon detection, quantum interference, and black hole entropy, the paper illustrates how physical properties emerge from informational processes. The discussion is framed by four guiding 'no's' that reject infinite regress, absolute laws, and continuum concepts, suggesting instead a participatory universe where observer-participancy, information, and physics form a self-consistent loop. The work concludes that understanding existence requires reinterpreting physics in purely informational terms, with quantum theory serving as both a guide and a challenge to our conception of reality.

title: Many-body physics with individually controlled Rydberg atoms
abstract: Recent decades have witnessed great developments in the field of quantum simulation—where synthetic systems are built and studied to gain insight into complicated, many-body real-world problems. Systems of individually controlled neutral atoms, interacting with each other when excited to Rydberg states, have emerged as a promising platform for this task, particularly for the simulation of spin systems. Here, we review the techniques necessary for the manipulation of neutral atoms for the purpose of quantum simulation—such as quantum gas microscopes and arrays of optical tweezers—and explain how the different types of interactions between Rydberg atoms allow a natural mapping onto various quantum spin models. We discuss recent achievements in the study of quantum many-body physics in this platform, and some current research directions beyond that. This Review Article outlines the techniques necessary for the manipulation of neutral atoms and making use of their interactions, when excited to Rydberg states, to achieve the goal of quantum simulation of many-body physics.

title: Many-body physics with individually controlled Rydberg atoms
abstract: Individually controlled Rydberg atoms have emerged as a powerful platform for exploring quantum many-body physics and simulating spin models. This review discusses the experimental advances enabling the trapping and manipulation of single neutral atoms in optical lattices and tweezer arrays, and details how their strong, tunable interactions when excited to Rydberg states naturally implement quantum spin Hamiltonians such as the Ising and XY models. The Rydberg blockade mechanism is highlighted as a key feature for generating entanglement and controlling collective dynamics. Recent experimental achievements are surveyed, demonstrating the versatility of these systems for studying quantum phase transitions, non-equilibrium dynamics, and entanglement generation. The article concludes by outlining future prospects for scalable quantum simulation, quantum information processing, and the exploration of novel many-body phenomena using Rydberg atom arrays.

title: New parton distributions for collider physics
abstract: We extract new parton distribution functions (PDFs) of the proton by global analysis of hard scattering data in the general-mass framework of perturbative quantum chromodynamics. Our analysis includes new theoretical developments together with the most recent collider data from deep-inelastic scattering, vector boson production, and single-inclusive jet production. Because of the difficulty in fitting both the D0 Run-II W lepton asymmetry data and some fixed-target DIS data, we present two families of PDFs, CT10 and CT10W, without and with these high-luminosity W lepton asymmetry data included in the global analysis. With both sets of PDFs, we study theoretical predictions and uncertainties for a diverse selection of processes at the Fermilab Tevatron and the CERN Large Hadron Collider.

title: New parton distributions for collider physics
abstract: We present new parton distribution functions (PDFs) for the proton, derived from a global analysis of hard scattering data within the general-mass framework of perturbative quantum chromodynamics. Incorporating recent theoretical improvements and the latest collider data—including deep-inelastic scattering, vector boson production, and single-inclusive jet production—we address tensions between high-precision DØ Run-II W lepton asymmetry data and certain fixed-target DIS measurements by providing two PDF sets: CT10, which excludes, and CT10W, which includes these asymmetry data with increased weight. Enhanced treatment of systematic uncertainties and more flexible PDF parametrizations improve both the fit quality and uncertainty estimates. We assess the impact of new experimental inputs, particularly the combined HERA-1 data, and evaluate the consistency of constraints from diverse experiments. The resulting PDFs are applied to predict key processes at the Fermilab Tevatron and CERN Large Hadron Collider, providing updated theoretical predictions and uncertainty estimates for collider phenomenology.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Cardiac Activation Mapping
abstract: A critical procedure in diagnosing atrial fibrillation is the creation of electro-anatomic activation maps. Current methods generate these mappings from interpolation using a few sparse data points recorded inside the atria; they neither include prior knowledge of the underlying physics nor uncertainty of these recordings. Here we propose a physics-informed neural network for cardiac activation mapping that accounts for the underlying wave propagation dynamics and we quantify the epistemic uncertainty associated with these predictions. These uncertainty estimates not only allow us to quantify the predictive error of the neural network, but also help to reduce it by judiciously selecting new informative measurement locations via active learning. We illustrate the potential of our approach using a synthetic benchmark problem and a personalized electrophysiology model of the left atrium. We show that our new method outperforms linear interpolation and Gaussian process regression for the benchmark problem and linear interpolation at clinical densities for the left atrium. In both cases, the active learning algorithm achieves lower error levels than random allocation. Our findings open the door toward physics-based electro-anatomic mapping with the ultimate goals to reduce procedural time and improve diagnostic predictability for patients affected by atrial fibrillation. Open source code is available at https://github.com/fsahli/EikonalNet.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Cardiac Activation Mapping
abstract: Electro-anatomic activation mapping is essential for diagnosing atrial fibrillation, yet current clinical methods rely on sparse measurements and interpolation techniques that neglect the underlying physics and uncertainty quantification. We present a physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework that incorporates the Eikonal equation governing cardiac wave propagation to generate more accurate cardiac activation maps from limited data. Our approach estimates epistemic uncertainty using randomized prior functions and leverages these estimates within an active learning algorithm to strategically select new measurement locations, thereby reducing predictive error. We validate the method on both a synthetic benchmark and a personalized left atrial model, demonstrating superior accuracy compared to linear interpolation and Gaussian process regression, especially at clinically relevant data densities. Active learning further improves mapping accuracy over random sampling strategies. These results highlight the potential of PINNs for efficient, physics-based electro-anatomic mapping with improved diagnostic reliability and reduced procedural time in atrial fibrillation care.

title: Physics and financial economics (1776–2014): puzzles, Ising and agent-based models
abstract: This short review presents a selected history of the mutual fertilization between physics and economics—from Isaac Newton and Adam Smith to the present. The fundamentally different perspectives embraced in theories developed in financial economics compared with physics are dissected with the examples of the volatility smile and of the excess volatility puzzle. The role of the Ising model of phase transitions to model social and financial systems is reviewed, with the concepts of random utilities and the logit model as the analog of the Boltzmann factor in statistical physics. Recent extensions in terms of quantum decision theory are also covered. A wealth of models are discussed briefly that build on the Ising model and generalize it to account for the many stylized facts of financial markets. A summary of the relevance of the Ising model and its extensions is provided to account for financial bubbles and crashes. The review would be incomplete if it did not cover the dynamical field of agent-based models (ABMs), also known as computational economic models, of which the Ising-type models are just special ABM implementations. We formulate the ‘Emerging Intelligence Market Hypothesis’ to reconcile the pervasive presence of ‘noise traders’ with the near efficiency of financial markets. Finally, we note that evolutionary biology, more than physics, is now playing a growing role to inspire models of financial markets.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: Physics and financial economics (1776–2014): puzzles, Ising and agent-based models
abstract: This review traces the historical and conceptual interplay between physics and financial economics from the late 18th century to the present, highlighting how physical models and concepts have informed economic thought and vice versa. It examines key puzzles in financial economics, such as the volatility smile and excess volatility, through the contrasting lenses of economics and physics. The paper explores the application of the Ising model and its generalizations to social and financial systems, drawing analogies between statistical mechanics (e.g., Boltzmann factor, logit models) and decision-making in markets. Recent developments including quantum decision theory and agent-based models (ABMs) are discussed as powerful tools for capturing heterogeneity, out-of-equilibrium dynamics, and collective phenomena such as bubbles and crashes. The review introduces the “Emerging Market Intelligence Hypothesis” to reconcile persistent market inefficiencies with near-efficient outcomes, and argues that evolutionary biology is increasingly influential in modeling financial markets. Overall, the paper underscores the value of interdisciplinary approaches—particularly those rooted in complex systems science—for understanding the adaptive, dynamic, and often unpredictable nature of financial markets.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: Physics of thin films
abstract: The investigation of the physical properties of matter has progressed so much during the last hundred years that today physics is divided into a large group of special branches, which are often very distant from each other. These branches arise because of the vast extent of the science itself, and are distinguished by the particular area studied, the method of investigation and so on. An independent and important branch that has developed recently is the physics of thin films. This deals with systems which have only one common property, namely, that one of their dimensions is very small, though all other physical properties of such systems may be different, as well as methods of investigating them. Usually, we investigate the physical characteristics of three-dimensional bodies. Their characteristic prop::!rties are often related to a unit volume, i.e. it is assumed that they are volume-independent. This assumption is legitimate as long as the dimensions are 'normal', i.e. more or less within macroscopic limits; but as soon as one dimension becomes so small that there is a considerable increase in a surface-to-volume ratio, that assumption is no longer valid.

title: Physics of thin films
abstract: This comprehensive work provides an in-depth exploration of the physics of thin films, encompassing their preparation methods, measurement techniques, formation mechanisms, and structural characterization. It systematically reviews chemical, electrochemical, sputtering, and vacuum evaporation techniques for thin film deposition, followed by detailed discussions on methods for measuring film thickness and deposition rates. The book examines the stages of film formation, nucleation theories, growth processes, and the influence of various factors on film structure and crystallography, including epitaxial growth. Advanced analytical techniques such as electron microscopy, electron diffraction, X-ray methods, and Auger spectroscopy are presented for the assessment of composition, morphology, and structure. The physical properties of thin films—including mechanical, electrical, magnetic, and optical characteristics—are analyzed with attention to experimental methods and underlying mechanisms. Finally, the applications of thin films in optics and electronics are surveyed, highlighting their roles in contacts, resistors, capacitors, inductors, ferromagnetic and superconducting devices, microacoustic elements, integrated circuits, optoelectronics, and integrated optics. This text serves as a foundational reference for researchers and practitioners engaged in thin film science and technology.

title: Physics potential and experimental challenges of the LHC luminosity upgrade
abstract: Abstract.We discuss the physics potential and the experimental challenges of an upgraded LHC running at an instantaneous luminosity of 1035 cm-2s-1. The detector R&D needed to operate ATLAS and CMS in a very high radiation environment and the expected detector performance are discussed. A few examples of the increased physics potential are given, ranging from precise measurements within the Standard Model (in particular in the Higgs sector) to the discovery reach for several New Physics processes.

title: Physics potential and experimental challenges of the LHC luminosity upgrade
abstract: This paper explores the enhanced physics opportunities and significant experimental challenges associated with upgrading the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC) to operate at an instantaneous luminosity of 10^35 cm^−2 s^−1, referred to as the Super-LHC (SLHC). The study evaluates the potential for more precise measurements of Standard Model parameters, such as gauge boson and Higgs couplings, improved determination of new physics parameters, extended discovery reach for high-mass phenomena including new heavy particles and extra dimensions, and increased sensitivity to rare processes. The impact of high luminosity on detector performance is analyzed, with particular attention to issues such as event pile-up, radiation damage, and the need for advanced detector R&D in areas like tracking, calorimetry, muon systems, trigger, and data acquisition. The paper assumes optimistic detector performance scenarios to estimate the physics gains achievable with a tenfold increase in statistics. Overall, the SLHC upgrade promises substantial advances in probing fundamental interactions while leveraging existing infrastructure, provided that key technological and engineering challenges can be addressed through targeted research and development.

title: Robust Independent Validation of Experiment and Theory: Rivet version 3
abstract: First released in 2010, the Rivet library forms an important repository for analysis code, facilitating comparisons between measurements of the final state in particle collisions and theoretical calculations of those final states. We give an overview of Rivet's current design and implementation, its uptake for analysis preservation and physics results, and summarise recent developments including propagation of MC systematic-uncertainty weights, heavy-ion and ep physics, and systems for detector emulation. In addition, we provide a short user guide that supplements and updates the Rivet user manual.

title: Robust Independent Validation of Experiment and Theory: Rivet version 3
abstract: Rivet version 3 is a major update to the widely used Rivet library, which provides a robust framework for the independent validation and comparison of experimental measurements and theoretical predictions in particle physics. This paper presents an overview of Rivet’s architecture, its applications in analysis preservation, event generator validation, and phenomenological studies, as well as its adoption by experimental collaborations. Key new features include enhanced support for systematic uncertainty propagation via event weights, improved handling of heavy-ion and deep-inelastic scattering analyses, tools for detector emulation, and mechanisms for more accurate run merging. The updated system introduces flexible kinematic cuts, advanced filtering functors, and expanded analysis options to facilitate modern collider data analysis workflows. A concise user guide is provided to assist new users with installation, running analyses, and contributing new routines. These developments position Rivet as an essential tool for ensuring reproducibility, transparency, and precision in the comparison of theoretical models with collider data.

title: Search for New Physics with Atoms and Molecules
abstract: Advances in atomic physics, such as cooling and trapping of atoms and molecules and developments in frequency metrology, have added orders of magnitude to the precision of atom-based clocks and sensors. Applications extend beyond atomic physics and this article reviews using these new techniques to address important challenges in physics and to look for variations in the fundamental constants, search for interactions beyond the standard model of particle physics, and test the principles of general relativity.

title: Search for New Physics with Atoms and Molecules
abstract: This review examines recent advances in atomic, molecular, and optical (AMO) physics that enable precision tests of fundamental physical laws and searches for physics beyond the Standard Model. The article surveys experimental and theoretical developments in using atoms and molecules to probe parity violation, time-reversal symmetry breaking via electric dipole moments, CPT and Lorentz invariance, possible variations of fundamental constants, quantum electrodynamics, general relativity, and the equivalence principle. It discusses laboratory searches for dark matter, dark energy, exotic spin-dependent and spin-independent interactions, and violations of quantum statistics. Key results are contextualized within broader efforts to address unresolved issues such as the nature of dark matter and energy, the matter-antimatter asymmetry, and the integration of gravity with quantum theory. The review highlights how advances in AMO techniques—such as laser cooling, atomic clocks, magnetometry, and interferometry—have led to unprecedented measurement precision, opening new avenues for discovery. Ongoing and future experiments are outlined, emphasizing the potential for AMO systems to reveal new particles or forces and to constrain or uncover deviations from established physical theories.

title: Self-organization and the physics of glassy networks
abstract: Network glasses are the physical prototype for many self-organized systems, ranging from proteins to computer science. Conventional theories of gases, liquids and crystals do not account for the strongly material-selective character of the glass-forming tendency, the phase diagrams of glasses or their optimizable properties. A new topological theory, only 25 years old, has succeeded where conventional theories have failed. It shows that (probably all slowly quenched) glasses, including network glasses, are the result of the combined effects of a few simple mechanisms. These glass-forming mechanisms are topological in nature and have already been identified for several important glasses, including chalcogenide alloys, silicates (window glass and computer chips) and proteins.

title: Self-organization and the physics of glassy networks
abstract: Network glasses exemplify self-organized systems whose unique glass-forming tendencies and phase behaviors elude explanation by conventional theories of gases, liquids, and crystals. This paper reviews the emergence of a topological theory that accounts for the formation and properties of glassy networks through simple, universal mechanisms based on network connectivity and constraints. The theory posits that the balance between interatomic constraints and degrees of freedom determines whether a network is floppy, rigid, or ideally isostatic, with the latter corresponding to an arrested, stress-free glassy state. Experimental evidence from chalcogenide alloys and other network glasses confirms key predictions, including the existence of a critical mean coordination number and the identification of two distinct topological transitions that bound an intermediate phase characterized by self-organization. This intermediate phase, observed in both insulating and electronic glasses, exhibits sharp compositional boundaries and is associated with a reversibility window in calorimetric measurements. The topological approach not only unifies understanding across diverse glassy materials but also establishes conceptual bridges to biophysical networks such as proteins, highlighting the broad applicability of self-organization principles in complex systems.

title: Strong coupling between surface plasmon polaritons and emitters: a review
abstract: In this review we look at the concepts and state-of-the-art concerning the strong coupling of surface plasmon-polariton modes to states associated with quantum emitters such as excitons in J-aggregates, dye molecules and quantum dots. We explore the phenomenon of strong coupling with reference to a number of examples involving electromagnetic fields and matter. We then provide a concise description of the relevant background physics of surface plasmon polaritons. An extensive overview of the historical background and a detailed discussion of more recent relevant experimental advances concerning strong coupling between surface plasmon polaritons and quantum emitters is then presented. Three conceptual frameworks are then discussed and compared in depth: classical, semi-classical and fully quantum mechanical; these theoretical frameworks will have relevance to strong coupling beyond that involving surface plasmon polaritons. We conclude our review with a perspective on the future of this rapidly emerging field, one we are sure will grow to encompass more intriguing physics and will develop in scope to be of relevance to other areas of science.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: Strong coupling between surface plasmon polaritons and emitters: a review
abstract: This review provides a comprehensive overview of the strong coupling phenomenon between surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs) and quantum emitters, such as excitons in J-aggregates, dye molecules, and quantum dots. The article introduces the fundamental physics underlying SPPs and strong coupling, using the coupled harmonic oscillator model to elucidate how hybrid light-matter states emerge when the interaction strength exceeds relevant energy scales, leading to observable effects like Rabi splitting. A historical perspective is offered alongside a detailed discussion of recent experimental advances that demonstrate strong coupling in various plasmonic systems. Theoretical approaches are critically compared across classical, semi-classical, and fully quantum mechanical frameworks, highlighting their applicability and limitations in describing strong coupling phenomena. The review concludes by outlining future directions for the field, emphasizing its potential to enable novel quantum optical systems and impact a broad range of scientific disciplines through advances in nanofabrication and photonic engineering.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: The microphysics of collisionless shock waves
abstract: Collisionless shocks, that is shocks mediated by electromagnetic processes, are customary in space physics and in astrophysics. They are to be found in a great variety of objects and environments: magnetospheric and heliospheric shocks, supernova remnants, pulsar winds and their nebulæ, active galactic nuclei, gamma-ray bursts and clusters of galaxies shock waves. Collisionless shock microphysics enters at different stages of shock formation, shock dynamics and particle energization and/or acceleration. It turns out that the shock phenomenon is a multi-scale non-linear problem in time and space. It is complexified by the impact due to high-energy cosmic rays in astrophysical environments. This review adresses the physics of shock formation, shock dynamics and particle acceleration based on a close examination of available multi-wavelength or in situ observations, analytical and numerical developments. A particular emphasis is made on the different instabilities triggered during the shock formation and in association with particle acceleration processes with regards to the properties of the background upstream medium. It appears that among the most important parameters the background magnetic field through the magnetization and its obliquity is the dominant one. The shock velocity that can reach relativistic speeds has also a strong impact over the development of the micro-instabilities and the fate of particle acceleration. Recent developments of laboratory shock experiments has started to bring some new insights in the physics of space plasma and astrophysical shock waves. A special section is dedicated to new laser plasma experiments probing shock physics.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: The microphysics of collisionless shock waves
abstract: Collisionless shock waves, governed by electromagnetic interactions rather than particle collisions, are fundamental to a wide range of astrophysical and space environments, including supernova remnants, pulsar winds, gamma-ray bursts, and galaxy clusters. This review synthesizes recent advances in the understanding of the microphysical processes underlying collisionless shock formation, dynamics, and particle acceleration. Emphasis is placed on the multi-scale, nonlinear nature of these shocks and the critical roles played by background magnetic field strength, orientation, and shock velocity in shaping instabilities and particle energization. The interplay between high-energy cosmic rays and shock structure is explored through a combination of observational data, analytical theory, and numerical simulations. Key instabilities—driven by resonant particle-wave interactions, return currents, and energetic particle gradients—are examined for their impact on magnetic field amplification and diffusive shock acceleration efficiency. The review also highlights recent progress in laboratory plasma experiments that probe shock microphysics, offering new perspectives on processes relevant to both space and astrophysical shocks.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: The Physical Implementation of Quantum Computation
abstract: After a brief introduction to the principles and promise of quantum information processing, the requirements for the physical implementation of quantum computation are discussed. These five requirements, plus two relating to the communication of quantum information, are extensively ex- plored and related to the many schemes in atomic physics, quantum optics, nuclear and electron magnetic resonance spectroscopy, superconducting electronics, and quantum-dot physics, for achiev- ing quantum computing. I. INTRODUCTION � The advent of quantum information processing, as an abstract concept, has given birth to a great deal of new thinking, of a very concrete form, about how to create physical computing devices that operate in the hitherto unexplored quantum mechanical regime. The efforts now underway to produce working laboratory devices that perform this profoundly new form of information pro- cessing are the subject of this book. In this chapter I provide an overview of the common objectives of the investigations reported in the remain- der of this special issue. The scope of the approaches, proposed and underway, to the implementation of quan- tum hardware is remarkable, emerging from specialties in atomic physics (1), in quantum optics (2), in nuclear (3) and electron (4) magnetic resonance spectroscopy, in su- perconducting device physics (5), in electron physics (6), and in mesoscopic and quantum dot research (7). This amazing variety of approaches has arisen because, as we will see, the principles of quantum computing are posed using the most fundamental ideas of quantum mechanics, ones whose embodiment can be contemplated in virtually every branch of quantum physics. The interdisciplinary spirit which has been fostered as a result is one of the most pleasant and remarkable fea- tures of this field. The excitement and freshness that has been produced bodes well for the prospect for discovery, invention, and innovation in this endeavor.

title: The Physical Implementation of Quantum Computation
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the physical requirements for implementing quantum computation, beginning with an introduction to the foundational principles and potential advantages of quantum information processing. It identifies and elaborates on five essential criteria for realizing practical quantum computers: scalable systems with well-characterized qubits, the ability to initialize qubits to a known state, long relevant decoherence times, a universal set of quantum gates, and qubit-specific measurement capability. Additionally, two further requirements related to quantum communication are discussed. The analysis connects these criteria to a broad spectrum of proposed physical implementations, including systems based on atomic physics, quantum optics, nuclear and electron magnetic resonance spectroscopy, superconducting electronics, and quantum dots. By examining the challenges and prospects associated with each approach, the paper highlights the interdisciplinary nature of the field and underscores the ongoing innovation driving progress toward viable quantum computing technologies.

title: The physics of gamma-ray bursts
abstract: Gamma-ray bursts (GRB's), short and intense pulses of low-energy $\ensuremath{\gamma}$ rays, have fascinated astronomers and astrophysicists since their unexpected discovery in the late sixties. During the last decade, several space missions\char22{}BATSE (Burst and Transient Source Experiment) on the Compton Gamma-Ray Observatory, BeppoSAX and now HETE II (High-Energy Transient Explorer)\char22{}together with ground-based optical, infrared, and radio observatories have revolutionized our understanding of GRB's, showing that they are cosmological, that they are accompanied by long-lasting afterglows, and that they are associated with core-collapse supernovae. At the same time a theoretical understanding has emerged in the form of the fireball internal-external shocks model. According to this model GRB's are produced when the kinetic energy of an ultrarelativistic flow is dissipated in internal collisions. The afterglow arises when the flow is slowed down by shocks with the surrounding circumburst matter. This model has had numerous successful predictions, like the predictions of the afterglow itself, of jet breaks in the afterglow light curve, and of the optical flash that accompanies the GRB's. This review focuses on the current theoretical understanding of the physical processes believed to take place in GRB's.

title: The physics of gamma-ray bursts
abstract: Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are among the most luminous and energetic events in the universe, characterized by brief, intense emissions of soft gamma-rays originating from cosmological distances. This review synthesizes observational advances and theoretical developments in GRB physics, focusing on the fireball internal-external shocks model. Observations from space- and ground-based instruments have established that GRBs are typically followed by long-lasting afterglows across X-ray, optical, and radio wavelengths, enabling host galaxy identification and redshift measurement. The fireball model posits that GRBs result from the dissipation of kinetic energy in ultra-relativistic outflows via internal shocks, while afterglows arise from external shocks with the surrounding medium. Theoretical analysis addresses relativistic effects, shock physics, particle acceleration, synchrotron and inverse Compton emission, and polarization. The review examines prompt emission mechanisms, afterglow modeling, and associated phenomena such as high-energy neutrinos, cosmic rays, and gravitational waves. Progenitor models involving massive star collapse or compact object mergers are discussed in light of energetic requirements and observed associations with supernovae and star-forming regions. Despite significant progress, key questions remain regarding the nature of the central engine and detailed emission processes, highlighting directions for future research in GRB astrophysics.

title: The physics of heavy Z' gauge bosons
abstract: The $\mathrm{U}{(1)}^{\ensuremath{'}}$ symmetry associated with a possible heavy ${Z}^{\ensuremath{'}}$ would have profound implications for particle physics and cosmology. The motivations for such particles in various extensions of the standard model, possible ranges for their masses and couplings, and classes of anomaly-free models are discussed. Present limits from electroweak and collider experiments are briefly surveyed, as are prospects for discovery and diagnostic study at future colliders. Implications of a ${Z}^{\ensuremath{'}}$ are discussed, including an extended Higgs sector, extended neutralino sector, and solution to the $\ensuremath{\mu}$ problem in supersymmetry; exotic fermions needed for anomaly cancellation; possible flavor changing neutral current effects; neutrino mass; possible ${Z}^{\ensuremath{'}}$ mediation of supersymmetry breaking; and cosmological implications for cold dark matter and electroweak baryogenesis.

title: The physics of heavy Z' gauge bosons
abstract: Heavy Z′ gauge bosons, arising from additional U(1)′ symmetries in extensions of the Standard Model, are well-motivated by grand unification, string constructions, and various TeV-scale physics scenarios. This review surveys the theoretical foundations, model-building aspects, and phenomenological implications of such Z′ bosons. It discusses their couplings, mass generation mechanisms, anomaly cancellation requirements, and possible kinetic mixing with the Standard Model Z boson. A broad range of models is considered, including those inspired by grand unification, extra dimensions, strong dynamics, and family nonuniversal couplings. Current experimental constraints from precision electroweak measurements and collider searches are summarized, along with prospects for discovery at future facilities. The presence of a Z′ can have far-reaching consequences for the Higgs and neutralino sectors, provide solutions to the supersymmetric μ problem, introduce exotic fermions, induce flavor-changing neutral currents, affect neutrino mass generation, and mediate supersymmetry breaking. Cosmological implications include potential roles in cold dark matter production and electroweak baryogenesis. The discovery of a heavy Z′ would thus have profound impacts on particle physics and cosmology, motivating continued theoretical and experimental exploration.

title: TWO-PERIOD GREEN'S FUNCTION IN STATISTICAL PHYSICS
abstract: Various aspects of the application of Green's functions in statistical physics are reviewed, and the future applications of two-period functions (retarding and advancing) are analyzed. The principle properties of the two- period Green's function and their simplest application in irreversible process theory, in the theory of superconductors, in ferromagnetics, and in electron- lattice reactions in common metals and semiconductors are discussed. It is also shown that the causal Green's functions can be successfully replaced with retarding and advancing Green's functions in the analytical expansion of the complex plane. Statistical mechanics sometimes employs the Motsubara temperature Green's functions which are not related to time; however, they are less adaptable than the temperature-time Green's functions. (R.V.J.)

title: TWO-PERIOD GREEN'S FUNCTION IN STATISTICAL PHYSICS
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of two-period (two-time) Green's functions within the framework of statistical physics, emphasizing their foundational role in the study of systems with a large number of interacting particles. Building on the formalism of quantum field theory, the work introduces temperature-dependent two-time Green's functions—causal, retarded, and advanced—as generalizations of correlation functions, highlighting their advantages for calculating observable quantities and constructing equations of motion. The spectral representations of these functions are discussed, demonstrating their utility in addressing the challenges posed by continuous energy spectra and large system sizes, where traditional perturbation theory encounters difficulties. The paper explores applications to the theory of irreversible processes, ideal quantum gases, superconductivity, ferromagnetism, and electron-lattice interactions in metals and semiconductors. By employing two-time retarded and advanced Green's functions instead of conventional causal functions, the approach facilitates analytic continuation in the complex plane and provides a unified framework for tackling a wide range of problems in quantum statistical mechanics. The results underscore the effectiveness and versatility of two-period Green's function methods for analyzing equilibrium and nonequilibrium phenomena in many-body systems.

title: A Short History of Sociological Thought
abstract: This text offers an account of the rise of sociological thought from its origins in the 18th century. Beginning with the classical sociology of Marx, Durkheim, Weber and Simmel, it goes on to examine paradigms of functionalism, interactionism, structuralism and critical Marxism, and ends by discussing salient 1990s sociological theory, including the theories of Foucault, Baudrillard, Giddens, Habermas and others. It critically engages with sociological theory throughout its development, offering students a path through competing traditions and perspectives that brings out the distinctive value and limitations of these.

title: A Short History of Sociological Thought
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the development of sociological thought from its origins in eighteenth-century social philosophy to contemporary theoretical perspectives. It traces the emergence of sociology as a distinct discipline, examining foundational figures such as Vico, Montesquieu, and the thinkers of the Scottish Enlightenment, and explores the rise of positivism and empiricism in the nineteenth century through the works of Comte, Saint-Simon, Mill, and Spencer. The analysis highlights Marxism’s contributions to understanding capitalist development, class formation, and historical determinism. The paper then examines classical sociology’s critique of positivism through Durkheim’s functionalism and Weber’s interpretive sociology, as well as theories of social action and domination. It further considers the evolution of Marxist thought after Marx, including the ideas of Lukacs and Gramsci. In its discussion of modern sociology, the paper reviews key developments in functionalism, action theory, symbolic interactionism, phenomenology, structuralism, and the sociology of knowledge and culture. The conclusion addresses ongoing debates concerning democracy, industrialization, legitimation, and the future trajectory of sociological theory. Through this historical survey, the paper elucidates how sociological thought has responded to changing social conditions and intellectual currents over time.

title: Feminist Praxis: Research, Theory and Epistemology in Feminist Sociology
abstract: This collection critically examines the intersections of research, theory, and epistemology within feminist sociology, foregrounding feminist praxis as both a methodological and political project. Through diverse contributions, it interrogates the academic production of knowledge, challenges traditional divides between quantitative and qualitative methods, and highlights the significance of auto/biographical approaches in feminist research. The volume explores the complexities of defining research topics, negotiating personal and professional identities, and analytically utilizing lived experience to produce situated knowledge. By engaging with written and visual texts, contributors demonstrate how feminist epistemologies disrupt conventional sociological paradigms and offer transformative insights into gender, class, ethnicity, and professional practice. This work advances feminist sociology by illuminating the reflexive processes underpinning feminist inquiry and advocating for methodologies that center women's experiences and challenge dominant power structures in knowledge production.

title: “Fundamental Causes” of Social Inequalities in Mortality: A Test of the Theory∗
abstract: Medicine and epidemiology currently dominate the study of the strong association between socioeconomic status and mortality. Socioeconomic status typically is viewed as a causally irrelevant “confounding variable” or as a less critical variable marking only the beginning of a causal chain in which intervening risk factors are given prominence. Yet the association between socioeconomic status and mortality has persisted despite radical changes in the diseases and risk factors that are presumed to explain it. This suggests that the effect of socioeconomic status on mortality essentially cannot be understood by reductive explanations that focus on current mechanisms. Accordingly, Link and Phelan (1995) proposed that socioeconomic status is a “fundamental cause” of mortality disparities—that socioeconomic disparities endure despite changing mechanisms because socioeconomic status embodies an array of resources, such as money, knowledge, prestige, power, and beneficial social connections, that protect health no matter what mechanisms are relevant at any given time. We identified a situation in which resources should be less helpful in prolonging life, and derived the following prediction from the theory: For less preventable causes of death (for which we know little about prevention or treatment), socioeconomic status will be less strongly associated with mortality than for more preventable causes. We tested this hypothesis with the National Longitudinal Mortality Study, which followed Current Population Survey respondents (N = 370,930) for mortality for nine years. Our hypothesis was supported, lending support to the theory of fundamental causes and more generally to the importance of a sociological approach to the study of socio-economic disparities in mortality.
venue: Journal of Health and Social Behavior

title: “Fundamental Causes” of Social Inequalities in Mortality: A Test of the Theory∗
abstract: This study tests the theory that socioeconomic status (SES) is a “fundamental cause” of social inequalities in mortality, maintaining its association with health outcomes despite changing mechanisms and risk factors over time. Drawing on data from the National Longitudinal Mortality Study, which tracked over 370,000 individuals for nine years, the authors examine whether SES is more strongly associated with mortality from preventable causes than from less preventable ones. The findings confirm that SES disparities are greater for deaths from causes amenable to prevention or treatment, supporting the theory that SES operates through flexible resources—such as money, knowledge, power, and social connections—that can be used to avoid risks and adopt protective strategies as new health threats and interventions emerge. These results underscore the enduring impact of social conditions on health and highlight the necessity of sociological perspectives in understanding and addressing persistent health inequalities.
venue: Journal of Health and Social Behavior

title: Handbook of Qualitative Research
abstract: The substantially updated and revised Fifth Edition of this landmark handbook presents the state-of-the-art theory and practice of qualitative inquiry. Representing top scholars from around the world, the editors and contributors continue the tradition of synthesizing existing literature, defining the present, and shaping the future of qualitative research. The Fifth Edition contains 19 new chapters, with 16 revised―making it virtually a new volume―while retaining six classic chapters from previous editions.

title: Handbook of Qualitative Research
abstract: The third edition of the Handbook of Qualitative Research, edited by Denzin and Lincoln, serves as a foundational reference for qualitative researchers, offering comprehensive updates and new topics that reflect the evolving landscape of the field. This edition expands its scope to include indigenous research, critical and performance ethnography, arts-based inquiry, narrative research, Foucault’s influence, ethics, online research strategies, and evaluation policies. The handbook is organized into an introduction and six parts: an overview of the discipline’s current state; a call for socially and morally engaged science; epistemological foundations; research methods; data collection and analysis techniques; interpretation, evaluation, and presentation of results; and future directions for qualitative inquiry. Each section integrates updated chapters from previous editions alongside new contributions, making this volume an essential resource for understanding both the theoretical and practical dimensions of qualitative research.

title: Handbook of the Sociology of Gender
abstract: This handbook provides a comprehensive view of the field of the sociology of gender. It presents the most important theories about gender and methods used to study gender, as well as extensive coverage of the latest research on gender in the most important areas of social life, including gendered bodies, sexuality, carework, paid labor, social movements, incarceration, migration, gendered violence, and others. Building from previous publications this handbook includes a vast array of chapters from leading researchers in the sociological study of gender. It synthesizes the diverse field of gender scholarship into a cohesive theoretical framework, gender structure theory, in order to position the specific contributions of each author/chapter as part of a complex and multidimensional gender structure. Through this organization of the handbook, readers do not only gain tremendous insight from each chapter, but they also attain a broader understanding of the way multiple genderedprocesses are interrelated and mutually constitutive. While the specific focus of the handbook is on gender, the chapters included in the volume also give significant attention to the interrelation of race, class, and other systems of stratification as they intersect and implicate gendered processes.

title: Handbook of the Sociology of Gender
abstract: The Handbook of the Sociology of Gender offers a comprehensive and critical overview of contemporary sociological theories and research on gender as a pervasive social construct shaping all aspects of human life. Edited by Janet Saltzman Chafetz and featuring contributions from leading scholars, the volume addresses gender across micro, meso, and macro levels, examining its influence within social processes, structures, and major institutions such as the economy, family, polity, legal systems, health care, education, science, sport, and religion. Emphasizing comparative cross-national and historical perspectives, the handbook also highlights within-gender differences related to class, race/ethnicity, sexuality, and age. Rejecting a singular focus on women or men, it instead explores the dynamic relationships between genders and their roles in both dominant and subordinate positions. Divided into four sections—covering foundational issues, macrolevel structures and processes, microlevel interactions, and institutional contexts—the book aims to provide in-depth analyses for professional sociologists, graduate students, and interdisciplinary feminist scholars seeking an authoritative synthesis of current knowledge in gender sociology.

title: Social ontology
abstract: This article extends and develops a theory I began in my book, The Construction of Social Reality. Its aim is to explore social ontology in a way that will make it clear that social ontology is both created by human actions and attitudes but at the same time has an epistemically objective existence and is part of the natural world. The fundamental concepts necessary to explain its creation and continued existence are: the distinction between observer-relative and observer-independent phenomena, the distinction between the epistemic and the ontological senses of the objective–subjective distinction, the notions of collective intentionality, the assignment of function, and constitutive rules. The upshot of the discussion is that the basic notion in institutional ontology is that of a status function. Status functions are the glue that holds society together because they create deontic powers, powers that work by creating desire-independent reasons for action. Thus, social ontology locks into human rationality. I discuss some of the implications of this work for sociology and anthropology.

title: Social ontology
abstract: This article investigates the problem of social ontology by extending the argument from The Construction of Social Reality (1995), focusing on how social reality is constituted through collective intentionality, the assignment of function, and constitutive rules and procedures. After clarifying key distinctions between observer-independent and observer-relative phenomena, the paper analyzes the logical structure of society, emphasizing the foundational role of language in enabling the existence of social institutions such as money, property, and government. Further developments include an examination of status indicators and cases where status functions are attributed without a physical substrate. The taxonomy of institutional facts is discussed, as well as the interplay between conceptual analysis and empirical data. The article concludes with reflections on the nature and varieties of institutional facts, arguing that social reality is created by observer-independent mental phenomena giving rise to observer-relative facts through collective acceptance and recognition.

title: Social Relationships and Health Behavior Across Life Course.
abstract: Sociological theory and research point to the importance of social relationships in affecting health behavior. This work tends to focus on specific stages of the life course, with a division between research on childhood/adolescent and adult populations. Yet recent advances demonstrate that early life course experiences shape health outcomes well into adulthood. We synthesize disparate bodies of research on social ties and health behavior throughout the life course, with attention to explaining how various social ties influence health behaviors at different life stages and how these processes accumulate and reverberate throughout the life course.

title: Social Relationships and Health Behavior Across Life Course.
abstract: This paper synthesizes sociological research on the influence of social relationships on health behavior across the life course, integrating findings from childhood, adolescence, and adulthood. Drawing on a life course perspective, the authors argue that social ties—encompassing social integration, support, control, and stress—shape health behaviors in both positive and negative ways, with effects that accumulate and reverberate over time. The review highlights how the structure and content of relationships change across developmental stages, influencing health behaviors differently depending on life stage and context. Evidence demonstrates that early social experiences launch trajectories that impact health well into adulthood, while evolving networks in adolescence and adulthood continue to shape behaviors such as diet, exercise, substance use, and adherence to medical regimens. The authors propose a conceptual framework that unifies disparate literatures and identifies key psychosocial mechanisms linking social ties to health behavior. They conclude by emphasizing the need for future research to further unpack these processes and inform policy interventions aimed at improving population health through the social foundations of behavior.

title: The Cambridge handbook of expertise and expert performance
abstract: This 2006 handbook provides comprehensive information about expert performance. It describes the processes, knowledge, and methods by which people climb to the highest possible levels of human performance. It highlights the research techniques and approaches that investigators use to gain insights about such extraordinary performance.

title: The Cambridge handbook of expertise and expert performance
abstract: This paper examines the evolving role of expertise in contemporary society, particularly in the context of unprecedented access to information, open innovation, and data-driven technologies. Contrary to claims that expertise is obsolete or easily replaceable, the authors argue that expertise remains vital not only as a repository of knowledge but as a dynamic capacity to systematically explore and address the unknown. Drawing on historical analysis and advances in design theory, the study highlights how expertise operates at the intersection of known and unknown domains, enabling both preservation and creative innovation. The paper discusses the cognitive, organizational, and institutional logics underpinning expert performance in uncertain environments and underscores the importance of expertise in responding to global challenges such as climate change and pandemics. Ultimately, the authors advocate for a renewed understanding of expertise as a process that continually redefines boundaries between knowledge and ignorance, fostering sustainable and responsible innovation through non-destructive creation.

title: The Sociology of the European Union
abstract: We seek to shape an agenda for the growing interest in using sociological approaches to study the European Union (EU). In order to deepen and broaden the Europeanization agenda, the article points to how sociology can help reveal the ‘social bases’ of European integration (i.e. processes of European Union), as well as identify effects on European society that might reconnect EU studies with key comparative political economy debates about the European ‘varieties of capitalism’ and its models of economy and society. Unfortunately, however, ‘sociological’ approaches towards the EU have mostly been wrongly equated with the ‘constructivist turn’ in EU studies, and its characteristic preference for ‘soft’ qualitative discursive methods and meta-theory. We argue that, rather than turning to culture, identity or social theory for inspiration, an empirical sociological approach to the EU would reintroduce social structural questions of class, inequality, networks and mobility, as well as link up with existing approaches to public opinion, mobilization and claims-making in the political sociology of the EU. To conclude, the article identifies some exemplary studies along these lines.

title: The Sociology of the European Union
abstract: This article sets out an agenda for integrating sociological approaches into the study of the European Union (EU), arguing that mainstream EU studies have largely neglected the social foundations and consequences of European integration. The authors critique the tendency to equate sociological analysis with constructivist, discursive, or meta-theoretical methods, and instead advocate for an empirical sociology that foregrounds issues of class, inequality, networks, and mobility. Drawing on comparative historical sociology and political economy, the paper calls for a deeper examination of the structural processes underpinning Europeanization and highlights the need to reconnect EU studies with broader debates about varieties of capitalism and models of society. By reviewing exemplary empirical works, the article demonstrates how a sociological perspective can enrich understanding of both the drivers and effects of European integration, ultimately proposing a more comprehensive research agenda that situates EU politics within its wider societal context.
